For anyone checking IMDb to see if it's worth watching, here's what you need to know: no action, no appealing characters, no apparent budget, and absolutely dreadful acting. It screams "bad movie," not least because the entire film takes place in a single room.

Hard to categorize, *Mother Night* defies easy classification—perhaps it's an avant-garde spy thriller? This excellent Vonnegut novel was, arguably, one of his most adaptable works, and its filmic rendition remains remarkably faithful. The indie production approach likely served it better than a big studio budget, especially given that intelligent, nuanced novels like *Mother Night* rarely get greenlit in today's Hollywood. This film, however, benefits from tight direction and a strong cast. Nick Nolte, whose performances only seem to deepen with age, retains his compelling everyman quality, allowing him to embody diverse roles. Sheryl Lee shines, beautiful and talented as ever; one often feels her career deserved far greater recognition, despite an unconventional start as a deceased character in a cult phenomenon like *Twin Peaks*. Ultimately, this is a thoroughly enjoyable film, even for those unfamiliar with the source material.

Having read through numerous comments, it's evident that science fiction audiences are divided into two distinct groups.

One group comprises the well-read, highly literate, and intelligent viewers. They possess a deep understanding of the genre's history and, crucially, recognize its potential for profound storytelling when handled by a talented creator. They are keenly aware that for many years, science fiction was relegated to the fringes of literature, often dismissed by critics as mere tales of ray guns and aliens for young teenagers. These discerning fans know the literary giants—Asimov, Heinlein, Bradbury, and Ellison—who elevated the genre from that low status. Through their work, these authors crafted intelligent, thought-provoking narratives that pushed boundaries and redefined the human condition.

These informed fans approach Hollywood's genre offerings with a critical, discerning eye, not out of cynicism, but because they believe the narrative must be paramount. They are not swayed by flashy computer graphics or relentless action sequences.

This film was a profound eye-opener, a cinematic experience I've revisited multiple times since my first viewing at the memorable age of four, and again at twelve. The director's compelling message resonates deeply: it's a powerful call to spiritual awakening, urging us to embrace faith in our daily lives and avoid the egregious error of dismissing or disrespecting the divine. It's an exceptional film that speaks equally to believers and non-believers.

A film severely lacking in moral compass. The protagonist, a drifter, accepts a contract to kill a man for money, only to be double-crossed by the mob. He then inexplicably falls for the victim's widow, moving in with her under false pretenses. When she uncovers his villainy, he "accidentally" kills her. His subsequent vendetta against the mobsters, framed as a "Walking Tall"-esque act of heroism, rings hollow. His initial act of murder-for-hire permanently strips him of any audience sympathy, rendering his subsequent actions morally bankrupt and impossible to connect with. Similarly, the widow, despite being portrayed as a compassionate woman running a homeless mission, loses credibility by swiftly entering a relationship with the drifter after her husband's death. Her reaction upon discovering his guilt—locking him inside her ownpresumably escapable—home—is equally illogical and undermines her character.

Twenty years ago, Michael Hawthorne, then a five-year-old boy, witnessed his father commit a horrific axe murder of his mother on a desolate road, followed by his father's suicide. Now, Michael (Gordon Currie) invites his girlfriend Peg (Stacy Grant) and best friends Chris (Myc Agnew), Jennifer (Emmanuelle Vaugier), Lisa Ann (Kelly Benson), Ned (Brendon Beiser), Mitch Maldive (Phillip Rhys), and Trish (Rachel Hayward) to celebrate Halloween at his grandparents' farm in the countryside. He instructs them to wear costumes embodying their deepest fears. With the help of his Native American friend Crow (Byron Chief Moon), Michael plans an ancient ceremony, using a carved wooden dummy named Morty (Jon Fedele), to permanently eradicate their fears. Michael's own greatest fear is succumbing to the same serial killer tendencies as his father. However, the ritual goes awry, and Morty transforms into his father, who then begins to murder his friends.

"The Fear: Resurrection" is a largely disappointing and aimless slasher film. Despite an intriguing premise—the elimination of each character's profoundest inner fear before it manifests—the execution is marred by a messy, cliché-ridden screenplay. The acting ranges from overly theatrical, as exemplified by Ms. Betsy Palmer, to notably weak.

Rancid Aluminium stands out as a uniquely bewildering and depressing experience, even among the low points of my life. The red flags were unmistakable: a complete lack of a premiere, no celebrity endorsements, and a conspicuous absence of critical reviews. My sole motivation for enduring the film was the desperate hope of catching a nap.

The narrative was an incoherent mess, utterly devoid of explanation, and plagued by idiotic narration. My brief moment of elation when the protagonist appeared to be shot was quickly extinguished by the disappointing revelation that he had, in fact, survived. My sincerest wish is for all involved in this cinematic atrocity to face the gallows.

While largely unintentional, the film did offer moments of humor. One particularly memorable scene involved the protagonist inexplicably masturbating in a public restroom stall, bizarrely instructing the occupant of the adjacent stall to cover his ears.

Words fail to convey the depth of my anger. Therefore, I will conclude with this: Rancid Aluminium is a film exclusively for sadists, wastrels, and regressives—those who actively seek self-inflicted torture.

Five years have passed since I endured that film, yet its memory clings to me like a persistent shadow. I entered fully forewarned of its supposed awfulness, a fact for which I can only fault myself. But like many, I dismissed the torrent of negativity. As a devoted Sandler fan, I simply couldn't conceive of one of his films being truly that irredeemable. I chalked it up to the usual detractors. I have never been more mistaken.

What unfolds on screen is a comedy utterly devoid of humor, an astonishing feat in itself. One might expect that in 90 minutes, they would accidentally stumble upon a moment, however fleeting, of comedic value. But no. It is simply, profoundly bad. This isn't a "so bad it's good" situation; it's just bad. There is no ironic laughter to be found, only despair. You yearn for a single joke, a solitary chuckle, but none arrive.

Recall *The Ring*, where viewers meet their demise seven days after watching a cursed tape? If this movie were on that tape, the end would be instantaneous, self-inflicted.

American World War II films, while often entertaining and effective as morale-boosting propaganda, frequently lacked realism. Though many remain watchable today, this historical inaccuracy often kept them from achieving true cinematic greatness. A prime example is John Garfield's *Air Force*, depicting a single B-17 performing an implausibly decisive aerial assault. *Pride of the Marines*, however, stands out as a refreshing exception. Its portrayal of a true story is remarkably accurate, which initially surprised me given the improbable nature of its events. Further research confirmed its fidelity to the extraordinary real-life achievements of two Medal of Honor recipients, illustrating a rare instance where truth proved stranger than fiction.

Having first encountered the story through the book, I was drawn to this film adaptation. While not strictly biographical, it offers a gripping and unsettling dive into the depths of evil and madness, with Michel Serrault delivering a truly unforgettable portrayal of Dr. Petiot.

The film is rich with striking visuals: Petiot's vampiric nocturnal travels, his black cloak billowing, are almost emblematic. Hints of expressionism abound, particularly Petiot's distorted silhouette ascending from the cellar where his victims await cremation, evoking classic 'Nosferatu' imagery.

Yet, it was the auditory experience that truly captivated me. The soundtrack is saturated with foreboding sounds, from the ominous opening music and wordless wails, to the persistent background din of knives being sharpened within the complex where Petiot operates his practice. Eerie tunes from a street peddler's saw, along with animalistic screeches from an unseen goat and howling cats, further amplify the unsettling atmosphere.

This film utterly lacks artistic merit and deserves no accolades. In fact, it barely warrants an audience. The cinematography award it received is baffling; the camera work is disorienting, constantly feeling as though the edges of the frame are crudely cropped, denying the viewer a complete visual experience. The narrative itself is abysmal, though I confess I couldn't endure the entire runtime. A particularly egregious scene involved soldiers partying in their barracks, with one coerced into drinking — a moment, among others, that painfully evoked the low-brow quality of a Steven Seagal movie. My strong recommendation: avoid this cinematic travesty at all costs.

The film, it seems, was conceived in a vacuum of knowledge, utterly devoid of any understanding of Nietzsche's life and philosophy, psychoanalytic principles, or the rich history of Vienna. Its creation appears to have followed a perverse sort of recipe: select a renowned intellectual you've never actually read, portray him as utterly deranged, introduce outlandish physicians tasked with his 'cure,' sprinkle in a few moderately attractive women, cast an actor whose most prominent feature is an exaggerated mustache, ensure every character speaks with an intolerably thick accent, intersperse nonsensical dream sequences, gratuitously insert another famous historical figure (like Freud) with no genuine connection to the main subject, pepper the dialogue with a handful of terms plucked from the genius's actual writings, and finally, over-amplify every conceivable element, especially the soundtrack. The resultant cinematic experience is one to be avoided at all costs.

As the director's nephew, I've spent years hunting for this film, and I can unequivocally state it's one of the worst movies ever made. Even my uncle, the director himself, no longer possesses a copy (I checked). I'm eager to finally present him with one.

With an average IMDb rating of 1.9/10 from 206 votes, it's astonishing this film hasn't yet secured a spot in the "bottom 100," likely ranking somewhere in the mid-30s if it had more votes. It's almost a shame it doesn't even receive the ignominy of a bottom 100 title.

This holiday season, I'll be gifting copies to my family—sure to be either the best or worst present they receive.

Originally hesitant to watch "Lost," a chance encounter with the polar-bear episode in Season 1 captivated me, and the show has held my attention ever since. (Not the polar bear, mind you.) So, bear with me as I enthusiastic ramblings.

"Lost" masterfully expands on the simple premise of a passenger plane crashing on a desert island. It delves into the characters' lives with unflinching depth, exploring their motivations, identities, and origins. The island soon emerges as a pivotal force, connecting various aspects of their lives—whether they're escaping their pasts (like Sawyer and Kate) or finding spiritual awakenings (like Locke and Claire). "Lost" also zeroes in on the island itself, revealing its mysterious horrors and their strange interconnections.

While television actors aren't typically acclaimed for their nuanced performances, the cast of "Lost" largely delivers spectacular portrayals, projecting

My brother and I stumbled upon this film late one Saturday night, or perhaps early Sunday morning, after a few drinks. What unfolded was a masterclass in cinematic absurdity, a film so riddled with blunders it became a joy to dissect.

From the opening scenes, the "luxury" ocean liner, which clearly doubles as a utilitarian roll-on/roll-off ferry, sets the tone. Its interior, adorned with cast iron fixtures and doors haphazardly labeled "staff" with adhesive stickers—only to reappear serving entirely different purposes in subsequent shots—is an absolute delight. The continuity errors are not merely noticeable; they are glaring, practically leaping off the screen.

The climax further solidifies its legendary status. The protagonist leaps from a lifeboat as the ferry, now a distant speck, explodes. Yet, in the very next shot, his son and his new girlfriend—the ship's PR director, a kung-fu expert, and former police officer dismissed for her maverick ways (yes, really)—are seen on the very same ferry, now speeding away from the blast. Then, inexplicably, the father materializes, embracing them. How? Who cares! It's pure, unadulterated cinematic magic.

This film boasts not a single redeeming quality. The casino, laughably small, resembles a large bedroom with just one gaming table. And when the heroes are chased by villains, there's only one predictable hiding spot. You guessed it.

In a desolate Texas desert town, a string of gruesome murders has cast a pall of fear. This film, while attempting a fleeting foray into mystery and even racial tension—the latter feels particularly shoehorned—ultimately caters exclusively to slasher enthusiasts. They will find themselves well-served by the abundant gore and nudity, hallmarks of the genre.

Dana Kimmell, notorious for her role in *Friday the 13th Part 3*, stars as the petulant, amateur teen detective.

*1/2 out of ****

MPAA: Rated R for violence and gore, nudity, and some language.

Despite its R-rating, I doubt this film will entertain anyone beyond their teenage years. It lacks a compelling plot, character development, and humor. Its sole offering is an abundance of nudity, featuring attractive women.

This movie's connection to the "American Pie" franchise is baffling, as it's a poor hybrid of eroticism and comedy, failing at both. I'd only recommend it if you're seeking nudity but are hesitant to procure a dedicated erotic film.

I'm giving it a 1/10 for the two fleeting smiles it elicited, and an additional 2/10 for the appealing cast.

A familiar pattern of cultic influence emerges once more. This observation isn't a plot spoiler, as the film's true conclusion reveals itself only after investigating the origins of this protracted, pseudo-scientific infomercial: Ramtha's School of Enlightenment.

My inclination is always to disengage from any religious or philosophical movement that relies on a veil of deception, akin to the Wizard of Oz. I'm grateful to Ramtha that I only viewed a borrowed copy of this film, recommended by a "friend." To have expended valuable resources on this New-Age indoctrination would have been truly regrettable. I can only hope that proponents are sincere in their belief that they can "walk on water" enough to follow that conviction to its "logical" conclusion: either demonstrate the ability, accept the consequence of failure, or cease making the claim. As a film, its entertainment value barely registers, meriting a strong "1," particularly for introducing arguably the most unlikable character in cinematic history (the photographer's roommate, truly cringeworthy!). If you feel compelled to watch this film, I suggest borrowing it from one of the individuals who, having been influenced, recommended it to you.

This early Adam Sandler film offers a glimpse into his nascent comedic persona, mirroring his real-life struggles as a comic in 1989. The protagonist's persistent belief in his untapped comedic genius and his exasperation with the material he's given feel less like a character trait and more like Sandler's own frustrations spilling onto the screen. The movie pales in comparison to his later blockbusters, even the delightfully silly *Billy Madison*. It's clear that, much like his character, Sandler hadn't yet honed his comedic voice into a consistently successful and humorous form when this film was made.

Much of the film's intended humor stems from Sandler's character engaging in self-deprecating monologues, frequently lamenting his unacknowledged comedic talent or his perceived unattractiveness and inability to connect with women. The viewing experience is further complicated by the film's unconventional approach; it eschews traditional cinematic conventions. Sandler frequently breaks the fourth wall, directly addressing the camera and the audience, often commenting on the film's meager budget or its questionable content. The result is an undeniably awkward and at times embarrassing watch. Upon its conclusion, I found myself wishing to erase the experience from my memory, fearing that its wider discovery might tarnish Sandler's career. Give this one a wide berth.

This film utterly failed to deliver, leaving any viewer who enjoyed it with questionable taste in cinema. From its high-school-caliber direction and cinematography—making *The Blair Witch Project* (a film I despise) look visually superior—to a storyline that squandered its potential from the opening minutes, it was an insult to watch. While some suggest it's a child's imaginative journey, this offers no excuse for such a poorly executed script. The scene with the "Indian in the store" perfectly exemplifies this: did the child's glance at an idol conjure an entire backstory about a Wendigo spirit? And why did the store employee, after dismissing the presence of anyone else, simply pivot to a price negotiation, completely abandoning the bizarre encounter? It's baffling.

To those who found the telecast boring or believe Halle Berry and Denzel Washington didn't deserve their Oscars:

This was, in fact, one of the most significant Academy Awards shows. Firstly, it marked a historic moment: a Black actress won the Academy Award for Best Actress. For too long, talented Black actresses have been overlooked by the Academy. Personally, I had stopped watching the Academy Awards due to the consistent lack of diversity among winners and nominees, feeling it was merely a self-congratulatory event for a homogenous group. The Academy had numerous opportunities to recognize brilliant Black actresses in the past, such as Alfre Woodard, Whoopi Goldberg, Diana Ross, and Mary Jean Baptiste, but failed to do so.

Secondly, Halle Berry undeniably deserved her Oscar. While some may argue the Academy was pressured, it was high time that deserving actresses, particularly those from underrepresented groups, received recognition. Though Nicole Kidman’s performance in *Moulin Rouge!* was commendable, it was crucial for Black artists to be acknowledged in these awards. As for Mr. Washington, the Academy owed him substantial recognition after past oversights.

Fans of "Deep Cover" will find much to appreciate in this film, especially since many of Laurence Fishburne's poetic recitations in "Deep Cover" originated from the lyrical script of "Once In the Life," a screen adaptation of a play Fishburne himself penned. For those who admire Fishburne's work, this movie offers an immersive experience, showcasing his fully developed performance in a raw and captivating way. While it incorporates the expected elements of a gangster film—gun violence and illicit substance use—its true strength lies in a beautifully crafted script and a surprisingly moving story, even leaning towards the emotional depth often found in a "chick flick."

This is an extraordinary film—dark, thrilling, seductive, and exhilarating. It masterfully evokes the feeling of clandestine nights and secret clubhouses, using its confined sets to metaphorically convey the entrapment of the characters' lives. The film is impeccably constructed, rich with clever foreshadowing and intricate relationships. Every emotion is meticulously reflected in the set design and camera work, a testament to its exceptional quality.

May 1938. Hitler's visit to Italy sets the stage for a momentous meeting with Mussolini, stirring a whirlwind of emotions, tensions, and displays of self-affirmation. Against this backdrop, a deserted city, a lonely housewife, and a curious journalist converge, their disparate worlds colliding. The film offers sanctuary to a woman burdened by a melancholy life, a brief respite for a timeless victim. It is a tale of solitude and silence, exploring life's hidden corners and the desire to fight for one's existence. A pivotal character emerges in the form of a book, a gift on a spring afternoon. This cinematic poem masterfully portrays the nuances of everyday loneliness, advocating for an ineffable connection with reality and one's inner self. The imagery of Il Duce, Antonietta's endearing awkwardness, Gabriele's patient yet fragile intensity, and the director's skillful artistry in imbuing the script with grace through two phenomenal actors elevate this film to a sublime experience. It is a work of subtle delicacy, a powerful commentary on hypocrisy and arbitrary judgment, on the essence of life and the abhorrence of tyranny. Loren and Mastroianni deliver magnificent, intelligent performances, solidifying this film as a clear masterpiece.

Despite numerous negative reviews, I found myself pleasantly surprised by this horror film. It proved to be a fairly enjoyable experience, exceeding my expectations. While the acting, with the exception of the remarkable Alice Krige, left something to be desired, the dialogue occasionally offered amusing moments, such as the line, "Just consider yourself lunch." Overall, I'd rate it a 7/10, considering it an above-average adaptation of Stephen King's work.

There must be a compendium, somewhere, of the worst gay films ever made. The kind with interminable shots of actors staring pensively into the void, or bizarrely extended scenes of cats consuming spaghetti. This particular cinematic endeavor is a dizzying tale of two boys who fall in love, swim, get trapped in grottos, one burdened by a depressed mother, the other motherless. They converse, perambulate, swim, engage in sexual acts, get inebriated, and eventually separate. One protagonist endures an eight-day hospital stay, followed by an abundance of fast-forwards and rewinds. And, of course, there are those lingering, pensive shots of one character lost in thought or simply existing in stillness. Perhaps this is a deliberate, albeit misguided, filmmaking gimmick, or perhaps it's a desperate attempt to pad out a film so devoid of plot that it would otherwise clock in at a mere fourteen minutes. Make no mistake, this is approximately the thirtieth gay film I've...

If Akira Kurosawa erred in creating *Dodes'ka-den*, it was in the context of his partnership with the "four knights" (Kobayashi, Ichikawa, and Konoshita). They sought a blockbuster, but Kurosawa, arguably their leader, delivered an abstract, humanist art film. Set in a desolate slum, the film depicted characters grappling with profound tragedies. Had he pursued the project independently or with a different studio, the outcome might have differed. This misstep, compounded by other financial and creative challenges, contributed to his 1971 suicide attempt. Yet, Kurosawa remained true to his artistic vision, showcasing the resilience of the human spirit amidst adversity, a hallmark of his dramas. While its setting is unconventional, this is not a flaw.

The compelling nature of *Dodes'ka-den* deviates from Kurosawa's usual style, primarily due to its strong character-driven narrative rather than a plot-centric one.

This film was a treat for any Pokémon enthusiast. It unveils new legendary Pokémon, a staple of the movie series, and enriches the character dynamics. However, I suspect its appeal may not extend to those outside the fandom, particularly most adults. While some dialogue felt a bit trite, this is often an unavoidable consequence of English dubbing. The animation was largely stunning, despite a few less polished moments. The villain, though somewhat clichéd, represents just one type in the franchise's diverse rogue's gallery. To those who didn't enjoy it, I respect your opinion, but I'm confident that Pokémon fans will adore it.

In a misguided attempt at humor, the film "Bulletproof" envisions a scenario where a motley crew of caricatured foreign adversaries unite south of the border, only to be comically defeated by Gary Busey's character. This movie serves as a regrettable illustration of 1980s cultural detritus, squandering the talents of its supporting cast, including L.Q. Jones and Thalmus Rasulala.

This quintessential Lars von Trier film, my personal favorite, surpasses even "Breaking the Waves" and the more recent "Dancer in the Dark." Its visual artistry is simply captivating, featuring remarkably original framing and superb performances—truly a must-see.

The criticism that *Full House* is "cheesy" often feels exaggerated. Most viewers seek enjoyment and relaxation from a TV show, not critical analysis (unless they're professional critics or story analysts). For the majority, a show like *Full House* serves as a perfect escape after a demanding day. It consistently delivers humor, but its appeal extends beyond simple jokes.

While the Tanner family is undeniably an idealized, hypothetical portrayal – a family truly without flaw – it's crucial to remember this is television, not reality. There's no inherent problem in presenting such a benevolent, albeit fictional, family. The show's enduring popularity and long run are testament to its widespread enjoyment, regardless of subsequent commentary.

Furthermore, *Full House* offers more than just entertainment; it subtly conveys messages that resonate across all age groups, however simple they might appear. Jesse's...

Having endured countless viewings of this film over the past two Christmases, courtesy of my children, I am uniquely positioned to assess this adaptation of Dr. Seuss's timeless story. And frankly, it falls short.

Succeeding a classic like Chuck Jones' animated special is a formidable challenge, yet this rendition distinguishes itself through its oppressive heavy-handedness and excessive padding, resulting in a numbing experience. While I acknowledge the presence of a few clever gags, the overriding impression is that of a cynical cash-grab, ironically, while simultaneously decrying the commercialization of Christmas.

Jim Carrey's performance, while predictably over-the-top, fundamentally clashes with the established character of the Grinch. Boris Karloff's portrayal was one of measured cunning, a slow-burning malevolence; Carrey's chaotic energy lacks this crucial nuance, a glaring misstep among many. The talent of actors like Jeffrey Tambor and Christine Baranski is regrettably squandered. Universal, why? While I understand certain venerable actors, much like their countrymen, are amenable to a wide array of roles, this particular film should be consigned to the archives.

This film, touted as the most expensive Canadian production ever shot in British Columbia, is a colossal failure, condemned to obscurity. Directed by a British filmmaker, it offensively portrays Canadians as over-sexed drug addicts and dimwits, completely devoid of genuine Canadian spirit—a baffling use of public funds. Meanwhile, the British character is inexplicably presented as the norm. The supporting cast is a collection of sitcom stereotypes, reminiscent of a perpetually shouted "Norm!" Visually, the film oscillates between picturesque postcard shots and murky, indistinct indoor scenes. The actors' constant fidgeting raises questions: Are they as disengaged as the audience, or is this a deliberate directorial choice? This cinematic misstep is best avoided. Instead, seek out the works of Bruce McDonald, a truly original Canadian voice whose films will captivate rather than alienate their audience.

This film ranks among the most disappointing I've ever encountered. My premiere viewing at SXSW left me profoundly underwhelmed, particularly given the director's admitted lack of familiarity with John Lennon's life. Though presented as a drama, the constant, unsolicited laughter from the audience at its sheer cheesiness was telling—never a positive indicator. The only redeeming qualities were the performances of Dominic Monaghan and Jason Leonard as Livien's comedic roommates and bandmates, providing much-needed levity in an otherwise overly solemn production. The gratuitous inclusion of Beatles lyrics felt absurdly misplaced. While the movie's narrative faltered, its soundtrack was, without question, a standout element and likely its strongest asset. Unless you're a devoted fan of Dominic Monaghan, I would strongly advise against watching this movie.

"Fear of a Black Hat" is a masterclass in comedy, a film that had me in stitches from beginning to end. I wholeheartedly urge you to see this movie if you have the opportunity; it is, without a doubt, the funniest film I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing. You won't regret it!

Curious about why you should watch the captivating nature documentary "Earth"? Let me explain. While I won't ramble endlessly, I must emphasize why this film is essential viewing. "Earth" offers a global journey, tracing the migration paths of three animal families: a polar bear mother and her cubs, whose story subtly entwines with the father's solitary hunt for food; a mother whale and her calf on an epic search for sustenance; and an elephant matriarch leading her substantial offspring across Africa. Directors Alastair Fothergill and Mark Linfield expertly capture not only the compelling sagas of these three families but also the survival instincts of countless other species. The cinematographic team—Richard Brooks Burton, Mike Holding, Adam Ravetch, and Andrew Shillabeer—demonstrate incredible skill, capturing breathtaking natural landscapes and innate animal behaviors, including stunning slow-motion hunting sequences.

The film excels in its central romance, which is beautifully portrayed and serves as the core theme. However, the love story unfolds against a backdrop that is excessively lyrical, visually elaborate, and ultimately unrealistic. Furthermore, the protagonist's psychology is perplexing and difficult to grasp, a sentiment mirrored by the film's equally enigmatic conclusion. While the movie may pique your interest, approach it with tempered expectations.

If this film is any indication, it's no wonder even cowgirls get the blues. I had higher hopes for Uma Thurman, which was my sole motivation for enduring this cinematic ordeal. The movie was dreadful, with the soundtrack being its only saving grace. It's truly a pity that a zero rating isn't an option for these reviews, because this film unequivocally deserves it.

Clocking in at over two hours, this film adaptation of Pearl Buck's renowned novel ambitiously covers extensive narrative ground.

Despite occasional melodramatic turns, the movie delivers visually impactful scenes, most notably a stunning locust attack that closes the film. Given its age, the special effects are remarkably well-executed, a testament to the crew's skill.

Award-winning actors Paul Muni and Luise Rainer deliver powerful, commendable performances. However, the casting of Caucasian actors in Asian roles, particularly the unconvincing portrayal by Walter Connolly, compromises the film's credibility. A remake featuring an all-Asian cast would significantly enhance the story's authenticity and appeal.

Thomas Clay's film, much like its young protagonist, seems to have gone astray. It's a production that meanders, portraying a troubled youth's descent into depravity, culminating in scenes of gratuitous violence. The film's central thesis, that violent imagery corrupts, is ironically undermined by its own content. One wonders if the director grasps the very connection he attempts to illustrate, or if he is simply out of touch with the pervasive nature of online content.

Emily Watson's portrayal of Natalia is, without a doubt, the most affectionate and passionate lead character I've encountered on screen. She reigns supreme in this film, undeniably its queen—or perhaps, in a fascinating twist, its king? The intricate interplay of chess matches and the families' power struggles for control and victory is simply breathtaking. Much like the film's chess masters, the director skillfully plays multiple simultaneous games with our minds, each weaving into either major or minor patterns. The early 20th-century Italian lake district, with its period details, costumes, and imagery, is captured magnificently; not an inch of space is wasted.

The film is brimming with brilliant scenes, too numerous to recount. I highly recommend setting aside enough time to watch it twice, perhaps a week apart. It's simply impossible to grasp all the poetry within its 64-square, multi-dimensional framework in a single viewing.

While I haven't read Nabokov's book, the film brings to mind another romantically triumphant, poetry-as-game movie: Barry Levinson's *The Natural*. That film famously discarded the bleak ending of Bernard Malamud's fatalistic novel in favor of a romantic impressionism.

This cinematic endeavor is a vacuous experience, utterly devoid of substance. One can only assume Rachel Griffiths's participation was a financial imperative. The abysmal lighting suggests a shoestring budget, making the viewing experience even more lamentable. I'm now contemplating extreme measures should I ever encounter Pete Postlethwaite again. The absence of a discernible plot or coherent script is baffling. My deepest regret is the irretrievable time squandered on this cinematic refuse.

The film felt like a series of scares without a cohesive story. So many potential plot points were introduced and then abandoned. We learned nothing about the room's history, its malevolent nature, or the significance of the "hour" countdown. Hints, like the camera in the vent, were never followed up on.

The "digital" appearance of the ghosts and the way objects vanished with a static sound suggested a high-tech haunted house, but this intriguing concept was never explored. Furthermore, the film was riddled with inconsistencies: electronics supposedly failed in room 1408, yet the TV worked, and despite no cell signal, the wireless internet functioned perfectly.

Ultimately, the movie relied on predictable horror tropes—reflections, things just out of sight, changing paintings, bleeding walls, and the "it was all a dream" cliché—without offering anything new or meaningful. It was shock for shock's sake.

My girlfriend and I stumbled upon this movie while channel surfing, hoping for a heartwarming Christmas film. We were sorely disappointed.

The lead actor, playing the soldier, delivers a performance utterly devoid of emotion. His expression remains unchanged whether he's felling trees, witnessing the woman he loves being kissed by another, or being pleasantly surprised by her. His acting was so poor it became a source of unintentional comedy for us.

Then there's the "cute" blonde, whose primary skill appears to be counting dots and cheating on her boyfriend – quite the catch! Her life's ambition seems to be living with her parents and continuing her dot-counting endeavors.

In essence, the plot revolves around an emotionless man falling for a dot-counting, unfaithful woman. It's incredibly predictable and a complete waste of time. The only takeaway is some bewildered laughter at its sheer corniness. I particularly "enjoyed" the scene where her dad declares his exclusive diet of French fries.

I might be in a small club of people who genuinely appreciate this film. Having seen it upon its release, I concur with the previous reviewer that "Up The Academy" was remarkably ahead of its time. The humor is quintessential MAD magazine, which makes me puzzled why the magazine seems to distance itself from it. Moreover, it was one of the rare early 80s films to boast an exceptional accompanying soundtrack, featuring the burgeoning punk and new wave bands from L.A. at the time. I still listen to that soundtrack constantly. While acknowledging that far worse films exist, I find "Up The Academy" funnier than "Porky's." It delivers consistent laughs, with jokes primarily targeting stereotypes or sexual escapades. Of course, no one ever claimed this was "The Maltese Falcon."

While not a John Cleese completist (though I found "Fawlty Towers" brilliant), I am a fan. Spotting this neglected gem on a Blockbuster shelf, I decided to give it a watch. What unfolded was a delightful surprise: one of the funniest 50-minute viewing experiences I've ever had. The writing embodies classic English "goon show" humor, so much so that it could easily pass as an audio sketch on a "Firesign Theater" album. Yet, the impeccable execution and timing elevate "Strange Case" into a jaw-dropping performance capable of forging lifelong British comedy enthusiasts.

The British excel at blending broad satirical lampoons with keenly observed character "tics" and precise timing, and both are masterfully employed here. Cleese's "Holmes" evokes shades of Arkin's and Seller's "Inspector Clouseau," yet his remarkable talent for physical comedy allows him to carve out a unique and memorable portrayal. However, the true revelation is Arthur Lowe as "Watson." He portrays the character as a genial yet invincibly obtuse imbecile, delivering each line with such superb timing and nuance that he becomes the undeniable highlight.

I remember the early days of Pay Per View, when renting a movie meant actually calling a number. As kids, we'd always wanted to rent Playboy, but that required a phone call to a live person. Summoning the courage, we'd ultimately be met with four hours of soft-core, poorly filmed garbage. 

This particular movie was also a Pay Per View offering, and I recall nearly every scene from its advertisement. In recent years, I've been on a quest to acquire all the great films from my childhood, and this was high on the list. It's the kind of movie that, once it's on, is hard to turn off. 

It boasts an all-star cast attempting the perfect bank heist, but, of course, nothing goes according to plan. While there are many good spoof bank capers, this one certainly earns its place among them. It delivers enough action and laughs to keep you engaged. Check it out if you dare!

This film does a disservice to the Australian film industry. Its lack of discernible values offers little beyond a fleeting distraction for the idle. To truly showcase the immense talent within our filmmaking community, we need projects with greater substance and artistic merit than this显然tacky production.

Though I hadn't considered myself an "Uwe Boll Hater," having seen none of his previous films, his movie "Seed"—named after its serial killer—has brought me close to joining that club. This film is utterly senseless, its plot a complete joke. Despite Boll's clear attempt to shock, 90% of the movie is simply boring.

Here's a summary:

1.  A hooded killer watches real-life footage of animals being tortured on TV, ostensibly from pelt farms. The film's opening tries to justify this with a ridiculous "statement about humanity" and a PETA address. Given that the movie delivers no coherent message and devolves into exploitative torture porn, this immediately sets a negative tone.

2.  A death by electrocution occurs, with an on-screen pretext that crudely telegraphs later plot points.

3.  Cops watch videos of starving animals, babies, and women.

John Carpenter's *Halloween* stands as a horror masterpiece, recounting the chilling tale of Michael Myers, an escaped mental patient who returns to his hometown on Halloween night to stalk and murder a group of unsuspecting babysitters.

This film remains, unequivocally, the pinnacle of the *Halloween* franchise. Carpenter demonstrates remarkable restraint, meticulously pacing the narrative and developing genuinely likable characters—a rarity in the horror genre.

Even more striking is the near absence of blood and gore, yet the film retains its unmatched ability to terrify, solidifying its place as the scariest *Halloween* installment to date.

*Halloween* notably marked Jamie Lee Curtis's film debut and a pivotal moment in the illustrious career of the late Donald Pleasence. It is, without question, a true classic.

Last night, while watching this film, I was struck by a profound sense of its lasting power. I have a strong feeling it's a film I'll return to repeatedly over the years.

It possesses all the hallmarks of a timeless story. Despite a few cultural references that may be lost on a Western audience, its core message resonates universally.

Richard C. Sarafian disowned this cinematic disaster, which first assaulted Japanese audiences before limping to direct-to-video release in the States. There, it languished in obscurity until the Turner networks, desperate for programming beyond infomercials, unearthed it from the depths of their archives to fill the desolate 3-6 AM slots. While the "Alan Smithee" pseudonym typically signifies a director's disavowal due to studio interference, Sarafian cannot entirely deflect blame. The cast, seemingly fresh from "Overacting 101," delivers a parade of cringeworthy dialogue. The plot is a tangled mess, and the special effects are utterly underwhelming. What isn't laughably bad is simply tedious. One wonders what compelled talents like Palance, Matheson, Boyle, or Heston to appear in such a dud—the source material, be it script or book, must have held some promise. Yet, the translation from page to screen went catastrophically awry. In short: avoid. It doesn't even possess the redeeming quality of being "so-bad-it's-good."

Altman's "H.E.A.L.T.H." masterfully reinterprets the classical four humors, transforming them into hilariously entertaining characterizations. Lauren Bacall embodies Phlegm as the guarded Esther Brill, whose life revolves around maintaining appearances and shielding her secrets. Paul Dooley's Choleric Dr. Gil Gainey frenetically flails, a chaotic seal barking his bizarre aquatic theories. Glenda Jackson's Isabella Garnell personifies Melancholy, channeling a Shakespearean Hamlet with her troubled, self-righteous pronouncements. Henry Gibson's Bobby Hammer delivers Bile with memorable lines. Amidst this colorful cast, James Garner's Harry Wolff and Carol Burnett's Gloria Burbank serve as relatively grounded figures, striving for normalcy amidst the extreme personalities gathered for H.E.A.L.T.H. — a farcical "world trade organization" for anything but genuine well-being.

During a visit to France around March 5th, I had the opportunity to attend the Cinélatino Rencontres de Toulouse, a film festival I'd long known about but never experienced. I decided to go, and it was there that I discovered "Cero y van 4."

The film is stunning. While the French subtitles may have slightly diluted its impact compared to how it might resonate with Mexican audiences, its shocking nature nonetheless came through.

"Cero y van 4" offers a biting satire of urban violence, kidnapping, and street crime in Mexico, painting a raw portrait of a bustling metropolis. It shares thematic echoes with "Secuestro Express," which also satirizes kidnapping, though with a more serious tone, featuring a remarkable Mia Maestro. Both films seem to explore a form of redemption narrative, questioning the limits of human endurance. While not a satire, "Man on Fire" also delivers a powerfully stark depiction of Mexico's streets. In its ability to deeply shock and affect viewers, "Cero y van 4" evokes comparisons to "The Brave One." Much like "The Usual Suspects," the film is punctuated by surprising plot twists.

This film presents deeply troubling content. Its portrayal of women is highly problematic, particularly scenes where female characters appear to be amused or flattered by their own abduction and sexual assault, framing rape as something enjoyable. This aspect alone makes it one of the most misogynistic films I've encountered.

Furthermore, the movie's depiction of Indigenous people is appallingly outdated, using white actors in "brownface" to play Native American roles, a practice that should have been long abandoned by 1968. The complete absence of actual Indigenous actors further highlights this issue.

Beyond these disturbing social commentaries, the film suffers from significant creative flaws. It features overt and poorly disguised homages to "The Hustler," boasts terrible acting, employs overly didactic musical cues that leave no room for viewer interpretation, and presents a confused narrative where it's unclear who the audience is meant to support.

It's perhaps unsurprising that Quentin Tarantino reportedly admires this film, despite his own cinematic work often featuring strong female characters. This preference, combined with anecdotal claims regarding his personal views, raises questions about his stance on misogyny. My decision to watch this movie is one I now regret.

**SPOILERS**

Jean-Paul Sartre's famous declaration, "Hell is other people," finds vivid illustration in *The Odd Couple*. Jack Lemmon and Walter Matthau, as Felix Ungar and Oscar Madison, portray two friends whose decision to cohabitate devolves into escalating frustration and uproarious comedy. The film culminates in Felix's departure, leaving behind a noticeably more refined Oscar.

Lemmon delivers a superb performance as the neurotic, fastidiously clean, and newly single Felix. Matthau, in a brilliant counterpoint, is equally captivating as Oscar, the slovenly sportswriter whose primary concern is winning poker games to support his children.

The brilliance of Lemmon and Matthau in their roles is twofold: it's a testament to Neil Simon's exquisite script and their undeniable chemistry as a duo. These two late, great actors, portraying friends with vastly different lifestyles but shared experiences with ex-wives and children, forged a partnership that is virtually inimitable. Their synergy was so profound that audiences clamored for more.

There's no flirting in this film, just immediate, unembellished action. The initial 15 minutes subject viewers to a grueling display of violence and sexual perversion. While I appreciate such elements in context, their presentation here, devoid of any meaningful framework, is simply repellent.

Having endured the opening's relentless torture and mayhem, the film abruptly shifts gears with the introduction of Donna. It transforms into a different entity entirely—not an improved one, but a dispassionate road movie. Attempts at humor fall flat, largely due to uninspired comedic cameos from actors like Judy Tenuta and Mink Stole, as well as several sex workers and drag queens, all of whom are underserved by the material.

The cinematography is deliberately disorienting, making this film unsuitable for anyone prone to motion sickness or, frankly, any form of discomfort. Indeed, it's difficult to ascertain the target audience for this film, beyond perhaps gay and bisexual S&M enthusiasts who favor poorly scripted, poorly filmed independent cinema that reflects their interests.

Sean Ellis's latest work was an incredible letdown.

Imagine gathering your friends, all buzzing with anticipation for Ellis's new film. You've got a vague sense of the plot, no spoilers, and sky-high expectations. It's late, the perfect atmosphere for this kind of movie.

Fifteen minutes in, you're telling yourself it has to pick up. At twenty-five, you wonder if you should just call it a night and save it for when you can truly appreciate its supposed subtle genius. Past the half-hour mark, you realize half your hyped-up audience is asleep, and you throw in the towel.

A few days later, having exhausted all other viewing options, you return to it, this time in the middle of the day, hoping a fresh mood will keep you engaged. Ten minutes later, you're fast-forwarding through unbelievably and needlessly long transitions and static shots. With any other filmmaker, you'd have given up, but there's *Cashback* and its legacy. Yet, even that legacy can only carry a film so far.

This film stands as a contender for the worst I've ever witnessed, critical acclaim notwithstanding. The fundamental issue, I believe, lies with Kundera's source material. It's not inherently unfilmable, but rather, like the vast majority of his oeuvre, it suffers from pretentiousness and excessive self-indulgence. Kundera appears deeply enamored with himself, leading to characters who are introspective to a fault and novels that, taken as a whole, strike me as misogynistic. Despite having engaged with numerous works across his bibliography—including his truly dreadful Socialist Realist poetry—I remain baffled by his enduring reputation. The very characteristics that make his novels such infuriating reads, particularly the pervasive self-absorption, were amplified to an unbearable degree on screen. Perhaps I simply missed something, though I doubt it. Furthermore, I find it astonishing that this production merits a place in the Criterion Collection; its cinematic significance frankly escapes me.

Reunion shows come in various forms, often with mixed results. One type brings back original cast members to reprise roles after decades. While some, like "Return to Mayberry," manage to be watchable despite flaws, others, such as the execrable "Return to Green Acres" or the silly-even-for-"Gilligan's-Island" "Rescue from Gilligan's Island," largely disappoint.

These revivals frequently suffer from weak scripts, often injecting a self-aware silliness that proves fatal to comedic timing. New characters are often shoehorned in haphazardly, disrupting established dynamics. Overall, these attempts to resurrect past glories rarely succeed.

A different kind of "reunion" show features the cast reminiscing and sharing anecdotes, interspersed with clips from the original series. Beyond this, there are also movie adaptations of shows, which are rarely successful, and biographical films about the show's history (like "The Brady Bunch" example).

I gave *Timecop* a perfect 10, but this sequel barely scrapes a 1.

The plot is incredibly dull and bears only a superficial resemblance to the original. Many elements from the first film were discarded, replaced by nonsensical new ideas. Despite being set in 2060 (if memory serves), time travel inexplicably becomes more perilous.

The action sequences are largely disappointing. Only the initial one truly impresses; the rest are few, far between, and remarkably brief. At one baffling point, the protagonist time-travels at least twice within mere minutes.

In summary, spare yourself the waste of time; this movie is utterly worthless.

This film felt like one I was *supposed* to enjoy, yet it left me cold. Its relentless pursuit of "artistry" came across as forced and ultimately vacuous – all style, no substance. While individual scenes boasted undeniable beauty and were pleasant in isolation, their cumulative effect was an arduous endurance test. The glowing reviews on the video box, coupled with my fondness for Shakespeare, prompted this rental, but I was sorely disappointed. I found it rather pretentious and, at times, dull.

Following the rape of his teenage girlfriend by Zebbedy Colt, also known as The Night-Walker, Harry Reems spirals into despair, seeking solace in encounters with lesbians. Concurrently, Colt, a figure often seen with a cane and dressed like a magician, continues his spree of sexual assaults. Eventually, Reems resolves to hunt Colt down and put an end to his violent acts.

Despite its controversial subject matter and a few marginally graphic moments, the film largely resembles typical 1970s pornography, suffering from clumsy execution. The rape and abuse scenes are surprisingly subdued, and its attempt to capitalize on the success of "Death Wish" is almost comical. R. Bolla, known for "Cannibal Holocaust," appears as a police officer. While Colt's character often leans into exaggeration, his outbursts are infrequent and ultimately too contained, leaving the impression that this "roughie" could have been considerably more intense.

This film was an endurance test, leaving me questioning how I made it to the end without resorting to the fast-forward button. Perhaps I missed the point, or perhaps I simply don't appreciate its supposed mystical atmosphere; personally, I found it as mystical as a trip to McDonald's.

The characters were uniformly terrible, possessing less development than those in a Tom & Jerry cartoon. I'm left wondering why I subject myself to such cinematic tripe. It's enough to make one consider joining a monastery or the Foreign Legion! Truly, an absolutely dreadful film in nearly every regard.

This exceptional film is a perennial favorite, one I've enjoyed on multiple occasions. Michael Caine delivers an outstanding performance, as is typical of his work. While Caine has developed a reputation for taking on a wide variety of roles regardless of a film's perceived quality, his portrayal of Sidney here is excellent.

From the very beginning, the writing is masterful. It's surprising to discover such sharp wit from Ira Levin, known for unsettling works like *The Boys from Brazil* and *Rosemary's Baby*. With a cast featuring Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, Dyan Cannon, and Henry Jones, and directed by Sidney Lumet, it's hard to imagine this film going astray.

I hesitate to reveal more, as spoiling any aspect of this movie would be a disservice. Simply watch it and cherish it.

This "horror" film is a rare misfire, managing to be both boring and unintentionally comical. Despite a promising beginning with an intriguing premise, it quickly devolves into a generic slasher, punctuated by gratuitous supernatural and sexual elements. Even the talented Alice Krige is squandered in a role undermined by ludicrous plot twists. Unless you have absolutely no other options, skip this one. Rating: 3/10.

During Joe Bob Briggs' tenure hosting Monstervision on TNT, I endured this film. Despite his best efforts, he couldn't salvage it. My only motivation for seeing it through was to provide my video production students with a prime example of what to avoid at all costs – a task that tested every fiber of my being. The experience was akin to witnessing your great-grandmother flirt with a teenage boy: utterly excruciating.

Frankly, setting the film strip ablaze would be a more engaging spectacle. I'm not exaggerating.

Should you encounter this movie in a bargain bin, I implore you: retreat as if from a venomous snake.

I typically avoid Farrelly Brothers films, and to my knowledge, I've never seen one. The same generally goes for Jimmy Fallon's movies, though I'm still atoning for my viewing of *Taxi*. My sole motivation for watching this particular movie was Drew Barrymore. There's something about her that just makes me smile; she's utterly captivating. I even sat through *50 First Dates* for her – that's how influential she is! This wasn't a groundbreaking baseball movie, nor was it intended to be. It was, at its heart, a love story: a tale of someone clinging to their one constant until finding a reason to let go. Despite a predictable conclusion, the journey there was thoroughly enjoyable and made it worthwhile.

Thirteen years after its release, I finally watched this cinematic gem, and its themes of brotherhood and fatherhood are timeless. The dynamic between the wilder younger brother and the more conventional older sibling is instantly relatable. While Craig Sheffer's portrayal of the elder brother felt somewhat restrained, Brad Pitt delivers a captivating performance, and Tom Skerritt perfectly embodies the father figure. The Montana fly-fishing scenes are visually stunning, revealing the unexpected allure of the sport. The film admirably preserves the essence of the novel, with only minor adjustments for the screen, a rare feat in book-to-movie adaptations. For those seeking a powerful yet understated emotional experience, this film is an ideal choice.

This Cheech & Chong film boasts the funniest jokes of the series. As my introduction to their work, I found it to be excellent, a recommendation from my father – truly a great role model! My grandmother even purchased it for me, fully aware of its content. What a family indeed! This movie is quite good and an ideal rental for those seeking a classic. However, be forewarned: it's not side-splittingly hilarious like *There's Something About Mary*. While it has its moments, it doesn't reach that level of constant laughter. Nevertheless, I encourage you to check it out; I'm sure you'll find it amusing, unless you happen to be an anti-drug activist.

This film was a complete misfire, leaving me questioning the choices of everyone involved. The director should be mortified by this output. It's baffling why anyone would greenlight such a creatively bankrupt project. The ending, particularly the character's demise, was unintentionally comical. I frequently had to avert my eyes or change the channel due to the sheer ineptitude of the performances. The actor portraying Heath was particularly abysmal, and I sincerely hope his career prospects are severely limited after this. Furthermore, I believe the director should be held accountable for this cinematic atrocity, perhaps even facing professional repercussions. My rating: 0.02 out of 10.

The film unfortunately falls flat, punctuated by gratuitous, ineffective nudity seemingly intended to jolt the audience. While Lena Olin delivers a masterful performance, Daniel Day-Lewis's dialogue is largely unintelligible. The director, Kaufman, struggles with the material, creating a disjointed narrative that awkwardly oscillates between domestic drama and political turmoil. Character motivations are inconsistent and unexplained, further contributing to the film's overall incoherence.

Approaching "Still Crazy," my expectations were low, anticipating merely another rock-and-roll film serving as boomer nostalgia. While it certainly offers that, it also delivers much more. Director Brian Gibson, known for his successful Tina Turner biopic, brings his distinctive style, making this, his final film, a fitting capstone.

The cast shines, with Bill Nighy perfectly embodying the band's frontman. Bruce Robinson, more recently known as a director, delivers a superb performance as the washed-up guitarist, a remarkable feat given his absence from the screen since the late 1970s. For those seeking a poignant and humorous film complemented by excellent music, "Still Crazy" is a must-see.

7.4/10

I received the novelization of "Kazaam" for my eighth birthday, and while it's often said the book is better than the movie, this was a notable exception. At least the film has the advantage of a relatively quick runtime.

The acting is abysmal, though this was hardly unexpected from a movie starring Shaquille O'Neal as a magical rapping genie who emerges from an ancient boombox (a confinement, I imagine, for very good reason). The child actor playing Max is particularly grating, portraying a whiny and unconvincing character. He's bullied by neighborhood kids, which, frankly, given his portrayal, is understandable.

The plot is uninspired and riddled with clichés: a neglected boy whose workaholic father is always absent finds a new friend who improves his life and ultimately helps him reconnect with his dad.

Even at the tender age of eight, I recognized the sheer absurdity of the concept. It's truly astonishing that anyone involved in this cinematic misstep managed to have a career afterward; it's an utter embarrassment that should never have seen the light of day. I could continue to enumerate this film's numerous failings, but...

A truly dreadful film! It beggars belief that it received a Golden Globe nomination, suggesting it must have vied against an exceptionally weak field. This movie takes the compelling story of the Renaissance's first renowned female painter and utterly mangles it. My grievance isn't with the creative liberties taken with historical facts; a compelling narrative could easily justify such deviations. However, the result is simply bizarre. By all accounts, the actual life story of this artist promised a far more engaging cinematic experience, leaving me baffled as to why they opted for such a remarkably insipid script. Perhaps the historical account lacked sufficient gratuitous nudity for their vision. The film concludes with a rushed, bullet-point summary of the artist's life – a brevity I desperately wish they had applied to the preceding two hours.

This film is practically a rehash, and a poorly executed one at that. The timeline is a mess, whether through laziness or indifference, making the entire experience a failure. It barely qualifies as a movie. I unfortunately encountered it as a bonus feature on the *The Boogeyman* disc, and it was so dreadful I felt my brain cells dying. Avoid this at all costs. Seriously, it should carry a warning: "May cause significant IQ drop upon viewing." My rating? A definitive 0/10.

In my opinion, this is a rather bizarre, yet humorous film. It leans more towards fun than fright, especially if you appreciate horror. While it brought to mind "Children of the Corn," it ultimately stands apart as a more enjoyable viewing experience.

Alright, alright, settle down, I was just kidding.

"Bustin' Out" is actually a more fitting and accurate title anyway.

This film delivers a satirical take on racism and crime dramas, courtesy of our X-rated animator friend, Ralph Bakshi, and it's one of his stronger efforts.

Regarding the crime aspect, it portrays a certain truth: organizations establish their power, defend it, and then boredom or stronger rivals potentially lead to their downfall. Watch it to see how it unfolds.

As for racism, I'm not so sure. With Scatman Crothers (RIP) and the "love walrus" (also RIP), both Black, serving as main perspectives, I largely interpreted it as an assault on racism. Richard Pryor's enjoyment of the film further supports this. And the inclusion of a younger Philip Michael Thomas (pre-"Miami Vice") was a pleasant surprise.

It's an animated "Blaxploitation" film, which is a good thing here—well-executed and impactful. It will undoubtedly make some viewers uncomfortable (like the lynching scene), but unfortunately, that's rooted in reality.

However, Ralph Bakshi truly should have reconsidered that initial title.

Last night, I finally watched "Starlight," and all I can say is... wow. Where to even begin? The comically amateurish special effects—seriously, Willie's eye lasers?—the dreadful acting, the leaden dialogue, the jarringly out-of-place stock footage, or the pervasive, self-important earnestness that permeates the entire film? It’s a truly singular experience, and for that, we should all be grateful. I hereby crown Jonathon Kay the rightful successor to Ed Wood.

I ignored the reviews and saw it anyway, only to find the critics were spot on. What a monumental waste of money, especially given its budget. Thankfully, *Kill Bill* was my next viewing. For truly terrifying cinema, look no further than *Crossroads*. Honestly, I'd rather watch *Girl in Gold Boots* again than sit through that drivel.

I wholeheartedly concur with jamrom4's assessment. This film was, without a doubt, the most abysmal cinematic experience of my life. Despite warnings, I foolishly subjected myself to it. About ten minutes into the agonizing ordeal, I mentally checked out, yet I endured to the bitter end, a decision I now profoundly regret. It was a repulsive, plotless mess that culminated in a preachy, undeserved conclusion. No film this execrable deserves to exist. I implore you, spare yourselves the terror of "Fatty Drives the Bus." I only wish I had heeded the same advice. Save yourselves from this cinematic abomination. I suspect its high ratings originate from those involved in its creation, individuals who, frankly, deserve to be erased from existence.

This film holds a special place in my heart, a true masterpiece I've revisited countless times, each viewing as profoundly moving as the last. My family has learned to brace themselves for the emotional impact it has on me, a testament to its powerful narrative. What elevates this movie beyond mere entertainment is its authenticity: it's a true story, penned by Antwone Fisher himself. The performances are exceptional, with each actor perfectly cast. Denzel Washington, a personal favorite, delivers what I consider his finest work in this film.

The story resonates with me deeply, particularly because of a young boy I once cared for, who, like Antwone, was born in jail. He was an incredibly precious child, and I had the privilege of witnessing his journey to adoption by a wonderful family who championed for him for nearly two years. I first saw this movie during a time of uncertainty for him, when his future was still hanging in the balance. Knowing he is now safe and loved brings me immense joy, a joy mirrored in Antwone's own happy ending as he found his family.

I am eager to learn more about Antwone's life since reuniting with his family. The film truly is extraordinary, and I cannot recommend it highly enough.

My prior indifference to Farrah Fawcett evaporated with her stunning performance in this film. Her portrayal was so raw, I can scarcely imagine the emotional toll of repeated takes. The movie itself was a grueling watch; its grim subject matter, depicting seemingly endless abuse, instilled a profound sense of helplessness. The narrative lost some of its intensity when her friends reappeared, and I found the ending unconvincing. While the director clearly favored high-angle shots and mirror reflections, I felt the pacing in the latter half needed more attention. Though undoubtedly a powerful play, the film, despite its merits, ultimately didn't quite resonate with me.

This film is an utter waste of time and money. Its creation is frankly baffling. The acting is abysmal, indicative of a severe lack of skill. The plot is flimsy, and the ending is utterly unsatisfying. The only redeeming qualities, if one can call them that, are the cinematography and perhaps the minimally acceptable sound design. The one silver lining is that if such a project can be made and even find financial success, it offers a glimmer of hope to screenwriters with genuine ideas and actors with actual talent.

**Warning: Spoilers Ahead**

This film was a complete letdown. It's yet another entry in the tired "Catholic/supernatural suspense thriller" genre, retreading familiar ground without an ounce of originality. We're subjected to the usual tropes: the conflicted priest, forbidden sexuality within the clergy, the entanglement of politics and faith, rampant church hypocrisy, and shadowy conspiracies. Add to that a predictable "new age of evil" prophecy and a series of uninspired good-versus-evil magical showdowns, and you have "The Order."

The plot, weak as it is, hinges on two concepts: Absolution (specifically, the Anointing of the Sick, or "last rites") and Excommunication. The twist, which I won't fully reveal, involves a "Sin Eater"—a device to bypass the conflict between these two states. This flimsy premise, combined with the aforementioned clichéd elements, makes for a truly dull viewing experience.

One scene particularly offensive was the intercutting of a priest's sex scene with images of the Virgin Mary, a blatant insult to Catholic sensibilities. The film limps to a close with Heath Ledger's character delivering a cringeworthy, self-important monologue about being a redeemer and damner of sins, devoid of love, as he dramatically walks into the darkness.

This is the film that launched the "Next Action Star" competition, and I'm genuinely relieved I wasn't involved, let alone won.

It's astonishing how quickly one can form an opinion about a movie – literally within the first ten seconds. The opening titles alone were enough! I endured part of this "teleplay" (as it was clearly made for TV) during my military service. The typical audience I was with, a mixed bag of average guys, usually settled for shows like *Las Vegas* just for the eye candy. So, the bar for entertainment was incredibly low; *The Girl Next Door* was practically high art by comparison (and not for its script, mind you). Yet, this movie's utter void of originality, compelling acting, coherent scripting, and virtually every other quality that makes a film watchable, made it effortless to switch the channel to *Las Vegas* (or was it *CSI*? I forget). Crucially, not a single person in the room objected, which is truly remarkable! For the love of all that is good, do not buy this movie. If it's on TV...

It seems most people rating this film a perfect 10 are devout Christians; as someone who isn't, I found it less compelling. While it might appeal to those seeking a Christian-themed movie, I can't recommend it for a general audience.

The characters and their illogical actions were a source of frustration. The film's central message—that teaching morality is incomplete without attributing it to Jesus—was particularly irksome. In one scene, the protagonist tells a boy that stealing is wrong, then asserts that this teaching originated with Jesus. This struck me as offensive. Are we to believe that the concept of "thou shalt not steal" was exclusive to Jesus, implying he authored the Ten Commandments or that stealing was acceptable before his time? Having rented this from Netflix, I regret not paying closer attention to the comments beforehand.

This film cleverly blends entertainment with incisive political commentary. Released as the Soviet Union teetered on the brink, it lampoons the Soviet mindset by setting its story in the USSR's nascent years, subtly questioning the very foundations of the revolution, both culturally and practically. While the rigid strictures of Soviet society had loosened by the late 1980s and early 1990s, the underlying ideology and mentality persisted, ripe for deconstruction. Fortunately, this profound philosophical critique is delivered within a hilarious and engaging narrative.

This Tom Hanks film captivated me! As a devoted fan, I'm consistently impressed by his versatility, from the profound drama of *Cast Away*, *The Green Mile*, *Saving Private Ryan*, *Forrest Gump*, *Apollo 13*, and *Philadelphia*, to the comedic brilliance of *A League of Their Own*, *Turner and Hooch*, *Catch Me If You Can*, *The Lady Killers*, *Big*, and *Toy Story*.

However, Hanks isn't the sole standout in this movie. Tyler Hoechlin, a promising up-and-coming talent, delivers a remarkable performance as Hanks' son. He's definitely an actor to watch. And, as expected, Paul Newman is brilliant, a true legend.

Even the supporting cast shines. The talented Jennifer Jason Leigh, whose unforgettable performances in *Bastard Out of Carolina* and *Single White Female* come to mind, gracefully portrays Hanks' wife, contributing significantly to the film's overall excellence.

This movie is pure enjoyment, especially for those of us who were young Ramones fans when it was released. I've rewatched it countless times, alone and with friends, and it remains as fresh and hilarious as ever. It brilliantly captures the timeless fanaticism for a band and the universal high school boredom with academic drudgery.

The film is packed with brilliant lines and scenes. From the running gag about our "permanent record" (a threat that, I can assure you, doesn't follow you far past graduation) to the iconic "static" exchange ("I'm getting some static." "Not as much as you're going to get," as Principal Togar approaches). We see the comically decrepit school board member attended by nurses, the Nazi-esque hall monitors' penchant for "body searches," and Principal Togar's dramatic "final solution" as he burns the Ramones' records (for younger readers, these were the vinyl predecessors to CDs). And, of course, there's Joey Ramone's deadpan observation, "Things sure have changed since we got kicked out of high school," immediately followed by Togar's exasperated query...

This show was a tremendous hit with me. Channel 4 aired what appears to be the sole season in the UK. Its characterization was spot-on, reminiscent of The Simpsons in its portrayal of a diverse small-town population.

The absence of a laugh track, a rarity for American TV comedies at the time save for *The Larry Sanders Show*, significantly enhanced the viewing experience. It lent an air of authenticity to the eccentric police characters, making their quirks feel genuine rather than performed.

Ultimately, this quirky gem thoroughly entertained me. I suspect it may have narrowly missed its target audience, and I believe it could have achieved cult status in the UK had it been broadcast at a more accessible time.

As always, I'm left wondering: where can I find this show to watch it again? Any leads would be greatly appreciated.

This film, surprisingly, faced widespread moral condemnation, denounced from pulpits more often than any other film before the restrictive Hays Code. Priests, in fact, warned their congregations that seeing it constituted a mortal sin.

This extreme reaction stemmed from several perceived transgressions:

Firstly, Jane's apparent enjoyment of sex was a major point of contention. A scene depicting her and Tarzan waking in their treetop shelter, with her sensuously stretching and playfully remarking, "Tarzan, you've been a bad boy!" strongly implied not only sexual activity but potentially a kinky element. This stood in stark contrast to later Hays Code regulations, which discouraged portrayals of women, especially, finding pleasure in sex.

Secondly, Jane's preference for Tarzan, a "savage" — albeit a resourceful and wise one — over the "civilized" and "respectable" Holt was deeply problematic. While initially swayed by a dress from London offered by Holt, her loyalty decisively shifted. This was particularly evident when Holt attempted to kill Tarzan, and both he and Jane believed Tarzan was dead. However, upon realizing Tarzan was alive, the allure of "civilization" completely dissipated for Jane. Tarzan's appeal, it seems, was undeniable.

Deemed too shocking for audiences in 1959, *THE BRAIN THAT WOULDN'T DIE* languished for three years, finally released in 1962 after significant edits. Today, its initial reception seems baffling; the film is a bizarre blend of lurid, lewd, and profoundly ludicrous elements.

The plot centers on a doctor obsessed with transplantation. When his girlfriend perishes in a car accident, he salvages her severed head, rushing it to his clandestine laboratory. There, with rudimentary tools like telephone cords, clamps, and what appears to be a baking pan, he revives her. However, gratitude is far from her mind. Instead, she’s furious, especially upon learning the doctor's plan to graft her head onto a new body.

The doctor proves remarkably fastidious in his search, seeking a body "built for speed." He cruises city sidewalks for unsuspecting women, frequents strip clubs, attends beauty pageants, and relentlessly pursues cheesecake models.

This film captures that magical moment when childhood innocence gives way to the confusing whirlwind of adulthood.

We meet Danni (Reese Witherspoon) at the precipice of this transition. She's a dreamy teenager, swooning over Elvis records and longing for love. Her older sister, Maureen, soon bound for college, appears to have it all figured out. Beautiful and effortlessly charming to boys, Maureen secretly struggles, dating a local "loser" (whose father is also somewhat fixated on her) and wishing for a decent boy to sweep her off her feet. Danni, like many teenagers, grapples with self-doubt, idolizing Maureen without recognizing her own inherent beauty.

Adulthood truly enters Danni's world with the arrival of Court Foster. Having recently lost his father, Court moves with his mother and two younger brothers to work their old family farm. He has been

Emma, as a novel, holds a special place in my heart, largely due to its titular character and her relationship with Mr. Knightley. Emma, despite her imperfections, possesses a fundamentally good heart that elicits forgiveness and affection from the reader. Her dynamic with Mr. Knightley is a masterclass in romantic tension and warmth: familiar yet respectful, playful yet profound, it generates that delightful flutter of romantic excitement. Knightley himself is the epitome of an ideal man, and Emma, for her era, embodies the spirit of an independent, intelligent, and confident woman – especially considering her youth at just 21, with ample room for growth and maturity. Who wouldn't aspire to be Emma, or to experience the unique reprimands of Mr. Knightley?

This particular adaptation, however, completely misses the essence of what I cherish about *Emma*. I found it unwatchable, failing to capture the warm, generous spirit that endears Emma to her readers. The Emma I know displays profound patience and warmth towards her father, and her bond with Mrs. Weston highlights her selfless capacity to prioritize a friend's happiness, even at the cost of her own companionship when she facilitates Miss Taylor's marriage. In this adaptation, Mr. Woodhouse's portrayal felt bizarre rather than endearingly quaint.

Despite my earnest attempts, including purchasing the pilot film on both VHS and DVD, I struggled to connect with this program. A significant hurdle was the apparent self-absorption of the two lead characters, David (Bruce Willis) and Maddie (Cybill Shepherd). While I acknowledge the clever and often acclaimed dialogue, which was undeniably a cornerstone of the show's popularity, it wasn't enough to draw me in.

The dynamic between the main characters often mirrored the "battle of the sexes" prevalent in classic screwball comedies, characterized by constant arguments, accusations, and shouting. While many viewers seemingly relished this bickering, I found it off-putting, which kept me from ever fully embracing "Moonlighting."

My sole source of entertainment came from Allyce Beasley's portrayal of the hapless aide, Agnes, whose limited screen time was a genuine disappointment. While Shepherd was visually appealing (and I assume Willis was equally so for female viewers), the incessant arguing between the leads ultimately deterred me.

This film has haunted me since our first encounter. My mother watched it on television back in '92, and I vividly recall being roused in the dead of night by her tearful cries as my father guided her upstairs. She was uttering phrases like, "Don't let her get me," or something similar. When I inquired about what had distressed her so, she revealed she'd been watching *The Woman in Black*. Naturally, I had to see it for myself, and despite being only eleven, she permitted me. It terrified me to my core. Since then, I've been virtually immune to the scares of other horror films!

This film plays more like high-budget children's television than a cinematic experience. The antagonist appears to be a massive, sentient cloud of chocolate-covered espresso beans, a theory seemingly confirmed by the subtitles' designation of it as 'Insomnia.'
