My initial excitement, upon hearing of a civilization eradicated by insomnia, quickly dissipated when it became clear this was no nihilistic martial arts epic. The film even ventures into experimental territory, featuring a villain suffocated by an old man's extraordinarily long, white eyebrows. *Zu Warriors*' coherence remains equally elusive, regardless of whether the subtitles are active—a troubling indicator. The special effects themselves evoke a dated aesthetic, somewhere between Ray Harryhausen and *Xena: Warrior Princess*. In a word, primitive.

While I've long admired Woody Allen's past work, only an uncritical fan could overlook the sheer dullness, meaninglessness, pretentiousness, and, most notably, the abysmal acting in this film. It's an empty intellectual exercise built on flimsy foundations. The decision to artificially craft an "actor Allen-clone" by having Will Ferrell mimic a younger Allen's mannerisms and dialogue was a disastrous misstep, yielding predictably ludicrous results. And as for the dialogue, what was presumably intended as profound philosophical reflection devolved into an unwitting and comedic parody of intellectual thought. A regrettable outcome indeed.

Seldom seen, this giallo unfolds with a languid, laid-back charm, eschewing genre clichés for a looser narrative. The plot centers on a woman's quest for her missing lover, a psychiatrist who inexplicably vanished. Her search leads her to a villa inhabited by an array of eccentric characters, where, in true giallo fashion, murder lurks close by.

The film boasts a strong cast, including Adolfo Celi (Thunderball), Alida Valli (Suspiria), Horst Frank (Cat o' Nine Tails), and a youthful Sybil Danning (an '80s scream queen). Rosemary Dexter, though unfamiliar to me, confidently carries the lead role.

A defining characteristic of *Eye in the Labyrinth* is its atypical jazz-rock fusion soundtrack. Composed by Roberto Nicolosi, the score evokes the style of Miles Davis, particularly his work on *In A Silent Way*. This excellent soundtrack significantly distinguishes the film from most gialli. Its fusion groove enhances the languid atmosphere and complements the sunny, coastal scenery that forms much of the film's backdrop.

Typically, an actor's debut film is forgettable, often showcasing the inexperience of everyone involved—and this film is no exception. Worse, even by 1982 standards, its quality is so abysmal it borders on hilarity. Shot in the Chicago area on a shoestring budget, the acting is predominantly stiff, wooden, and cartoonish, reminiscent of a poorly executed high school or community theater production. Dialogue is frequently drowned out by traffic noise and delivered with an unnatural, forced declarativeness. The scenes feel contrived and disjointed, and bizarrely, characters—both children and adults—show no signs of aging despite the passage of years within the narrative.

While I believe compelling Christian films can appeal to broad, secular audiences, creators often prioritize "The Message" or personal connections to the project over fundamental filmmaking principles.

*The Unborn* stands out as a commendable low-budget horror film, effectively tapping into anxieties surrounding pregnancy. Brooke Adams delivers her usual strong performance, ably supported by B-movie veteran James Karen, though the rest of the cast is fairly typical for the genre. Surprisingly, Gary Numan's score is a definite highlight. Henry Dominic's screenplay offers an intelligent take on the subject, despite a subtle undercurrent of misogyny. Rodman Fender's direction is competent, if unremarkable, occasionally resorting to gratuitous jump scares. Fans of Brooke Adams, whose talent often goes underappreciated in film, will find her performance here particularly rewarding.

*The BFG* is a beloved Roald Dahl classic, yet this animated adaptation fails to capture its magic. While John Hambley's script largely adheres to the original story, the film is hampered by bland animation, a sluggish pace, and uninspired voice acting. What should be a joyful, vibrant adventure instead devolves into a tedious and dull experience. Uninitiated young viewers would be far better served by reading the book first, as this film risks deterring them from a true children's classic.

The story follows young orphan Sophie (voiced by Amanda Root), who endures a bleak existence at an unfriendly orphanage run by the cruel Mrs. Clonkers. One night, peering out her window, Sophie spots a colossal figure tiptoeing down the village street. Realizing it's been seen, the figure reaches through the window, plucks Sophie from her bed, tucks her into its enormous pocket, and vanishes into the night. Sophie soon discovers she has been abducted by a giant.

*Full House*: A show where forgetting to brush your teeth somehow warrants a 30-minute episode, complete with noisy kids and a lecturing dad. And let's not forget Uncle Joey's bizarre antics and Uncle Jesse's leather-clad posing, all while the family pontificates on their departed mother's hypothetical actions. It's a series of drawn-out, nonsensical adventures that will not only bore you to tears but also prematurely age you.

This iconic French film from the 1970s, a cornerstone of the era's sexual liberation cinema, features Gérard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere in memorably sardonic roles. It stands among the dark psychological dramas Blier masterfully crafted in the '70s and '80s, alongside works like "Serie Noire," "Buffet Froid," and "Beau Pere."

A previous comment incorrectly translated the title. While the protagonists are indeed "going places," the French title, literally "the waltz dancers," is a metaphor for the movement of testicles, a far cry from the commonly used English version.

A visually stunning film, yet a missed opportunity. Imagine discovering Atlantis—what's your first move? Exploration, of course! This was a chance for Disney to transport viewers to an extraordinary world. Instead, they fell back on tired tropes.

This film was a fascinating paradox: simultaneously the worst and the best movie I've ever encountered. Perhaps its charm lies in embracing the delightful absurdity inherent to many made-for-TV sci-fi originals. The line, "I like my dinosaur meat well done!" stands out as a particularly memorable and hilarious quote.

The plot feels like the product of a particularly vivid, pot-induced dream. One can almost picture the writing team, post-all-night revelry involving dance-offs and mind-altering substances, brainstorming this gem: space marines dispatched to a dinosaur and medieval-house infested alien planet to safeguard a science team. Brilliant! It perfectly fulfills the entire checklist for a classic sci-fi original: guns, dinosaurs, medieval elements, space travel, and delightfully terrible acting.

I highly recommend watching this movie, though perhaps not owning it.

The film suffers from a lack of compelling characters; the protagonist, in particular, embodies the least appealing traits of Woody Allen, Paul Reiser, and Paul Provenza. Furthermore, the plot relies on transparently artificial scenarios, such as the predictable rollerblading incident, which are so contrived they become off-putting.

The film masterfully portrays the subtle complexities of gender segregation, often a source of societal friction, with remarkable tenderness. Its humor, though tinged with bitterness, is incisive. The decision to cast mostly non-professional actors lends an authentic, almost documentary-like quality, enhancing its realism and tangibility.

The most captivating scenes unfold as the girls, ostensibly forbidden from observing, are spellbound by a soldier—their supposed overseer—broadcasting a game. For Iranians, the post-victory street celebrations, replete with familiar cheers and dancing, will undoubtedly evoke a profound sense of national pride. Even for non-Iranians, the film's universal appeal is undeniable.

Christmas, a holiday marked by both sacred and secular traditions, ideally encourages goodwill among people. Yet, this spirit seems lost on Ebenezer Scrooge, a 19th-century London merchant and moneylender.

Scrooge's nephew observes his uncle's complete disdain for Christmas, which Scrooge dismisses as "humbug." Scrooge, much like his 20th-century parallel, Mr. Potter of Bedford Falls, New York, has long shed any semblance of humanity, becoming a hardened and cynical individual.

However, as Charles Dickens masterfully narrates, redemption is always within reach. Through the intervention of a solitary ghost and three spirits, Scrooge is given a path to transformation.

"A Christmas Carol" endures as a timeless holiday classic, yet its profound social commentary on 19th-century Great Britain is often overlooked, much like that found in "Oliver Twist." The film vividly portrays the lives of the middle and lower classes. The Cratchits, though a step above the destitute characters in "Oliver Twist," nonetheless face a constant struggle to maintain their meager standing.

This film is a masterclass in design, flawlessly executed from its intricate sets to its evocative lighting and immersive soundscape. The plot unfolds ingeniously, with a script that draws viewers into a sophisticated narrative where characters pursue a deceptively simple goal.

Paxton delivers a career-defining performance, his every mannerism and vocal intonation perfectly calibrated. Each shot is meticulously crafted, and the film continuously delivers unexpected twists, particularly after the first hour. While perhaps not the year's top film, it is a brilliantly refined gem, best appreciated by those who enjoy intellectual challenges.

My babysitter was a huge fan, so I grew up watching many of the older episodes. I'm not particularly fond of Scooby Doo, so I'm not sure why I even bothered to leave the TV on when this show premiered. To my surprise, I found myself thoroughly enjoying it. For me, Shaggy and Scooby were the only truly interesting characters (I can practically feel the glares from fans of the others), so I appreciate the show's decision to focus solely on them. This might, however, alienate fans of the original series. I'm impressed with the voice acting, especially Dr. Phinius Phibes. His voice was captivating even before I realized he was voiced by Jeff Bennett. And Jim Meskimen’s portrayal of Robi sounds like he's genuinely having a blast. I also get a kick out of the techies, with their subtly autistic personalities and their clear desire to play Dungeons and Dragons or reenact scenes from Star Wars (though not explicitly named as such in the show, of course).

"The Crush" presents itself initially as a charming romantic comedy, following the lives of forty-something friends in a style reminiscent of a British "Sex and the City." The film maintains this pleasant tone for roughly its first two-thirds.

A particularly enjoyable aspect was the reversal of the "trophy hunk" stereotype, though the character's development felt somewhat underdeveloped (and, frankly, more of Kenny Doughty's physical presence would have been appreciated). The film heavily emphasizes the older woman/younger man dynamic, a stark contrast to the way the opposite pairing was handled in either version of "Sabrina" (neither of which I find appealing), or even in real-life relationships like those of Douglas/Zeta-Jones or Dion/Svengali.

Beyond Andie MacDowell's expatriate character, the cast features welcome, familiar faces from British dramas and comedies, including the sharply witty Anna Chancellor. However, the plot twists that emerge in the final act feel forced and contrived. It was only during the end credits that a deeper issue became apparent: much like "Sex and the City," the film's writer/director, debutant Scot John McKay, is male. This led me to suspect his true intention may have been to write a story about three gay men, perhaps exploring their coming-out journeys.

Having first encountered this film via MST3K, and despite the uproarious humor of the commentary, I found the movie itself to be far from terrible. While its low budget was evident and the plot occasionally convoluted, it possessed a distinctly Hitchcockian quality. Indeed, watching the unedited version, I was genuinely entertained. This film is ripe for a contemporary Hollywood remake.

Redline: A soulless rip-off, devoid of *any* redeeming qualities. It’s not just that it lacks a complex plot or surprising twists; it lacks *anything* engaging whatsoever. The experience is akin to a porn film where the narrative bookends are fleeting and forgettable – except here, you don’t even get what you paid for. Mind-numbingly dull, its race sequences defy belief, and the exquisite cars are utterly wasted, their beauty tarnished by appearing in this cinematic void. While the lead actress may be attractive, her presence alone isn't enough to rescue this disaster. One can almost picture the director randomly assembling plot points and dialogue, leaving the film’s structure to pure chance. No genuine racing enthusiast could endure, let alone enjoy, the racing depicted here.

Kirstie Alley stars in this film, appearing slightly trimmer, alongside a bleached-blond MacGyver lookalike. The plot revolves around a fifty-year-old screenwriter facing age discrimination, leading her to enlist her younger nephew to pose as the script's author. This unoriginal premise underpins a poorly executed movie, plagued by lackluster acting, insipid dialogue, and a preposterous storyline. A perplexing subplot involves a writer's inexplicable admiration for Alley's character. The actor portraying Alley's brother delivers a wooden, miscast performance, making their shared scenes unbearable. This film is best avoided.

This film may very well be the worst I've ever encountered. I once again fell victim to an enticing synopsis and appealing cover art, a mistake I've since learned from, especially after a similar experience with "Malevolence."

I typically enjoy horror films set in isolated, natural environments like woods, deserts, or farms. While this movie claims to be set in the Texas woods, the production quality suggested it was filmed in someone's backyard. The overall production values were abysmal, and the acting was, without exaggeration, the worst I've ever witnessed.

Furthermore, the plot bore no resemblance to the description on the back cover. This movie was so remarkably terrible that neither a major retailer like F.Y.E. nor local used DVD shops would even take it. I've seen my share of bad films, "Troll 2" being a memorable example, but this one undeniably surpasses them all. I genuinely believed nothing could be worse than "Troll 2," but I was mistaken. Avoid this movie at all costs, even if offered for free.

This visually striking and sophisticated game unfolds as a "story within a story." We follow Bart Klever, a screenwriter, as he grapples with his latest script—which, in a clever twist, is simultaneously the screenplay for the film we are experiencing. His struggle with the text, alongside the intimate environment of his flat where he works and cares for his daughter, becomes a central narrative theme.

The confined space of the apartment provides fertile ground for playful optical illusions, employing light, color, and even a pair of cats. This seemingly simple domestic setting is further complicated by the fluctuating dimensions of the evolving script. Displayed on a computer monitor, this mutable text is continually shaped by the filmmaker's interventions, acting as a counterpoint to the equally shifting environment. As the viewing angle constantly changes, fundamental questions arise: What constitutes "truth" versus "illusion"? Which of the depicted worlds holds primacy? And can any element serve as a fixed point of reference within this dynamic narrative space?

This film suffers from a cheap and unappealing aesthetic, failing to captivate its young audience, with the sole exception of a moderately amusing toilet humor gag. Christopher Lloyd's performance feels uninspired and weary, though the script's weak attempts at humor certainly don't elevate it. Elizabeth Hurley delivers an cringeworthy, amateurish portrayal in what was intended to be a comedic role. Only Jeff Daniels and Darryl Hannah manage to escape embarrassment. Ultimately, this movie feels utterly unnecessary, particularly when its inevitable comparison to Robin Williams' often brilliant improvisations in "Mork & Mindy" highlights its creative shortcomings.

This film paled in comparison to its predecessors. It lacked the same energy, excitement, and strong performances from actors willing to fully embrace their roles. The script, too, was a significant letdown. Several plot points left me utterly bewildered. Why does Farrah, seemingly uninterested in a serious career, have a manager who appears to be wasting his time? And if Kate and Barney are true "artists," why would they participate in such overtly commercialized television, reminiscent of a Shakespearean actor forced into a sitcom? They weren't established figures, nor were they destitute. While the historical detail of the poster's release preceding Farrah's show was accurate, the notions of Silverman rejecting "Funniest Home Videos" and "American Idol" pitches, or Spelling promising to create a show for Tori, are clearly fabrications.

Furthermore, the portrayal of Aaron Spelling's role was particularly irksome. He's depicted as the showrunner and creator, neither of which he was, and the origin of *Charlie's Angels* is presented in a laughable manner. The film also fails to explain how Spelling and Goldberg were able to enforce Farrah's oral contract when others had written agreements. Additionally, the absence of Farrah or Bernstein's perspective on this is a glaring omission.

The 1999 film boasts commendable production quality, featuring an attractive and capable cast. It refreshingly avoids common action film clichés: no endless, inaccurate shootouts or gratuitous, high-cost car destruction.

Interiors are convincingly modern and well-equipped, though the anachronistic, 1950s-esque computer lab stands out. Also, the unusual, pancake-batter-like makeup on the corpses, intended to suggest calcification, was unintentionally amusing and scientifically questionable.

However, the film's central premise—a computer virus transmitted through screens that transforms into a deadly biological pathogen—is, in my opinion, one of the least believable in sci-fi horror.

This film is captivating, primarily for three reasons.

Firstly, its aesthetic beauty is striking. The bold color palette, extraordinary costumes, and picturesque sets create a visually rich experience. The cinematography, while appearing lavish, complements the look without seeming overtly expensive.

Secondly, the narrative resonates deeply. As a fan of stories where misfits and loners form an unconventional family, I found this film particularly engaging. Unlike many of its genre, it skillfully avoids clichés, presenting flawed yet incredibly likable characters. Alan Larkin's performance is a standout (his character, the van, and the road trip theme evoked fond memories of last year's *Little Miss Sunshine*). I was also impressed by Fabrizio Bentivoglio's nuanced portrayal, though Til Schweiger's performance occasionally felt a touch overdone. The humor, often derived from their botched attempts at tricks, and the emotional depth intertwine seamlessly throughout the film, culminating in a highly satisfying ending.

Finally, the overarching magician theme is brilliantly executed. Much like a skilled magician directs the audience's gaze to create an illusion, this film expertly guides the viewer, achieving its desired effect.

The title truly speaks volumes. I saw this film with my father upon its release, and as a Korean War veteran, he held the subject of the movie in high esteem. My only critique is the film's narrow focus on a brief chapter of his life. It's astonishing to consider the epic biopic that could have been made from his entire life story, and the immense production costs such an endeavor would entail.

Some criticisms leveled at the man's character are, in my opinion, cheap shots. The film's central theme of "Duty, Honor, Country" is far more than a slogan; it embodies the profound dedication of one individual to his nation.

It's ironic that Gregory Peck, given his liberal leanings, managed to capture such a nuanced understanding of the man. He masterfully portrays the general's unwavering courage, balanced with his profound humanity.

This clever film, a timeless journey through love, features Buster Keaton as a perpetual suitor. From the Stone Age to ancient Rome and the Roaring Twenties, Keaton's signature wimpy persona battles Wallace Beery for the heart of his beloved. While undeniably cheesy, the Roman segment stood out, particularly the hilariously unconvincing lion costume and the bizarre chariot race in the snow. Yet, it was Keaton's extraordinary acrobatics that truly captivated. Though not his finest work, this exceptional and enjoyable film offers wholesome, old-fashioned fun across all eras. Don't miss it!

When I first heard about this film, I braced myself for widespread derision, especially given its target demographic. To my surprise, it garnered appreciation from audiences beyond the age of seven. While I did find some enjoyment in it, that was primarily due to my sister (who is ten) and I gleefully mocking it throughout.

Jordan, I must be frank: your performance was a significant Weakness. A film struggles when its lead can't deliver, and unfortunately, neither the script nor the plot offered any redemption. Pamela’s character, in particular, was incredibly weak, verging on pathetic.

Despite these shortcomings, I did find some strong performances, notably from Spencer, Hollywood, and Ronnie. However, their efforts weren't enough to salvage the movie.

Two aspects of this film remain particularly perplexing:

1.  The implausibility of Spencer's character falling for hers. While in reality, there's only a four-year age difference between the actors, "Go Figure" made it seem far greater. Jordan is undeniably pretty, but her portrayal in the film...

I might be overestimating this film's quality, but it's Halloween, I've just experienced "Knott's Scary Farm," and I'm in the mood for a delightfully cheesy Halloween movie. Plus, it only cost me a dollar.

Normally, I'd fast-forward through a movie like this, hunting for the highlights. Yet, for some reason, I resisted the urge. From the opening scenes, it was clear this wasn't a "real" movie, not even a B-movie. It falls more into the vein of a made-for-TV "horror" film, reminiscent of something shot on a shoestring budget with a camcorder. (Honestly, I half-expected one of those overly-muscled college guys to wander out in his underwear at any moment.) There are no cutaway shots – multiple camera setups were obviously out of the budget – and the lighting is flat. Despite all this, there's something oddly refreshing about watching a director with limited resources manage to pull off a halfway decent film. Their commendable effort, even with severe limitations, deserves recognition. This movie certainly has its merits: the acting is surprisingly competent, and the cinematography, while a bit too bright to be truly scary, is quite good.

Sidney Franklin's *The Good Earth* endures as a classic, distinguished by its timeless narrative and exceptional performances. Luise Rainer's portrayal of O-Lan, which earned her an Oscar, is particularly remarkable; her transformation is so profound that she is almost unrecognizable. With minimal dialogue throughout the lengthy film, Rainer masterfully conveys emotion through her facial expressions and body language, embodying her character so convincingly that unfamiliar viewers might easily believe she is Chinese.

The film's exploration of a rags-to-riches tale and universal human themes ensures its continued relevance. As Wang Lung and O-Lan escape famine and poverty to achieve financial prosperity, they discover that possessions alone do not equate to a meaningful life. True fulfillment returns only when they reconnect with the land after battling a locust plague—a scene made unforgettable by special effects that remain visually stunning. This enduring formula, presented through the unique lens of a Chinese family (especially groundbreaking for 1937), solidifies the film's classic status. *The Good Earth* powerfully conveys the invaluable truth that wealth pales in comparison to the richness of friends and family.

The claim that this film is a bad movie is simply unfounded. In reality, it stands as the finest movie I have ever witnessed. Its narrative is excellent, and the performances delivered by the cast are among the best I've seen. I would not offer a single critique of any actor's work. This movie is, and will forever remain, unparalleled.

Busy Phillips delivered a remarkable performance, masterfully blending both comedic and dramatic elements. While Erika Christensen was strong, Phillips undeniably stole the show. This was a welcome follow-up to her previous film, *The Smokers*, which fell short of expectations. It would be a travesty if Busy Phillips is not recognized with a nomination for this film. Bypass *Mona Lisa Smile* and instead see *Home Room*.

Despite my disdain for Hollywood, my love for cinema often compels me to endure subpar theatrical releases. Such was the case with "Vanilla Sky," a film I'd hoped would honor its Spanish predecessor, "Open Your Eyes," either through faithful adaptation or innovative reinterpretation. Instead, it awkwardly attempted both, failing spectacularly.

The film's opening held promise, particularly with the inclusion of Radiohead, a band I admire and wished had a more prominent role. However, the musical journey ultimately veered into the perplexing with "Good Vibrations" by The Beach Boys blaring during the climax. This jarring shift exemplifies the film's inconsistent and often ill-fitting soundtrack. While a few club scenes boasted decent tracks, the inexplicable choice of "Good Vibrations" at a critical juncture was more irritating than impactful, especially given its complete irrelevance to the plot. Meaningful song choices, like Radiohead's "Kid A" perhaps serving as a primary theme, would have significantly elevated the experience.

Visually, the club scene was a highlight, credit where it's due. Beyond that, the film reeked of an arrogance that presumed audience comprehension. Yet, those who might grasp its nuances are likely the same ones who prefer the subtitled original, leaving the majority alienated.

Upon the US entry into World War I, Hollywood was compelled by the government to produce propaganda films. Among these, *THE LITTLE American* stands out, largely due to its star, Mary Pickford.

Pickford portrays a young woman conflicted between two suitors: Jack Holt, a German, and Raymond Hatton, a Frenchman. Their enlistment in the war, however, postpones her choice.

A pivotal moment occurs when the ship Pickford is on, laden with munitions, is sunk by the Germans—a scene reminiscent of the Lusitania incident. From a lifeboat, Pickford delivers a powerful condemnation to the German commander. Later, as a prisoner of war in a château, she encounters both Holt and Hatton.

Director Cecil B. DeMille crafts a singular, striking scene within the film. As Pickford and Holt navigate a ravaged village, they encounter a bombed church with only a single wall intact. Against this wall hangs a large crucifix. In a surreal sequence, the wall collapses, yet the figure of Jesus remains suspended mid-air. This moment of profound artistry contrasts sharply with the film's otherwise direct and unembellished style.

I watched "I, Robot" on DVD last night and, upon reviewing its IMDb reception this morning, was struck by how divisive it has proven among critics—a division unfortunately marked by considerable acrimony.

This polarization baffles me, as the film is neither exceptional nor truly terrible. Its most salient characteristic, for me, is its depressingly unoriginal nature. It's disheartening to witness American audiences readily embrace such clichéd, uninspired retreads as groundbreaking cinema. "I, Robot" is a pastiche through and through: its plot is a clumsy marriage of Asimov and contemporary action tropes; Will Smith reprises his familiar role as a cynical, quick-witted hero; and the special effects are clearly derivative of films like "The Matrix."

In essence, "I, Robot" embodies the quintessential modern action film: superficial plotting, forced witty banter, and relentless adrenaline. Smith's performance is unremarkable, but this is hardly surprising—he seems to be Hollywood's latest, unsuccessful attempt to mold a Black Bruce Willis. The narrative, incidentally, is riddled with plot holes of varying magnitudes.

In Bridgeport, deranged high school teacher Richard Fenton (Johnathon Schaech) harbors a dangerous obsession with his teenage student, Donna Keppel (Brittany Snow). After he murders her family to ensure she stays with him, Richard is apprehended and sentenced to life in prison. Three years later, a traumatized but recovering Donna, still undergoing psychological treatment and medication, attends her prom. Accompanied by her boyfriend Bobby (Scott Porter) and two other couples, she heads to the Pacific Grand Hotel for the celebration. Unbeknownst to them, the psychopathic Richard has escaped prison and is now staying on the same floor, relentlessly pursuing Donna and brutally stabbing anyone—friends or hotel staff—who stands in his way.

This utterly forgettable slasher, "Prom Night," is a rehash of tired clichés, devoid of any genuine originality. Its nonsensical plot is superficial and absurd, further marred by Johnathon Schaech's abysmal portrayal of the deranged killer. The screenplay's predictability is truly astounding, allowing viewers to foresee every development. I rate this film a three.

Title (Brazil): "A Morte Convida Para Dançar" ("The Death Invites to Dance")

This film is arguably one of the worst I've encountered recently.

I fail to see the appeal of Heath Ledger; his appearance in the film was, to my eye, disfigured. Had I known of his real-life relationship with Naomi Watts, I might have understood her character's attraction, but instead, I spent an agonizing two hours questioning her judgment.

Similarly, I struggle to understand the widespread admiration for Orlando Bloom. His disheveled beard and perpetually startled expression in this film did little to convince me of his 'heartthrob' status.

While Rachel Griffiths delivered her usual strong performance, Geoffrey Rush appeared disengaged, as if eager to conclude filming.

The narrative's attempt to elicit sympathy for bank robbers and murderers felt misplaced and ineffective. Unlike the genuinely entertaining *Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid*, this film was trite, replete with clichés, and frankly, dull. Our only reason for enduring it was the misguided hope that it would eventually improve, a hope that proved futile.

The final 10-15 minutes, though intended to be dramatic, were unintentionally amusing. The scene where Heath Ledger's gang is besieged in a frontier hotel, with women and children suffering due to their presence, is not inherently humorous. However, their subsequent exit, clad in what appeared to be armor, was comically absurd, reminding us instantly of the Black Knight from *Monty Python and the Holy Grail*.

This film simply didn't resonate with me. It struggled to engage me on an intellectual, emotional, or aesthetic level. The dense, uninvolving dialogue made it difficult to connect with or care for any of the characters, leaving me hard-pressed to find redeeming qualities.

While I understand that familiarity with obscure Catholic theology may be key to its appreciation, and acknowledge my own unfamiliarity as an atheist, I've seen numerous films tackling religious themes that transcended specific doctrines, finding universal appeal in their exploration of the human condition.

"The Bourne Ultimatum" plunges viewers into a high-octane chase from its opening moments, an explosive start to Jason Bourne’s (Matt Damon, delivering a masterful performance) relentless pursuit of the CIA black-ops architects who molded him into a lethal assassin. His ultimate goal: unearthing his true identity. David Strathairn joins the cast as a chillingly detached puppet master, complementing returning veterans such as the excellent Joan Allen and the virtually absent Julia Stiles.

As with its predecessor, the film employs Paul Greengrass’ signature shaky, hand-held camera work, which, while occasionally disorienting during lulls, perfectly enhances the tension and claustrophobia of the intimate combat sequences. It proves equally effective in the thrilling chase scenes, predominantly foot pursuits across rooftops, punctuated by spectacular vehicular destruction. A hallmark of the Bourne series is its exhilarating global scope and its audacious portrayal of technology and communications, often bending the laws of physics and pre-dating current capabilities. The Bourne films inhabit a gritty, hyper-realistic world, brimming with technologically-driven marvels, where coincidences seem to defy all logic.

This animated film, though unusual in its presentation, delves into themes of depth and emotion rarely seen in children's movies. We follow a young girl at summer camp, plagued by low self-esteem and a lack of friends, save for a pair of equally despondent siblings. Reaching her nadir, she makes a desperate pact with a devil-like entity. What makes this film remarkably true to life is the protagonist's journey: from the depths of despair, she experiences remorse, undergoes a profound transformation, and ultimately teaches this dark, mystical creature the human concept of love. Concurrently, the twin siblings find their own redemption and self-worth by aiding small bears. Despite its peculiar elements, the film offers a profoundly positive message for children and remains an enjoyable experience. Stephen Bishop's poignant musical contributions further enhance its appeal.

This film is perfect for a cozy night in, best enjoyed with a glass of wine, by the fire, and with your feet up. It's an undemanding watch, ideal for unwinding after a long day. While undeniably unrealistic, it's remarkably funny and thoroughly entertaining. Don't expect gritty realism; its charm lies in its humorous premise—the idea of a businessman not only agreeing to slum it but actually finding joy in the experience. I highly recommend it.

Ealing comedies are consistently excellent, but this particular film stands out as a masterpiece.

Its core premise revolves around the discovery that a small section of London's Pimlico district is, in fact, sovereign Burgundian territory, not part of the UK. The narrative then follows the residents as they contend with two immediate challenges: safeguarding the treasures unearthed by a bomb blast and fending off black marketeers who, realizing the area is exempt from British law, exploit the absence of rationing. When the government imposes a blockade, trapping them within their own street, we witness their tenacious fight against the system.

Forced to ration food and water in their principled stand, they paradoxically find themselves in a more dire situation than before the discovery. This forms a crucial moral cornerstone of the film. Their nadir arrives when their food supply dwindles to nothing, prompting them to consider surrender. However, in a heartwarming twist, the entirety of London rallies to their aid, inundating them with provisions, thereby empowering them to persevere in their struggle.

The film's execution is flawless, underpinned by superb acting.

I vividly recall watching a film at the age of five, believing it to be a typical cartoon, until bras and bullets unexpectedly filled the screen. This movie, while undeniably controversial and designed to provoke, possesses a dark humor and profound depth that I find compelling. It's a cult classic I highly recommend.

Fans of this genre might also enjoy "Fritz the Cat" and "The Nine Lives of Fritz the Cat," both of which I believe Ralph Bakshi directed. These films follow a cat navigating the struggles of family, street life, and employment. As soon as I was old enough, I sought out and rented all of these animated features.

During its initial release, this particular film, due to its controversial title "Coonskin," was also distributed under the name "Street Fighter." Ralph Bakshi's filmography also includes "Cool World," featuring a young Brad Pitt, and "Heavy Traffic," another animated exploration of street life through the eyes of a young man.

The film is a chaotic, patronizing "world music" nightmare. It's a poorly executed tourist film, made unbearable by its incoherent sequences. Lacking transitions or visual explanations, it jumps haphazardly between India, Egypt, South America, and Africa, presenting a jumble of "third-worlders with baskets on their heads," as one reviewer aptly put it. Their endless, seemingly meaningless walking footage feels like a forced attempt at profundity. For a truly impactful "life in transformation" theme, a much more cohesive setting, like Mexico (easily accessible from Koya's prime shooting locations), would have been far more effective.

Instead, the filmmakers opted for a jumbled global itinerary, rendered even more tedious by mind-numbingly overcranked filter shots. The only faint praise I can offer is that it narrowly avoids the abysmal depths of *Naqoyqatsi*.

While I generally appreciate Renny Harlin's directorial approach and commend the cinematographer for some impressive shots, this particular film, unlike his strong efforts in "Elm Street 4" and "Die Hard 2," suffers from a critical flaw: a complete lack of a coherent script. The dialogue, a common weak point in this genre, reaches an unparalleled level of absurdity here. The sheer quantity of truly dreadful lines is astounding, and their delivery is equally abysmal, reminiscent more of a cheap adult film than an action-adventure. It's almost as if Harlin believed that elongating the delivery of each line would somehow compensate for the script's deficiencies. He was mistaken.

The unfortunate reality is that talented actors are wasted in ill-conceived roles, burdened by insipid dialogue. Even factoring in my usual disinterest in Stallone's performances, his acting here outshines Lithgow, Turner, and especially Rooker, which speaks volumes about the film's shortcomings. It's perplexing, given Lithgow's brilliant portrayal of a villain in "Ricochet," that he's so underutilized.

Insights Gained from "The List":

Despite decent cinematography, a capable lead actress, and the presence of Malcolm McDowell, the film ultimately failed to engage.

Blockbuster's return policy does not cover cinematic disappointment.

Even in the face of questionable material, Malcolm McDowell's commitment to his craft remains evident.

Chuck Carrington's performance suggests a need for further acting development.

The screenplay would have benefited from professional refinement.

This viewing experience felt like a divine test, costing an undue amount for its quality.

The film's unstructured narrative and lack of resolution resulted in a disengaged audience.

Apparently, a simple cross drawn by a landlord can avert death – a compelling argument for cordial tenant-landlord relations.

A maid's song possesses surprising resuscitative powers.

Chuck Carrington's acting still leaves much to be desired.

Bringing this film home is likely to incur the wrath and ridicule of roommates.

No apologies will be sufficient for this cinematic misstep.

You can't help but adore the schlocky horror films of the 1970s. Unlike the monotonous slasher flicks of today, these K-tel-esque cinematic treasures deliver genuine scares without succumbing to tired formulas.

This particular B-movie chronicles the disastrous production of another B-movie. Faith Domergue, known for *This Island Earth*, plays an aging B-movie queen starring in a film based on a series of gruesome murders that occurred in a family home. Her director and boyfriend, who bears a striking resemblance to Gordon Jump but with an edge, is filming on location and under immense time pressure. The Ken-doll-esque co-star unearths a book of Tibetan chants, which they decide to incorporate into the script for added "realism." As it turns out, realism is precisely what they should have avoided.

John Carradine, long past his quest for the 17th gland in *The Unearthly*, now ekes out a modest living as the estate’s caretaker. He diligently performs his duties, but consistently finds himself at odds with the director.

The horror gradually intensifies: a dead cat, John Carradine digging a grave, ultimately leading to a staggering seven murders. At least the advertising was honest. It's truly a shame the ghoulish events unfolded as they did.

I'm curious about the pickup truck John T. drove in the movie. It appeared to be a mid-to-late 1970s Ford. This film holds a special place for my wife and me, as it was the first memorable movie we watched together as a married couple. The truck particularly interests me because it resembles the first one I drove, and I recently acquired a similar model. I'd love to restore it to match the one in the movie.

The movie's music and acting were also fantastic. Does anyone know who played John's aunt and what she's doing now? Also, I'm curious if John had a stunt double for the intense tower scene where he nearly fell. Finally, what year was the Mustang Debra W. drove? It looked like a 1960s model. Thanks for any information!

This Three Stooges classic, "Sing a Song of Six Pants," rivals "Disorder in the Court" as a personal favorite. It's an absolute laugh riot that no Stooges fan should miss.

The film follows the boys as janitors in a recording studio, where they overhear Christine McIntyre's stunning rendition of "Voices of Spring." Christine is on the cusp of a record deal, but she's hesitant to confess her career aspirations to her father and prove her talent. After Christine and others depart, the Stooges playfully put on her record, with Curly comically impersonating Christine. The record executive, mistaking Curly for Christine, invites him to perform at her party. Naturally, a man they've offended is also in attendance, and after the Stooges sabotage his solo, he vows revenge.

"Sing a Song of Six Pants" is a quintessential Stooges film, earning a perfect 10/10.

*The College Girl Murders* weaves a complex web of intrigue. A deranged scientist engineers an almost imperceptible, lethal gas. Yet, before he can capitalize on his breakthrough, a mysterious, hooded monk wielding a whip brutally murders him. When a co-ed succumbs to the gas in a church, Scotland Yard is called in, but the killings persist. Who can apprehend this elusive killer, who seemingly vanishes and reappears within the college grounds at will?

**What Works:**

*   **The Killer:** The killer's striking ensemble—a vibrant red, KKK-esque outfit, complete with matching gloves and a stark white, effectively wielded whip—is undeniably memorable. While the notion of such a flamboyantly dressed killer stalking a girls' school is far-fetched, it's one of the most sinister costumes I've encountered.

*   **Groovy 60s Music:** I'm eager to find the title music for *The College Girl Murders*. Its jazzy, hip, 60s vibe was absolutely captivating.

*   **Bizarre Touches:** Beyond the killer's outlandish attire...

The film's central concept captivated me: identifying "intruders" within the fragile Self, manifesting on various levels—predominantly subconscious, yet occasionally allegorical. These intruders are a pervasive presence throughout: from the protagonist's reclusive life on the Swiss-French border, to his recurring daydreams and nightmares, and even within his ailing post-transplant body. In a poignant turn during the latter half of the film, he himself becomes the intruder, returning to an ancient French colony in a bid for atonement.

The overarching tone is one of bitterness rather than pathos, laden with regret, guilt, and a pervasive sense of failure. It paints a grim portrait of old age—ostensibly independent, yet hollow and profoundly lonely within. The director masterfully crafts images to evoke fleeting sensations of anxiety and desire, rather than explicit meanings. Some are mesmerizing, even possessing a dry humor, akin to an absurdist play only a somnambulist could envision.

(BIG SPOILERS) Having previously experienced Takashi Miike's unsettling and brutal exploration of Japanese feminine ideals in *Audition*, I found *Visitor Q*—likely a play on "Visitor: Question"—to be a disturbingly graphic examination of the family unit. Miike’s surreal portrayal of familial dysfunction appears to strive for a Lynchian sense of disorientation and cinematic style, yet ultimately falls short in terms of intrigue and execution.

The film immediately immerses the viewer in a series of bizarre scenarios, beginning with the patriarch, Kenichi Endo (whose performance was notably strong), paying for sex with his estranged daughter, Fujiko. Upon his return home, he is assaulted by "the visitor," Kazushi Watanabe, who, wielding a sizable rock, inexplicably accompanies him back to the family residence. Meanwhile, the mother, Shungiku Uchida, endures abuse from her son, Jun Muto, who is himself a victim of bullying at school. The visitor, upon entering the home, menacingly integrates himself into the family dynamic. Over time, and with the visitor's peculiar influence, the family's relationships undergo a perverse transformation, evolving through acts such as breast milking, murder, and retention.

The enduring capacity for evil perpetrated in the name of religion, despite historical lessons and modern enlightenment, consistently astounds and appalls me. The calculated actions of the Catholic Church in 20th Century Ireland stand out as a particularly egregious example.

*A Love Divided* poignantly recounts the real-life ordeal of a family torn apart by bigoted intolerance and prejudice, all under the guise of an absurd Church doctrine. The film opens with idyllic scenes of rural Irish life, introducing Sheila and Sean Cloney, a happily married couple with two young children. Sean is Catholic, and Sheila is Protestant, yet she readily agrees to raise their children in the Catholic faith. Initially, there's no hint of discord between Catholics and Protestants in the village. However, this harmonious existence shatters when Sheila expresses a wish for their elder child to attend the Protestant school. The local priest, deeming this a "sin," promptly intervenes, turning Sheila's husband and the entire Catholic community against her.

This film exemplifies the challenges faced by technically proficient directors of music videos and commercials when transitioning to feature-length cinema. While the visuals, cinematography, lighting, CGI, and even sound design are meticulously polished, creating an undeniable sense of high production value, these strengths ultimately cannot compensate for significant narrative weaknesses.

The core issue isn't merely a "bad" plot, but rather a near absence of one. A substantial portion of the dialogue consists of uninspired exclamations like "What the hell was that?" without offering any resolution or explanation to either the characters or the audience. Much of the remaining dialogue feels improvised and unguided, suggesting a lack of a coherent script or clear direction for the actors.

Skye Bennet's performance stands out, perhaps precisely because her character, an autistic girl, is largely spared the burden of the woefully inadequate dialogue afflicting the rest of the cast.

Do you enjoy unraveling mysteries and navigating intricate narratives? If so, this film is a must-see. Francis Leclerc (son of legendary French-Canadian singer Félix Leclerc) delivers a brilliant and clever cinematic experience. Leclerc's signature style of flashy cinematography and intelligent editing shines through, brilliantly supported by Roy Dupuis's dynamic and praiseworthy lead performance.

The plot centers on Alexandre Tourneur, a veterinarian in his forties who awakens from a coma, having been inexplicably disconnected from life support. Tourneur grapples with amnesia, struggling to recall who caused the accident while he was tending to an injured deer on the road. As he fights to remember, his behavior grows increasingly unusual, suggesting an unsettling transformation.

This isn't a horror film, but it's a deeply mysterious and exceptionally well-acted one. While I have my own theories about the ending (my hypothesis points to the Indigenous character as the cause of the accident), the film intentionally leaves its conclusion open to diverse interpretations.

I highly recommend this film, rating it 9.5/10.

This film offers a welcome dose of cheer during a somber time, highlighting the simple power of friendliness. Morgan Freeman portrays a character remarkably similar to himself—a successful actor nearing 70. His journey to a small, unassuming grocery store, intended for role research, quickly charms both staff and patrons. Among them is Paz Vega's character, a captivating yet cantankerous young woman overseeing the "10 items or less" checkout lane.

*10 Items or Less* makes no grand pronouncements; instead, it gently chronicles the blossoming friendship between Freeman and Vega. The elder offers guidance in exchange for a ride home, a necessity after his assigned driver fails to appear and he finds himself without a crucial phone number. On a melancholic Sunday in New York City, this movie proved to be the perfect antidote to my blues.

Ladies and Gentlemen, please do not be deceived by the "A Stanley Kubrick Film" label. This is, regrettably, a film hailed as one of the most terrifying horror movies ever made, yet it is profoundly flawed. True horror should instill a fear so deep that it chills one to the bone at the mere thought of it in the dead of night. "The Shining," however, offers no genuine horror; instead, it presents a naive and foolish attempt at generating suspense. The effectiveness of such attempts, when divorced from reality, is self-evident.

The film's only redeeming qualities are the stunning vistas of the icy valley and the grand hotel itself, where much of the cast was accommodated. As for the performances, Jack Nicholson appears as a lost, lethargic soul, seemingly unsure of his character's motivations. Little can be said for the other bald, colored actor, who spends most of his time doting on a child actor. The film's shortcomings cannot be attributed to external factors; the tragedy is that it has been made, and poor Kubrick is no longer with us to rectify it.

It's hard to believe this film, with its laughable acting and one of the most preposterous plots imaginable, was released as recently as 1984. The premise beggars belief: a stout Texas sheriff, Joe Don Baker, is tasked with escorting an Italian he illegally arrested in Mexico all the way back to Italy. Adding to the absurdity, the title offers no clue about the film's content; it's as generic as any wannabe action/cop movie title could be.

Thankfully, I experienced this cinematic misadventure only through the protective filter of MST3K, with Mike and the Bots providing a constant stream of hilarious commentary. Their observations ranged from the female lead's uncanny resemblance to Elaine from *Seinfeld* ("None of them are spongeworthy") to relentless riffs on Baker's physique. While perhaps not as abysmal as *Mitchell*, Baker's reputation certainly precedes him here; when his name appears in the opening credits, Tom's dry remark, "I wish I was illiterate so I wouldn't have to read that," perfectly encapsulates the sentiment.

This *Columbo* installment excels with its well-crafted script, masterfully incorporating all the beloved hallmarks of the series: Columbo's unique rapport with suspects, the gradual unfolding of the mystery, the presence of his dog, and the compelling cat-and-mouse dynamic, which is particularly strong here. The writing also delivers welcome comedic relief, often centered around Columbo himself. Remarkably, this is achieved despite the concept—Columbo pursuing a mystery novelist—not being entirely new to the series.

The film also benefits immensely from James Frawley's exceptional direction. Frawley, who would go on to direct five more *Columbo* movies in the '70s and '80s, imbues the movie with distinct style and several truly memorable sequences.

While it's one of the slower-paced *Columbo* entries despite its moderate runtime, this deliberate approach works remarkably well here, largely due to the outstanding acting performances. As is often the case with *Columbo* films, the cast features either a prominent contemporary star or a revered veteran from early cinema.

I confess, Al Pacino is a guilty pleasure of mine. He was a phenomenal actor until *Scent of a Woman,* after which he seemed to overdose on his own persona, a state from which he never truly recovered. I’d heard next to nothing about *City Hall* growing up, and I’d hoped it would be a hidden gem—an overlooked, perhaps even prescient, intelligent, and captivating political thriller. It isn't.

*City Hall* muddles its plot with an excess of characters, names, and "realistic" urban issues, initially suggesting a broad and impactful narrative. You might anticipate a mind-blowing reveal. However, these numerous subplots and digressions ultimately lead to rather predictable urban tropes: the corruption of power, two-faced politicians, and mafia ties to law enforcement. While this setup theoretically could generate thrilling tension, that sense of danger and unpredictability never materializes.

Instead, the film unfolds predictably, culminating in a series of "confession" monologues. These are clearly intended to form a modern fable, imparting a lesson on the moral ambiguities inherent in the "real world" of politics.

The iconic theme song, "Arthur's Theme (Best That You Can Do)" by Christopher Cross, remains as captivating today as it was upon its release. This enduring melody perfectly encapsulates the spirit of New York City, much like the film itself.

Dudley Moore CBE delivers a memorable performance as the charmingly flawed, inebriated millionaire, Arthur Bach, engaged to the character played by Jill Eikenberry, later known for her role in *LA Law*. Arthur's life is managed by his devoted British butler, Hobson, portrayed with brilliant wit and warmth by Sir John Gielgud OM, who deservingly earned an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his impeccable performance.

The narrative takes an unexpected turn when Arthur falls for Linda Marolla, a diner waitress portrayed by Liza Minnelli. Minnelli, though not given a musical number, shines in a role that showcases her versatility, a stark contrast to her Oscar-winning turn in *Cabaret*.

The film also features a standout performance by Geraldine Fitzgerald as the formidable Bach matriarch, guiding the family's financial destiny with a commanding presence that arguably warranted an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Adding to the stellar cast, Barney Martin, beloved as Jerry's father on *Seinfeld*, portrays Liza's endearing father.

*Arthur* is a testament to exceptional filmmaking, a product of superb writing, compelling performances, and masterful direction.

Robert Duvall's performance in this film is remarkably ill-suited, characterized by a vocal delivery that uncannily resembles William F. Buckley. His acting, overly theatrical and melodramatic, consistently undermines any genuine dramatic engagement. Whether this was an intentional bid for attention or an accidental misstep, it stands out as the sole memorable aspect of an otherwise entirely forgettable movie. This film could serve as a cautionary example in acting classes, illustrating precisely what aspiring performers should avoid. Thankfully, Duvall's career evolved, and he abandoned such affected accents, going on to deliver far more compelling work. While he excels as a character actor, his range seems somewhat limited. In stark contrast, Klaus delivers a subtle and far more commendable performance.

This film, a captivating drama inspired by the life of Grey Owl in 1930s Canada, resonated with me in the same deeply moving way as 'Rudy' and 'Awakenings.' It focuses on a pivotal and tumultuous period late in Grey Owl's life.

The narrative centers on a Canadian Indian trapper who unexpectedly becomes an advocate for beavers threatened by over-trapping. Remarkably, he also foresees the decline of natural habitats and the unsustainable consumption of Earth's resources—ideas surprisingly well-received in the 1930s. He quickly rises to prominence as a public speaker, captivating audiences with his urgent message.

While Pierce Brosnan's casting might initially seem unusual, it proves to be a compelling choice; his performance, alongside Annie Galipeau's, is truly remarkable. Galipeau, a powerful actress, creates a refreshingly natural dynamic with Brosnan, unlike the often contrived pairings seen in recent Bond films.

I highly recommend this film to anyone who appreciates compelling drama, stunning cinematography, or environmental themes. It's also suitable for families, though younger children (under 10, depending on maturity) might find the narrative challenging to follow.

I can't recall who recommended this film, but they raved about it. It's undeniably bizarre, akin to rubbernecking at a highway accident. As the saying goes, truth is stranger than fiction, and this truth is truly something to behold. I'm baffled by the decision to release a fictionalized account of this documentary later this year; how could one possibly improve upon the original?

The story follows Jackie Kennedy's aunt and cousin, who retreat from New York society to a secluded life in the Hamptons. There, they become reclusive, devolving into what can only be described as "crazy cat ladies." Their hidden existence would have continued had the city not intervened to condemn their squalid property, leading to Jackie's eventual rescue. This film was made after that intervention, and throughout, I couldn't help but wonder just how dire their situation was beforehand. It's a dark, utterly fascinating glimpse into the underbelly of high society.

My anticipation for this film, especially given its production, was immense. However, it proved to be a profound disappointment, a stark departure from the whimsical spirit of Dr. Seuss. Its vulgarity and poor taste were undeniable, qualities I believe Dr. Seuss himself would have disapproved of.

"How the Grinch Stole Christmas" handled its subtle adult humor with far more grace; my children, to this day, remain oblivious to it. In stark contrast, "The Cat in the Hat" brazenly paraded its vulgarity, exposing my children to far more than I would have wished.

As someone who grew up cherishing Dr. Seuss, it was disheartening to witness such a timeless classic desecrated on the big screen. I can only hope that "Horton Hears a Who" manages to deliver a adaptation that truly honors Dr. Seuss's legacy.

This film is an affront to intelligence. It's truly baffling how anyone could greenlight a premise where three children single-handedly defeat dozens of ninjas, all while peppering the script with witless humor. The movie is a disaster, redeemable only as a time-filler or for its unintentional comedic value.

A theatrical troupe faces a horrific ordeal when a mysterious killer, "The Fiend," begins to systematically target them. Meanwhile, two tenacious reporters and their bumbling photographer embark on an investigation into "The Fiend's" crimes, only to find themselves drawn into the killer's crosshairs. Just as the protagonists believe they have unmasked the culprit, a shocking twist challenges their assumptions and raises new questions about the killer's true identity.

Filmed on a shoestring budget, Sam Katzman's adaptation of "The Hunchback of Notre Dame," retitled "A Face in the Fog," cleverly utilizes real Hollywood locations, particularly in its latter half, to compensate for the absence of elaborate studio sets. While the film's direction could be more polished—a poorly chosen camera angle during a fight scene, for instance, detracts from the action—the cast, primarily composed of performers transitioning from silent to sound films, delivers commendable performances given the limitations.

Ernest Hemingway famously called Paris "a moveable feast." Indeed, countless artists have immortalized the city in paintings, novels, songs, poems, memorable quotes, and films. As the celebrated director Max Ophüls once said of Paris: "It offered the shining wet boulevards under the street lights, breakfast in Montmartre with cognac in your glass, coffee and lukewarm brioche, gigolos and prostitutes at night. Everyone in the world has two fatherlands: his own and Paris."

Paris has long been synonymous with love and romance. This is beautifully captured in "Paris, Je T'Aime," a collection of eighteen short films by talented directors worldwide, subtitled "Petite romances." Each segment introduces us to one of the City of Light's twenty arrondissements and its inhabitants – Parisians of all ages, genders, colors, and backgrounds navigating love in its myriad forms and stages. Some of these "petite romances" observe the unexpected encounters of strangers that spark instant interest, closeness, and potential relationships, such as the initial meeting between Podalydès and Florence Muller on a Montmartre street in the opening film, or for Cyril...

For years, I eagerly anticipated seeing this film, impressed by James Merendino's directorial talent, especially after his excellent work on *SLC Punk*, one of my favorite movies. The opening ten minutes of this film promised a worthy successor; however, it quickly lost momentum and began to drag. While the acting and direction were superb, and the overall production flowed seamlessly, the script unfortunately did not. My attention often wavered, sustained primarily by the captivating presence of Claire Forlani, arguably the most beautiful woman in the world. Although a decent film, it ultimately fell short of my high expectations.

(P.S. Keep an eye out for fantastic cameos by Chi McBride and Chris McDonald.)

This is, without a doubt, the funniest movie I've ever seen. From the moment the four delinquents are dispatched by their fathers to Wienberg Military Academy, the film establishes a consistently hilarious tone that never lets up.

Describing this movie is a challenge because its humor is so perfectly executed and brilliantly conceived. At first glance, it might seem like just another run-of-the-mill 80s teen sex comedy. However, it's far more than that! Courtesy of the creative minds behind MAD Magazine, *Up the Academy* delivers a unique formula and style I've yet to see replicated by any of Hollywood's "funniest" productions since. The film is brimming with such delightfully infantile and corny humor, you'd be forgiven for thinking the writers themselves were 14-year-olds. If you appreciate a good dose of immaturity, this is a must-see. A true classic. *****

I bought this movie solely out of my profound admiration for Gackt and, even more so, Hyde. Initially, I anticipated a visually appealing, albeit somewhat clichéd, film, given its rather outlandish synopsis. However, having just finished watching it, I am compelled to declare its brilliance to the world.

Hyde and Gackt delivered truly heart-wrenching performances. My eyes still burn from the tears shed throughout the latter half of the movie. The story is utterly engrossing, fostering a deep empathy for the characters by its conclusion. The vampiric element, often mishandled in film, is subtly woven into the narrative, lending an exotic normalcy to the setting rather than feeling like an arbitrary addition.

I initially rated it 9 out of 10. Upon reflection, I struggled to find a reason to withhold that final point.

This film is truly exceptional. If you have the opportunity, you should eagerly seek it out. While it bears little resemblance to its 1932 predecessor, Al Pacino's portrayal of Tony Montana is masterful and captivating.

Pacino possesses a unique ability to imbue any line with profound impact and brilliance. If you appreciated the use of expletives in *Pulp Fiction*, then *Scarface* offers another compelling example of an actor's command over language. It is, in its own way, quite remarkable.

Despite its rapid pacing and disregard for strict chronological realism, the film remains surprisingly easy to follow, though it demands your complete attention to fully grasp every detail. Personally, I find that three hours fly by when watching this movie; it is simply that engaging.

This film stands as a testament to exceptional acting and direction, so much so that one forgets its original production year.

I stumbled upon "Act I" over a decade ago purely by chance, a discovery even the tape's cover didn't hint at. It captivated me, intimidated me, and shocked me. Though it faded from memory for nearly a decade, I eventually recalled it and purchased both acts, finding them even more compelling than my initial experience.

My only critique concerns the Tank Police: despite their constant claims of being at war with crime, justifying tanks and heavy artillery, they appear to have an easy time with criminals. This disconnect is either never shown or suggests their "state of war" is merely propaganda, a point never explicitly explored.

While I doubt the original Japanese version could match the Americanized one, some narrative nuances were likely lost in translation. However, this is forgivable.

Chris Rock leads this remake of *Heaven Can Wait* (a re-imagining of 1941's *Here Comes Mr. Jordan*), a comedy about an aspiring comedian whose untimely death leads to an unexpected journey in a new, albeit temporary, body. Unlike the Warren Beatty version, where the protagonist was a backup quarterback for the Los Angeles Rams, Rock's iteration features Lance Barton, a struggling and undeniably untalented stand-up.

The film cleverly showcases Rock's comedic brilliance by casting him as a terrible comedian. It's akin to Tom Hanks portraying a subpar actor. Lance's ambition is to perform at the legendary Apollo Theater on a non-amateur night, but his attempts inevitably result in raucous boos, earning him the nickname "Booie." His jokes are weak, his delivery agonizing—Lance is the antithesis of the real Chris Rock.

While working as a bike messenger, Lance is en route to test out new material when he's struck by a truck.

I received the first Bill & Ted movie for Christmas and was so captivated that I had to buy the sequel when I stumbled upon it in a store. This installment, in my opinion, matched the humor of the original, though it spun a significantly stranger tale. The depiction of their personal hell and their challenge to Death, particularly their choice of mundane games like Clue, was hilarious. My only minor critique would be Station and Death joining the band; otherwise, it was a fantastic film.

This film feels like a joke, and not a good one. It's impossible to believe it was made in 1993; the fashion and music scream 80s. I suspect it languished on a shelf for years before some desperate distributor unleashed it upon an unsuspecting world.

There's a plot, of sorts. A reclusive man encounters a bearded stranger who informs him that if he meditates while singing his favorite song, he can transform into anyone he wishes. His song of choice? "London Bridge Is Falling Down." This inexplicable preference, barely a minute into the film, sets the tone for the monumental stupidity that follows, and believe me, it gets worse.

The protagonist, whom I can only assume is "the nostril picker" from the title given two separate scenes of him engaging in the act, decides to transform into a woman to get closer to...

A masterful film from Powell and Pressburger, prompting me to delve deeper into their body of work. It provocatively blurs the lines between perception and reality, highlighting the challenge of distinguishing one from the other. Visually stunning and expertly performed, despite David Niven's unconvincing portrayal of a 27-year-old. It was also a treat to spot a youthful Richard Attenborough. This is a film that lingered in my thoughts long after the credits rolled.

Skip this movie if you're looking to understand quantum mechanics; a used textbook for $9 would be a far better investment. I'm concerned my money might be funding something akin to a Kool-Aid shipment to Guyana.

The filmmakers seemed to juggle multiple, often contradictory, themes without successfully conveying any. They appeared to touch on:

1.  Science as the ultimate arbiter of human behavior, implying determinism.
2.  The limitations of science in explaining human behavior, suggesting free will.
3.  The inherent coolness of science.
4.  A belief in human divinity.
5.  Solipsism.
6.  The perceived difficulty of following in Sarah Norman's footsteps.
7.  A thinly veiled suggestion to ingest a hallucinogen for an enhanced viewing experience.

This film embodies my worst cinematic fears. Its arrogant and irresponsible portrayal of the Colombian conflict is so clichéd and unintelligent that it's an affront to the entire Colombian populace. The performances are abysmal, from Grisales (whose nude scene is utterly lamentable) to Bejarano, and from Fanny Mickey (who appears to have stepped out of a Tim Burton nightmare) to Díaz. Díaz, despite his notable effort to imbue a one-dimensional, clichéd, and poorly written character with life, is left with little more than a mustache to work with. The gratuitous, cheesy gore-fest of an ending is so bad it would make Ed Wood wince. The film fails on every conceivable level: cinematography, art direction, costumes, makeup, editing, and most egregiously, directing. Jorge Alí Triana has always been a poor filmmaker, but his previous works at least possessed a modicum of dignity. I can find no redeeming qualities in this squandering of resources, save for the hope that Colombian filmmakers will learn a crucial lesson in honesty, integrity, and responsibility from this malevolent fiasco.

My introduction to this film was purely serendipitous. It was the winter of 1990 in Alaska, and an Australian friend was sharing our minuscule apartment. Alaskan winters can be harsh, driving most indoors to seek solace in heavy drinking and whatever television fare presented itself. I, however, stumbled upon this cinematic masterpiece in a snowbank outside a thrift store, instantly recognizing its hidden value. It's quite possibly the best bad movie ever made. For the next fortnight, we watched it incessantly, fueled by copious amounts of alcohol. We even found ourselves tilting or inverting the television for a more complete viewing experience. This film is a true diamond in the rough, promising endless laughter and lasting memories. Should you ever encounter it for rent, I implore you: liberate it. You won't be disappointed!

I initially expected *The Sentinel* to be a mediocre movie, but I was pleasantly surprised. While not a cinematic masterpiece, it's incredibly entertaining, boasting well-executed action sequences. The film brought to mind TV series like *24* or *Alias*, and even Wolfgang Petersen's thriller *In the Line of Fire*. If you're looking for an groundbreaking thriller, you'll likely be disappointed. However, go in with an open mind, and you'll find *The Sentinel* to be an enjoyable experience.

Rating: 7

If you're looking for "The Gamers" by Dead Gentlemen Productions, this isn't it. This film lacks humor and feels like a waste of time.

The positive reviews here appear to be disingenuous, likely crafted by individuals associated with the production, attempting to generate artificial interest.

As a mockumentary, it falls flat. Any comparison to works like "Spinal Tap" or those by Christopher Guest is unwarranted and misleading.

The film's mean-spirited tone makes it hard to imagine anyone familiar with the subject matter finding it amusing. While self-deprecating humor is valuable, those targeted by this lampooning would likely feel insulted rather than entertained.

Its offensiveness stems not from any grand, satirical tackling of taboo subjects, but from its pervasive and pathetic banality.

This is, without a doubt, one of my all-time favorite films. Its tightly crafted dialogue, brimming with relentless puns, is exceptional, the cast delivers superb performances, and the plot showcases remarkable originality.

But don't just take my word for it—experience this movie and discover its delights for yourself.

Despite a star-studded cast that could form its own galaxy, THE HOUSE OF SPIRITS ultimately proves to be a contentious film. While its noble messages—championing liberal democracy and open-mindedness over fascism and racism—are undeniably commendable and likely widely supported, the film relentlessly bludgeons the audience with them, exhibiting as much subtlety as my blunt summary.

The viewing experience devolves into watching flawless, virtuous characters confront irredeemable villains, creating a narrative as suspense-free as a poorly staged professional wrestling match.

The film shines brightest when focusing on its central figures: Jeremy Irons as the complex patriarch, Meryl Streep as his talented wife, and Glenn Close as her sister-in-law. Their interactions lend the movie momentum and appeal. However, THE HOUSE OF SPIRITS is burdened by an excessive number of subplots and a constantly shifting parade of characters who appear and disappear like targets in a shooting gallery. This prevents any meaningful connection with them, leading to audience disengagement and boredom.

This episode, the first regular filmed *Columbo* movie, paradoxically aired as the second, following Steven Spielberg's "Columbo: Murder by the Book." It nonetheless stands out as one of the series' stronger entries.

Director Bernard L. Kowalski's creative vision is palpable, explaining why he was tapped to helm three more *Columbo* films. His innovative shot sequences elevate this movie, imbuing it with a distinctive style, palpable passion, and meticulous attention to detail. Each frame contributes to a visual tapestry that surpasses the typical made-for-TV movie, solidifying its place among the best-directed *Columbo* installments.

This *Columbo* entry is particularly original for several reasons. The murder itself is presented as a spontaneous, almost accidental act, leaving the killer no opportunity for pre-planning a "perfect crime." Instead, the focus shifts to the killer's frantic efforts to eliminate evidence and dispose of the body. Furthermore, the killer is portrayed not merely as the perpetrator of the crime, but begins to take on the role of an unexpected ally.

A truly singular talent, Sandra Bernhard began her career as a stand-up comedian in the 1970s. Her breakthrough arrived in 1983 with her role alongside Jerry Lewis and Robert De Niro in Martin Scorsese's underappreciated gem, "The King of Comedy." While her film career didn't fully blossom, she did appear in memorable, if quirky, films like "Dallas Doll" (1994) and "Dinner Rush" (2000). Yet, it was the roles she crafted for herself that most showcased her unique genius.

Her magnum opus, "Without You I'm Nothing," a film adaptation of her wildly successful off-Broadway show, catapulted her to stardom and, for a time, made her Madonna's closest confidante. Through ten impeccably staged scenes, Sandra transforms from Nina Simone to Diana Ross, shares anecdotes from her childhood, discusses Andy Warhol and San Francisco, and delivers captivating renditions of songs by Burt Bacharach, Prince, and Sylvester. Director John Boskovich masterfully captures Bernhard's 90-minute tour-de-force performance, which is at once sensuous and hilariously original. This film is essential viewing for any Bernhard devotee, a testament to her unconventional beauty and extraordinarily distinctive artistry.

For a mere fifty cents at the flea market, I eagerly acquired this.

Initially captivating for about fifteen minutes, it quickly devolved into a repetitive and dull experience.

While it was interesting to see Mick and the band in their prime, the excessive dialogue overdubbing made it difficult to discern their conversations and music.

The skits, with their politically dated, naive, and simplistic humor, reminded me of a poorly conceived, acid-fueled Monty Python. I found myself more engrossed in the late 1960s English backdrops than in the silly skits themselves.

This film serves as a poignant reminder of how drastically times change, and how quickly once-significant content can become utterly nonsensical. Despite a good song, this DVD has played it to death.

Revisiting a cherished childhood film in its restored version has proven to be a surprisingly engaging, if at times perplexing, afternoon experience. The complete cut of *Bedknobs and Broomsticks* significantly enhances narrative coherence, with the reinserted scenes—particularly those featuring McDowall—seamlessly connecting plot points.

However, the remastering choices for these previously excised sequences are somewhat unsettling. It appears the original audio tracks were either lost or damaged, leading Disney to re-dub the footage with new dialogue. While this initiative had potential, its execution falters due to the unavailability of many original cast members (some for understandable reasons). The resulting quality is noticeably subpar; lip-syncing is frequently imprecise, and, most jarringly, David Tomlinson's character is voiced by an actor whose tone bears no resemblance to Tomlinson's—indeed, I detect a faint German accent.

Despite these audio shortcomings, the inclusion of the full-length songs (save for "Step in the Right Direction") is a welcome addition, and the film's inherent charm and magical essence remain undimmed. One cannot help but chuckle at young Paul's innocent gaze as he coos at Angela Lansbury and the ensemble.

This film isn't for me. As a man nearing 50, my entry into independent cinema was recent and accidental, sparked by a late-night TV viewing of "Clerks." Its technical amateurism was striking, yet equally so was its brilliant script. My interest in this film's director piqued when he cited "Clerks" as an influence in a local paper interview. When he then named "The Station Agent"—a film I'd just watched on DVD—as his primary inspiration, I knew I had to see it.

The experience echoed my "Clerks" discovery, despite vast differences in content. Both films, despite technical flaws, are elevated by exceptional writing. "Clerks" portrays a day in the life of a man stuck in inertia, avoiding self-reflection. "Less Like Me," in contrast, depicts a man who appears to deliberately cultivate constant busyness.

I went into this movie expecting a drama about a man with a supernatural gift, ostracized by society. What I got, however, was a delightful surprise.
