My friend and I found it incredibly romantic (the appealing lead actor certainly didn't hurt!), and it offered a compelling blend of plot development, action, and humor. A running gag about the characters not learning each other's names until the third act had the entire theater roaring with laughter. In short, it defied my expectations in the best possible way. I’ll definitely be pre-ordering the DVD.

Reportedly in gestation for years, this television reunion of two of sitcom history's most cherished characters began poorly and rapidly deteriorated. Mary Richards (Mary Tyler Moore) and her best friend Rhoda Morgenstern (Valerie Harper) reconnect in New York after a lengthy estrangement, catching up on their lives. A seemingly straightforward premise, yet sadly, neither character has experienced anything noteworthy enough to warrant a film adaptation in the intervening years. Consequently, the screenplay resorts to a parade of tired plot devices, largely centered around older women in the workplace, utterly failing to capture the original show's unique charm and sophistication. The supporting cast is instantly forgettable, the humor is absent, and the once-vibrant chemistry between Moore and Harper has vanished. Moore reportedly delayed this project for years, awaiting "just the right script." If this was her definition of "right," one can only imagine the quality of the scripts she rejected. The characters' age is not the issue here...

This isn't just a funny movie; it might be the funniest I've ever seen. Robert Harling's script is practically flawless—don't just read the quotes, rent the DVD. The delivery is what truly elevates the dialogue.

Sally Field delivers a comically over-the-top performance unlike anything she's done before, and Kevin Kline is effortlessly hilarious. Robert Downey, Jr. is brilliant as always, and Kathy Najimy, in a small role, is a riot as the beleaguered costumer. I wasn't previously a fan of Elisabeth Shue, but she's fantastic here as the sole grounded character amidst a cast of caricatures on the set of "The Sun Also Sets." Hemingway must be spinning in his grave—or perhaps he's laughing too hard.

Five stars. Hilarious.

This fantasy series, a follow-up to 'The Baron' from Monty Berman and Dennis Spooner, captivated me as a child and remains a favorite. It chronicled the adventures of three superhuman spies, predating 'The Six Million Dollar Man'. Stuart Damon and William Gaunt, as Craig Stirling and Richard Barrett, shared undeniable on-screen chemistry, complemented by Alexandra Bastedo's captivating portrayal of Sharron Macready. The late Anthony Nicholls was a wonderfully gruff Tremayne. The strongest episodes, arguably, were penned by Tony Williamson, Terry Nation, and Brian Clemens, with Spooner's own 'The Interrogation' holding its own against 'The Prisoner'. It's a shame a second series never materialized; the concept held such promise. One can only wonder: would Craig and Richard have vied for Sharron's affections? What if Tremayne had uncovered the full extent of the Champions' powers? Did they possess unrevealed abilities? These questions, sadly, remain unanswered.

This film presents an unusual love story. While not exceptional, Nicole Kidman's performance single-handedly elevates it, overshadowing the rest of the cast—though Ben Chaplin delivers a commendable portrayal of Hertfordshire life, with shots of St Albans and Hemel Hempstead town center capturing the area's authentic essence. What begins as seemingly an ordinary episode of the British TV series "Heartbeat" quickly transforms into a gritty gangster escape thriller. Though ultimately a small, unremarkable film, it serves as decent weekend entertainment. It's a worthwhile watch, particularly if you're a lonely thirty-something who might find kinship with the hero, John.

Everyone faces a moment when they must rise again, and for Jack Dundee (Robin Williams), an embarrassed Taft resident, that moment arrives in "The Best of Times." The actor, known for his energetic radio performance in "Good Morning, Vietnam," here tackles the football field. Dundee aims to re-stage a pivotal game that cost his high school a coveted title. However, his former teammate, Reno Hightower (Kurt Russell), isn't so quick to agree.

While perhaps not a career highlight for either star, Williams and Russell prove to be an effective comedic duo. The film also features some truly amusing character names that are sure to elicit a chuckle. It's worth a watch.

Steer clear of this film at all costs; it is, unequivocally, the worst I have ever encountered. While most movies possess at least one redeeming quality, this one is utterly devoid of any. A truly horrendous experience.

In a summer also plagued by cinematic misfires like *Snakes on a Plane* and *The Da Vinci Code*, my assertion might seem audacious. Yet, I stand firm: *Superman Returns*, much like *King Kong* six months prior, is excessively long, self-indulgent, and drowning in CGI. Frankly, it's maddening.

Richard Donner's vision for his *Superman* films prioritized realism, and I believe his pragmatic approach to special effects remains unsurpassed. Bryan Singer, however, overwhelms us with so much CGI that it shatters immersion, constantly reminding the viewer they're watching a wannabe blockbuster. This film seems to equate audience impressiveness solely with a $250 million budget (an utterly irresponsible sum), poured into ostentatious visual effects that fail to deliver. We've seen every trick CGI can offer and been to every digital landscape. There's no genuine atmosphere or engagement here. For a film composed almost entirely of such digital artifice, the conclusion is self-evident.

Many fanboy critics, however, claim the film possesses "soul."

Thirteen when I first saw it, I'm now rewatching this series on DVD, three decades later. The opening credits' imagery remains vivid, having shaped my worldview and perception of humanity. My parents, who watched it with me, fostered engaging discussions afterward. This program ignited my passion for history, leading to top marks in my school's public exams.

Sir Laurence Olivier's narration is timeless perfection. One senses that those who lived through WWII would recognize this as their defining historical account. I can't imagine ever tiring of it. Perhaps a similar Cold War series could be considered, though finding a successor to Sir Laurence is an insurmountable challenge.

Buy it!

Mario Lewis, writing for the Competitive Enterprise Institute, has produced a comprehensive 120-page refutation of the film, which he argues should be retitled "A Convenient Lie." His detailed report, "A Skeptic's Guide to An Inconvenient Truth," is available at www.cei.org. A concise 10-page version can be found at www.cei.org/pdf/5539.pdf. These analyses suggest that concerns over "global warming" are comparable to the discredited Y2K predictions, a scare also supported by Gore, along with the pseudoscientific film "The Day After Tomorrow," which was based on a book by Whitley Strieber. Lewis's work mirrors the critical debunking efforts of figures like James Randi on psychics, Philip Klass on UFOs, and Gerald Posner on JFK conspiracy theories, aiming to dismantle the claims presented in Gore's film and the broader "global warming" narrative.

Unjustly accused of his unfaithful wife's murder, Scott Henderson (Alan Curtis) finds himself in a dire predicament. The night of the killing, he was with a mysterious woman who vanished without a trace, refusing to disclose her identity. As the police investigate, witnesses at the locations they visited together recall only Henderson, alone. Sentenced to death, his devoted secretary (Ella Raines), driven by her love for him, embarks on a desperate quest to unmask the true killer.

Despite its origins as a B-film from Universal, featuring a cast primarily of character actors and a fading star in Franchot Tone, this low-budget production transcends its limitations to become one of the finest film noirs of the 1940s. Curt Siodmak's masterful direction and a superb script, adapted from William Irish's (Cornell Woolrich's) excellent novel, propel the narrative with remarkable speed and visual flair. A standout scene—the infamous jam session between Raines and Elisha Cook Jr.—pulsates with an incredible, palpable sexual energy, a surprising inclusion given the era's censorship.

Only a handful of minor imperfections mar its otherwise near-perfect execution, most notably a dreadful performance by Tone.

The critics who lauded this film must have a limited cinematic diet.

It's a perplexing piece, seemingly capturing a delusional man's home videos of his dysfunctional, idiotic "family," complete with a live "teabagging" scene. Enough said.

Spare yourself the wasted time. Any hope that it improves is utterly unfounded.

My anticipation for this Australian film was high, hoping our cinema had finally produced a gem. Unfortunately, I was mistaken.

This slasher film was a truly dismal effort. I commiserate with Molly Ringwald, who traveled all the way to Australia only to be associated with such a poor production.

The acting, particularly from the Australian actor attempting an American accent, was abysmal, and the plot was equally weak.

Initially, the film's title struck me as uninspired—a clear echo of the cheesy "Stab" from Scream 2. However, I was prepared to overlook it if the movie delivered.

WARNING!!! MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD!!!

The ending was arguably the film's biggest failing. I anticipated a shocking reveal concerning the killer's identity, but the twist—that the killer wasn't human—transformed what began as a seemingly realistic slasher into an unwatchable horror film.

Save yourself the disappointment; avoid this movie.

I own all three remakes of this plot, on VHS, and the DVD of this particular version. Each offers enough script variation to remain entertaining and re-watchable. I wonder if any other film has been remade three times with such consistently all-star casts. Beyond the excellent main stars in this one, the supporting actors are superb. William Tracy, as Pepi, is a particular standout; his scene-stealing performance led me to seek out his other films, though most are unfortunately unavailable. As others have said, this one is a must-buy.

If this film indeed had a $20 million budget, one is left to wonder about its allocation. The computer-generated imagery is remarkably poor, to the point where even a monkey might produce superior results. It spans three hours and is, regrettably, a cinematic misstep. Though, I concede, the depiction of machines and Martians might have been impressive on an original PlayStation 1 or early 1990s PC game, had such a title existed.

It's truly perplexing to consider the fate of that budget. Pendragon Films could have, with the same $20 million, crafted a compelling movie using traditional models and computer-controlled cameras, akin to George Lucas's techniques from 1975-1983. Furthermore, they could have cast actors who appeared to invest some effort into their roles, or at least into the film's demise.

This film is, in all likelihood, the worst ever made. I would willingly endure a 24-hour continuous screening of "Ishtar" rather than watch this again. My disdain for it is absolute. I assert this is the worst film ever made because, unlike other notoriously bad films such as "Plan 9 from Outer Space," "Attack of the Killer Tomatoes," or "Santa Claus Conquers the Martians," which often achieve a cult status for their sheer awfulness, this film occupies a unique and unenviable position.

Rated NR (would be R for pervasive strong language and crude sexual humor). Quebec Rating: 16+ (should be 13+). Canadian Home Video Rating: 18A.

Eddie Murphy's 1983 special, *Delirious*, marks his debut stand-up comedy routine. Released during a period when he was making waves in films like *48 Hrs.* and *Trading Places* and a regular on *Saturday Night Live*, *Delirious* is one of two stand-up comedy films he made, the other being *Raw*. While I personally found the subject matter in *Raw* more humorous, *Delirious* is undeniably funny. Murphy delves into his childhood and playfully lampoons celebrities like Mr. T and Michael Jackson. *Delirious* is a must-see for any fan of stand-up comedy films.

My intention was to watch a documentary about Puerto Rico, but the film primarily focused on Nuyoricans and their experiences. My own visits to Puerto Rico have presented a different picture than the one often portrayed, particularly regarding poverty; the struggling individuals I've encountered there have generally been recent arrivals from Haiti, the Dominican Republic, or Cuba.

I find the concept of "Spanglish" misguided. One either speaks Spanish or does not, and based on what I heard, the latter seems to be the case.

I do not view Pedro Albizu Campos in the same light as Martin Luther King Jr. While King was a truly great man, Campos's significance appears limited to the small fraction of the population who advocate for Puerto Rican independence, which I estimate to be around one percent. To the majority, his views might seem extreme. I believe that pursuing independence for Puerto Rico is an impractical idea. The socio-economic conditions in independent nations such as Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, and throughout South and Central America and Mexico, offer sufficient evidence of the challenges that can arise from such a path. This documentary, rather than exploring Puerto Rico itself, seemed to be centered on the struggles of Nuyoricans.

Regarding the comment about the lack of African representation in the show, the documentary's subject matter was Puerto Rico, not Africa. Perhaps Denzel Washington will produce a film on that topic soon.

Early color films are a delight. Who knew 1940s fashion wasn't all drab?

Margaret Rutherford is the undeniable star of this film. Her "eccentric" attire is surprisingly appealing, and she boasts an enviable hourglass figure. However, I believe she was given excessive creative license. Her characterization, likely honed over many performances, suffers from a lack of restraint; it feels as though no one dared tell her to cut a joke once it landed. This leads to an overabundance of manic antics, which clashes with the character's otherwise surprisingly grounded nature. The humor of Madame Arcati lies in the subversion of typical medium portrayals—usually delicate women in flowing gowns. Arcati, instead, behaves more like a no-nonsense retired headmistress, ready to tackle any challenge with gusto. Unfortunately, the film fails to fully exploit the comedic potential of this contrast between her breezy, commonplace demeanor and her outlandish beliefs.

It's tiresome how American viewers feel compelled to pepper their descriptions with "Brit," "stiff," "upper," and "lip" simply because the cast (apart from Cummings) is English. Despite this stereotype, the three main characters frequently lose their tempers and engage in surprisingly risqué banter, such as the memorable line: "Did he make love to you? Yes, but very discreetly—he was in the cavalry!"

A fantastic, yet often overlooked classic, *The League of Gentlemen* stands as one of the greatest modern comedies. Its dark, bizarre humor far surpasses the tired, formulaic approach of its inferior — though more widely recognized — successor, *Little Britain*. Truly special, it emerged during a relatively quiet period in British comedy.

Before its arrival, there was nothing quite like *The League of Gentlemen*. While seemingly a simple sketch show on the surface, it quickly unfurls into a vivid, sinister, and incredibly hilarious universe teeming with brilliant comedic creations. What truly distinguishes it from its rivals is its narrative approach. Rather than rehashed, indistinguishable sketches, each individual or group of characters embarks on unique journeys and storylines. Every return visit offers a fresh surprise.

Across three series and a Christmas special, the fictional town of Royston Vasey gradually becomes populated by a populace as grotesque as it is hilarious.

The film falters significantly in its final thirty minutes, a point many reviewers have noted. However, its struggles begin much earlier, plagued by a predictable plot and a remarkably uninspired performance from Kate Capshaw. Her inability to connect with her character detracts from every scene she inhabits. While Connery and Fishbourne deliver solid performances, the pervasive manipulation of scenes for dramatic effect over genuine emotion creates an pervasive sense of artificiality. The ending, in particular, is simply bizarre. It's as if the filmmakers, acutely aware of the cinematic "mess" they had created, tried to compensate with an overwhelmingly loud and "dramatic" score. Every minor scare is punctuated by a crescendo of orchestration, reaching a level of absurdity that borders on comedic. This film serves as a prime example of major league cinematic failure; otherwise, it's best avoided.

Ettore Scola stands as a pivotal figure in Italian cinema. My parents and I once watched his *C'eravamo tanto amati* on a summer evening; we enjoyed it, though not with the same fervor we held for *A Special Day*. I consider Scola somewhat underrated, perhaps overlooked due to the mixed reception of his later works. Thus, last night, my mother and I settled in to re-experience this masterpiece. The film's writing, direction, cinematography, score, and production design were all subtly precise, but what truly captivated me was the undeniable chemistry between Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni. Both deliver exceptional performances as Antonietta and Gabriele. Antonietta, a housewife with six children, is married to a zealous Fascist who desires another child to win a state prize for large families. Gabriele, in stark contrast, is an outspoken anti-Fascist. Their paths intersect on a singular day in 1938—the day Hitler visited Mussolini in Rome. I won't reveal more of the plot; this film is an absolute must-see.

"Like the first touch of pleasure and guilt, like a spontaneous youthful flirt of fascination and fear, like a climax of contrary emotions," effused one movie enthusiast after a screening of *LOVE AT THE TOP*, the mistranslated title of Michel Deville's stylish film, *LE MOUTON ENRAGE*.

Writing for *The New York Times* shortly after its 1974 premiere, Vincent Canby offered a contrasting view: "LOVE AT THE TOP, which opened yesterday at the 68th Street Playhouse, is a 1973 French comedy that dimly recalls a number of nineteen-fifties English comedies about the rise and rise of cynical young men possessing—and possessed by—ambition." He did note, however, a key distinction: *LOVE AT THE TOP* eschews the English class system. (January 27, 1975).

While individual critics offered their assessments, time has proven the true arbiter. Over three decades later, *LE MOUTON ENRAGE* stands out as a film where decadence appears innocent, liaisons are youthfully enthusiastic, and emotions are remarkably manipulative.

For Romy Schneider's admirers, it's hardly necessary to mention that this film...

This rather uninspired made-for-television movie, which premiered on TBS, features Antonio and Janine in pursuit of a killer computer virus, and not much else. Of particular interest to trivia enthusiasts, its debut coincided with the real-life "Melissa" virus's global emergence in email inboxes.

Some films are so bad they're good; this is decidedly not one of them. Though based on a true story, its fidelity to the original events was questionable at best. The acting was abysmal, the direction uninspired, and the pacing rushed—as if the filmmakers were eager to simply finish and move on.

Melissa Joan Hart, never a particularly acclaimed actress in my opinion, operates within the realm of low-budget productions. Here, as in many of her roles, she undermines her characterizations through excessive overacting and rapid-fire delivery, seemingly mistaking speed for dramatic intensity. Her performance consistently reminds the viewer of the film crew and camera, rather than drawing them into the character's experience. This undermines the entire production, eroding any potential merit it might have possessed.

Perhaps the only redeeming moment was the character's demise, though even that lacked a satisfying impact.

This film is an utter failure, a masterclass in cinematic ineptitude. It defies enjoyment, even for enthusiasts of B-movies. Spare yourself the invaluable time; this production is irredeemable. Its flaws are pervasive, encompassing poor acting, direction, and a truly abysmal script, all indicative of a fundamental misunderstanding of entertainment. Having acquired the DVD for a mere three dollars, I now regret the expense and would readily pay someone to relieve me of it. Its impact was so negative that destruction seems insufficient. As a connoisseur of B-movies—from killer toys to quirky lagoon monsters—I can confidently state that this offering falls far short. It doesn't even achieve the "so bad it's good" status; it's simply pathetic.

I stumbled upon this film by chance in the early 90s, with no idea what I was getting into. Many horror enthusiasts might have overlooked it, mistaking it for a standard prison drama, while others who did see it were perhaps disappointed because it defied their expectations. These factors likely contribute to its low rating, but I urge genre fans to disregard that and give it a watch.

It excels in every aspect, from its compelling script and pervasive atmosphere to its powerful acting and the chilling depiction of the prison itself.

This film is a true gem, one I still cherish on video to this day. Don't miss it.

Underrated and multi-layered, *52-Pick Up* boasts a complex yet coherent plot, elevated by career-defining performances from its cast. Ann-Margret, Roy Scheider, and John Glover deliver perfectly cast, deeply nuanced portrayals. Particularly striking are Vanity, whose unexpected talent hinted at a serious acting career, and Kelly Preston, whose character leaves a lasting impression. This film is a must-see for anyone seeking an action-packed, gritty, and intricate narrative.

I initially struggled to categorize the film: was it a documentary, propaganda, or dramatic piece? Given its production era, it likely blended all three.

While the dramatic arc was somewhat predictable, the film promised — and delivered — engaging scenes. The training regimens and equipment, in particular, appeared remarkably authentic.

The movie truly coalesced for me in its final act. The realism of these concluding scenes, at least as I perceived it, was unlike anything I'd frequently encountered. It drew me into the action, allowing me to imagine the thoughts of the young combatants. This compelling realism was, however, occasionally juxtaposed with the challenges of casting convincing Japanese soldiers, especially at a time when authentic Japanese actors might have been scarce.

Ultimately, the film serves as an excellent window into the American mindset of 1943, as the war with Japan raged. It also notably included a subtle jab at Japan, referencing past aid provided by the USA.

I rarely criticize films; I prefer to highlight their strengths rather than dwell on their weaknesses. However, this particular movie offered almost no redeeming qualities. One has to question the purpose of producing something of such low caliber.

Significant portions of the film feature close-ups of Anne's face as she breathes deeply, accompanied by melancholic violin music. The remaining scenes are plagued by poor, wooden acting. Rupert Penry-Jones delivers an entirely expressionless performance. Jennifer Higham, portraying Anne's younger sister, exhibits anachronistic mannerisms. Anne herself is depicted as consistently meek and self-effacing throughout the entire film, offering no discernible reason for Captain Wentworth's eventual affection.

Furthermore, the production utterly fails to capture the period setting, with numerous egregious errors. These include characters running out of a concert, kissing in the street, and strolling hatless through the streets—a scene inexplicably included, especially given its source material's romantic significance. In conclusion, this film is a deeply disappointing and altogether terrible viewing experience.

Al Pacino's delivery of the eulogy over the child's coffin is flawless, a performance so powerful it would overshadow even Shakespeare's Mark Antony.

The script's brilliance, whether attributed to Paul Schrader or Ken Lipper, deserves commendation. Its rich, intelligent dialogue makes the film a must-see for those who appreciate strong screenwriting. The narrative itself unfolds compellingly, maintaining its grip until the very end, save for the concluding voice-over.

Beyond the exceptional dialogue, the film offers little else of note. John Cusack, for one, has certainly delivered more impactful performances. It's also worth noting the film's distinctly male-centric perspective, with female characters relegated to the periphery.

**7/10 (Kids), 6/10 (Adults)**

This *Lion King* semi-sequel spins off Timon and Pumbaa, retelling the original story from their perspective, including their first meeting. While Disney's tendency for inferior sequels and TV series based on minor characters is often met with skepticism, this entry manages to rise above. Kids and fans will likely overlook any flaws, drawn in by the abundance of jokes, songs, and engaging elements. Its success lies in the enduring charm of its central characters, a brisk pace, clever in-jokes referencing the first film, and humor that appeals to older viewers. The animation, though less flamboyant than the original, remains high quality, reflecting the relaxed "Hakuna Matata" ethos of the plot.

The film's framing device sees Timon and Pumbaa watching the events of the first *Lion King*, frequently pausing to offer humorous commentary, much like a live audience. We learn of Timon's near-outcast status...

This summer, a glut of blockbusters and film revivals—some quite disappointing—left me longing for a movie I could simply enjoy.

For those who prefer a concise overview (no spoilers here): This film is more mature than *Ella Enchanted*, featuring some questionable violence, significant death, and a few bloody scenes, making it unsuitable for young children. Yet, it avoids being overly corny or exceeding its scope. Envision a slightly more serious, more magical *Princess Bride*, and you'll have a good idea.

-------------------------------------------------------------

I'm not the most frequent moviegoer, perhaps catching a film once or twice a month on an active streak. As a devoted Sci-Fi/Fantasy fan, I quickly tire of repetitive plots and films that prioritize spectacle over substance. This movie, however, proved to be a rare gem.

By August, my expectations for big-budget films were so fractured that I deliberately avoided *Bourne*.

Michael Stearns portrays Mike, a character grappling with sexual frustration and a peculiar moral compass concerning sexuality. He's comfortable observing nude dancers but is repulsed by consensual sex between men and women. Mike believes that women engaging in sexual acts forfeit their "innocence" and "beauty." This conviction drives him to stalk couples in the Hollywood Hills, observing them from afar before fatally shooting the men with a high-powered rifle.

The film's apparent main purpose is to showcase explicit sexual content repeatedly, with the plot feeling secondary. This approach will likely appeal to many heterosexual men, given the prolonged scenes of nudity and sex, which offer significant titillation. The voyeuristic element is amplified by Mike's use of a rifle scope, through which he observes couples for extended periods before acting. This unsettling dynamic is further emphasized by an intrusive, albeit atmospheric, musical score.

This movie is a plotless, 80-minute parade of deranged characters, whose activities are limited to drinking and delivering abysmal jokes. The soundtrack is unbearable, the humor falls flat, and the female characters are offensively portrayed as either "slutty idiots" or "total geeks." It strongly appears to be the product of a 14-year-old boy's imagination, one who equates coolness with binge drinking and believes women exist solely for male gratification, with any dissenting opinions relegated to "geek" status. Furthermore, beyond a few character names and a minor appearance by Mr. Levenstein, the movie bears no substantive connection to the original American Pie series. The sole redeeming quality lies in the attractive female cast. Save yourself the trouble and avoid this film; its 5.4 rating is misleadingly inflated, as it deserves no higher than a 2.

While trailers for this film might highlight scenes of violence or non-mainstream sexuality, these are mere fragments, strategically chosen to pique interest. The film's true message, however, runs deeper: it portrays individuals, constantly downtrodden in their professional and personal lives, who channel their frustrations into oppressing others—often women at the lowest rung of this power dynamic.

Experiencing a film as unflinching as *Hundstage* can be challenging, yet it pales in comparison to the harsh realities faced by those depicted.

Technically, the film echoes *Short Cuts* in its episodic structure, but distinguishes itself with a documentary-like approach. Its cast, resembling everyday neighbors, perform with raw authenticity, devoid of glamour or, most disturbingly, hope. This realistic portrayal amplifies the film's impact, forcing viewers to confront the existence of countless individuals living lives of quiet desperation, their struggles often hidden beneath society's polished veneer. It's a stark reminder that beneath the surface, industries like pornography thrive, domestic violence persists unreported, and hopes are routinely shattered. Many of us, myself included, know such individuals.

If you seek a film that offers no easy escapism, then...

"Shore Leave" stands as *Star Trek: The Original Series'* inaugural foray into lighthearted science fiction, a style later mastered with "The Trouble with Tribbles." It offered a welcome reprieve for both the Enterprise crew and its audience from the universe-ending stakes often seen in episodes like "The Corbomite Maneuver."

The Enterprise discovers a seemingly idyllic M-class planet, prompting an away team to investigate. Soon, a series of absurd and seemingly perilous events unfold, yet they appear to be manifestations of human emotional extremes within a bizarre blend of fantastic mystery (McCoy's journey through the looking glass), psychological thriller (Kirk's relentless stalker from his past), and romantic comedy (which speaks for itself).

As the least serialized installment in the *Star Trek* franchise, it's easy to overlook the abundance of high-stakes, potentially disastrous dramas in *TOS*' first season. Unlike subsequent series writers, the *TOS* production team was unafraid to boldly go where no television series had gone before.

Is *this* the Christmas movie HeidiJean saw? A "great" one? Hardly. It was a dull, bland, and utterly uninspired affair, devoid of any genuine imagination or heart. My enduring thought throughout was: who on earth cast Carly Pope in the lead? Her performance was shockingly devoid of personality, completely lackluster. Baransky, as always, was a standout, offering the only glimmer of interest in the entire production. One might even speculate her involvement was the sole reason this project ever saw the light of day. Perhaps my expectations for a Lifetime movie airing just over two weeks before Christmas are too high, but I couldn’t help but feel that with a different director and a recast JJ – with an actress capable of eliciting even a shred of sympathy – this could have been a charming little film.

The film opens with a voiceover, a creative choice I immediately found disappointing. Given the boundless possibilities available to filmmakers, relying on narration to establish setting and introduce characters struck me as a simplistic and ultimately betraying act. I believe voiceovers, particularly those that spell out location, time, or the inner thoughts of characters, undermine the very essence of visual storytelling. A director's true skill lies in conveying these elements through compelling imagery and action, not through expository dialogue.

Despite this inauspicious start, the film quickly blossoms into a striking and sustained cinematic experience. It meticulously portrays the lives of a middle-class family, individually and collectively, with remarkable realism. The director possesses a clear talent for capturing authentic slices of life. For instance, the seemingly unusual behavior of a father making private phone calls from the bathroom initially raises an eyebrow, yet it resonates with the often-unconventional realities of daily existence...

This film sets a new low. Its promising title belies the shocking lack of talent on screen; with a cast of 20, not a single actor manages a convincing performance. My wife, a discerning critic, wisely retreated to bed just twenty minutes in.

The film captivates, seamlessly weaving flashbacks of a bizarre childhood with chilling tales of serial murder. Its inherent plot—the very essence of its story—is entertaining. Director Bill Paxton masterfully leverages this compelling narrative, keeping viewers consistently engaged.

From start to finish, the film builds anticipation, its first-class creativity evident in every frame. It is an exquisitely crafted, rare gem, devoid of lulls as the narrative flows seamlessly and swiftly from scene to scene.

The film powerfully illustrates the extreme lengths to which disillusioned individuals can go, committing horrific acts against loved ones and perpetrating evil in the name of 'God.'

This show is, in my opinion, an abysmal failure. The humor is utterly flat; I grasp the punchlines perfectly well, but they simply aren't funny. The entire production is horrendous, and the fact that I understand it only compounds its terribleness. The sole redeeming character I recall from the entire series was a hobo in a single episode, but even that fleeting positive is overshadowed by the overall dreadful quality of the show. It's unequivocally unfunny.

I find the claim "only smart people get it" particularly irritating. If those who utter such a statement are truly intelligent, why do they resort to disparaging others they don't know, dismissing them as unintellectual? It's akin to asserting "the sky is red" without ever bothering to look outside.

Ultimately, this is the worst show I have ever witnessed. The jokes are consistently terrible, even when comprehensible. The protagonist's supposed "controversy" feels incredibly forced and uninspired. Furthermore, the reliance on crude humor involving bodily fluids, often delivered through painfully bad acting, is truly dumbfounding. I genuinely cannot fathom what "smart" viewers find appealing in this. To judge and dismiss others without any personal knowledge strikes me as anything but an intelligent observation.

While many new sitcom formats have emerged, the classic, multi-camera setup with a studio audience and indoor set remains the most effective. *That '70s Show* exemplifies this perfectly. When the show premiered, its cast, including Kurtwood Smith, Debra Jo Rupp, Topher Grace, and Ashton Kutcher, were relatively unknown. Grace and Kutcher, who brilliantly portrayed their adolescent characters, are both departing this year to pursue other ventures. I lament Topher's departure, as the show initially revolved around his character, Eric, and his close group of friends. Ashton, however, has become a modern-day John Travolta, echoing Travolta's romance with Diana Hyland with his relationship with Demi Moore. The unfamiliarity of the cast was a distinct advantage, as celebrity casting can often detract from a show's authenticity. I particularly miss Mo Gaffney as Don's girlfriend Joanne, and Lisa Robin Kelly as the original Laurie; her replacement simply couldn't capture the same essence. The casting of Tommy Chong as Steven Hyde's beloved, albeit perpetually stoned, father figure was inspired. And it was a joy to see Tanya Roberts on screen again, after her memorable role in *Charlie's Angels*.

This show earns a disappointing 2 out of 10. My significant letdown stems primarily from the poorly developed storyline; its fleeting incidents prevented any clear moral from emerging. While Brenda Song delivered a commendable performance, Shin Koyamada appeared to struggle with his role. Although I understand the desire to incorporate Western elements, the show sorely missed crucial Chinese cultural elements, particularly in its portrayal of the villain, whose robotic appearance clashed with traditional Chinese aesthetics. The most egregious flaw, however, was the inclusion of inaccurate and distorted facts.

Some might argue that, as a "kid's show," it shouldn't be held to high standards. Yet, other Disney productions like *Mulan* demonstrate superior storytelling and presentation. Ultimately, I believe Disney films warrant more thorough research and planning. A compelling show requires more than just a sequence of martial arts moves.

This film, a masterclass in captivating storytelling, defies the simplistic allure of car chases and romantic comedies. Its power lies in intelligent dialogue, a hallmark of director Rohmer, which meticulously details human reactions to crisis. Far from boring, every moment is riveting, thanks to authentic conversations between characters facing dire circumstances.

Rohmer's "talky" style, often a point of criticism, is in fact his greatest strength, a characteristic shared with literary giants like Shakespeare. Just as "Hamlet" thrives on its verbal exchanges, this film navigates complex themes and conflicting values through insightful discussion. It delves into the inherent tension between aristocracy and egalitarianism and explores the ultimate test of loyalty when old friendships are challenged.

While I don't want to be a killjoy, Brad Sykes has directed at least two of the most uninspired and clichéd films I've ever seen, including this one and *Camp Blood*.

The acting is abysmal, the print quality is dreadful, and the entire production screams, "seriously, you could do better yourself." Perhaps this film is a challenge to us all, encouraging us to flood YouTube with our own zombie-related amateur hour.

I purchased this for a mere pound, but it's important to remember that you can't put a price on 71 minutes of your life. You'd be wise to steer clear of this cinematic turkey, even if it's bargain-basement priced.

"Live each moment as if it's your last," they say. If that's true, then don't squander a single one on this film. While Nichole Hiltz offers some fleeting visual appeal, ultimately unfulfilled, David DeLuise's performance suggests he's better suited for television or commercials. The plot is flimsy, the dialogue abysmal, and as for "The Art of Revenge," there's no art to be found.

Having attended an advance screening today, and without strong prior affection for either Dane Cook or Steve Carell, I found myself pleasantly surprised by this film.

*Dan in Real Life* centers on a widower raising three daughters, who, during a family weekend getaway, encounters his dream woman at a bookstore, only to discover she is his brother's girlfriend.

The film boasts impressive production quality: the soundtrack, cinematography, and performances are all excellent, with Steve Carell's portrayal being particularly noteworthy. My primary reservation lies in the underdeveloped characters, specifically Dane Cook's. The dynamic between Dane and Steve's characters remains largely unexplored, which could have enriched the depiction of Dan's internal struggle over his feelings for his brother's girlfriend. Despite this, *Dan in Real Life* stands as a strong, endearing movie—a welcome change from the year's influx of horror and action films.

This film's sole redeeming quality is Lola Glaudini's striking presence, particularly her physique. It's a shame the production didn't fully utilize her, as a more daring role might have elevated an otherwise unremarkable viewing experience. While other actresses appear, none possess Glaudini's captivating allure. Armand Assante's appearance is notably aged, a stark contrast to his past roles.

"Consequence" is a quintessential B-movie. Despite a promising premise, the execution falters, suggesting a disconnect between creative ideas and their realization. The cinematography is notably poor, detracting significantly from the visual experience. Uninspired direction leads to a bland thriller, characterized by predictable twists and underutilized talent. Though Lola Glaudini delivers a commendable performance as a femme fatale, even her efforts can't salvage "Consequence" from its ultimate fate as forgettable, uninspired cinema.

I'm writing in response to Chris_m_grant's comment on "Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life," where he praised the 1924 documentary as a "fantastic" portrayal of "early 20th century geography of today's Iraq."

I want to express my gratitude to Chris, and to everyone interested in the Bakhtiari Nomads, the Zagros mountains, and the landscapes depicted in "Grass." The traditions you witnessed in the film have thrived for centuries and will continue as long as life itself endures. As a native of this region and a Bakhtiari myself, I deeply appreciate your engagement.

Chris, I apologize for any inconvenience, but I must clarify a point in your comment: the Bakhtiari region of Zardkuh is located in Iran, not Iraq. Iran and Iraq are distinct and separate nations. Mistaking an Iranian for an Iraqi is akin to mistaking an American for a Mexican.

Thank you,

Ziba

Someone needs to tell Shaq to stick to basketball. This movie wasn't even entertainingly bad; it was just bad. Shaq plays a genie living in a boombox – a truly "original" take on the lamp. He's tasked with helping a young boy, played by the equally annoying Francis Capra. The storyline was flimsier than *Waterworld*, the acting was abysmal, and I doubt anyone who actually enjoyed this film would ever admit it.

The visit to their children and grandchildren was strained. May and her husband found a disquieting unfamiliarity among the "kids" and grandchildren, a distinct lack of the expected warmth. The evening concluded abruptly when May's husband, after a pointed comment about his daughter's cooking, declared his sudden illness and insisted on returning home. He passed away that night.

Now a widow, May felt adrift. Her marriage, while lacking passion or excitement, had at least offered her purpose. She had been needed, and despite years of neglected personal desires, her days had been filled.

Overwhelmed by depression and a profound lack of motivation, May sought refuge with her daughter, Paula. Soon after her arrival, Paula unleashed a torrent of pent-up resentment, accusing May of a lifelong lack of emotional investment and nurturing. May appeared taken aback, even surprised, yet she seemed to lack the energy or inclination to truly address the accusations. Her defense, "I'm your mother and I love you," rang hollow.

While the original "Cube" had an intriguing premise, its unlikable characters and subpar acting always detracted from my enjoyment. Consequently, I wasn't particularly eager to see its sequel. However, news of a third installment, rumored to be a prequel, piqued my interest. I hoped it would rectify the flaws of its predecessor and introduce a compelling cast. My hopes, sadly, were misplaced.

"Cube Zero" begins promisingly, introducing two characters responsible for monitoring and maintaining the labyrinthine deathtrap. The filmmakers effectively establish a sense of mystery through the depiction of their daily routine. This raises numerous questions: why are people sent to the Cube, and what is the true nature of those who orchestrate the entire operation? These questions are left for the viewer to ponder. Despite some weak acting, the film's first half progresses relatively well.

As the narrative unfolds, one of the "watchers" begins to

Missing the film's opening might explain my strong dislike, though my extensive study of the Roman Republic's fall means I already knew the story—which, ironically, could also be why I disliked it.

The film's historical inaccuracies are numerous, almost comically so. They're so pervasive, it suggests a deliberate disregard for authenticity, which in a strange way, makes them almost forgivable. What's baffling are the sporadic, intense efforts at historical accuracy that ultimately sow confusion. For instance, Antonius' marriage to Octavia is introduced with much fanfare, only to be dismissed two scenes later, serving no plot purpose and without Octavia ever appearing. Similarly, the inconsistent use of "Marcus Antonius" and the anglicized "Mark Antony" is jarring.

Setting aside historical accuracy, the film still falters due to its leading lady. She portrays a character utterly devoid of dignity, instead coming across as hysterical, melodramatic, and completely unrestrained.

Greetings. I'm Paul Raddick, also known as Panic Attack, from WTAF, Channel 29 in Philadelphia. I'm here to discuss a truly dreadful film, *Going Overboard*, which, despite its abysmal quality, somehow launched Adam Sandler's career before quickly fading into obscurity.

*Going Overboard* centers on Sandler's character, an aspiring comedian who lands a gig on a cruise ship. My initial impression was that he simply failed, but the plot takes a bizarre turn. Sandler encounters women who supposedly enjoy films like *History of the World Part I* and *Rebound*. These women were intended to be engaged, but in a shocking twist, they are executed by Sawtooth, a cannibal of unparalleled viciousness. While *Going Overboard* was a critical low point for Sandler, he found greater success in films such as *Big Daddy*, *Billy Madison*, and, Jen Leone's personal favorite, *50 First Dates*—Drew Barrymore was undeniably captivating in that one. *Spanglish* is a vastly superior film; *Going Overboard* is utterly worthless. End of transmission.

transports viewers on one family's impossible odyssey, immersing them in every step of their arduous journey. With stunning performances and breathtaking cinematography, it achieves a heartbreaking realism. The film's final line, imbued with a poignant hope, resonates as one of the most powerful in recent memory.

Please, save yourselves the trouble and skip this film. It's a complete waste of time, utterly devoid of purpose, with a nonsensical plot and abysmal acting. I'd rather endure a beating than sit through it again.

This all-time favorite, a cornerstone of my childhood, remains as vivid in my memory today as if I had just seen it. Its groundbreaking, award-winning special effects were remarkable for their time. Miklos Rosza's iconic score, arguably the finest in cinematic history, perfectly complements the timeless adventure. Sabu shines as the Thief, while Conrad Veidt's portrayal of the grand villain is unforgettable. My copy is always close by, ready for another journey into its magic. And watch out—Rex Ingram's genie is still eager to escape!

**ELVIRA, MISTRESS OF THE DARK (1988)**

**Director:** James Signorelli

**Starring:** Cassandra Peterson, W. Morgan Sheppard, Daniel Greene, and Edie McClurg

**Plot:** After quitting her television show, Elvira (Cassandra Peterson) journeys to the small, devout town of Fallwell, Massachusetts, to claim her inheritance from a recently deceased aunt. Her grand plan is to leverage this newfound wealth to launch a Las Vegas show. However, her inheritance proves less glamorous than anticipated: a dilapidated house, a poodle, and a mysterious magic cookbook. While navigating the peculiarities of Fallwell, Elvira endeavors to earn money, invigorate the local teenagers, win the affection of a handsome local (Daniel Greene), evade being accused of witchcraft, and safeguard the cookbook from her sinister uncle (W. Morgan Sheppard), who harbors apocalyptic intentions for its power.

**Review:** My admiration for Cassandra Peterson and her iconic persona, Elvira, is immense. Peterson is a remarkably successful, beautiful, and witty woman, and her portrayal of Elvira amplifies these qualities with a morbid charm and a delightful, often naive, humor – not to mention a truly impressive bustline. This film effectively showcases her captivating allure.

A significant strength of the movie lies in its "fish out of water" premise. The stark contrast between Elvira, adorned in her signature low-cut black dress, and the conservative environment of Fallwell creates a comedic dynamic that is consistently entertaining.

This 1981 follow-up to Joe Dante's "The Howling," a standout in the sparse subgenre of quality werewolf films, unfortunately fails to live up to its predecessor. While sharing the "Howling" name, "Stirba" is a standalone story, entirely disconnected from the original's characters and plot.

The film centers on Stirba, portrayed by Sybil Danning, who leads a Transylvanian cult of predominantly female werewolves. Danning's character undergoes a curious transformation, shifting from an aged, shapely woman to a blonde bombshell with notable cleavage, her transformations intensifying with sexual arousal. Opposing her is Christopher Lee as Stefan Crosscoe, a seemingly weary occult investigator. He journeys to Stirba's domain with an American couple, whose friend fell victim to the werewolf cult.

For viewers seeking explicit gore and nudity, this film delivers. It features graphic depictions of violence, including exploding eyeballs and a particularly disturbing scene involving a impaled dwarf.

Evaluating films from the early sound era, including this one, presents a unique challenge, differing significantly from standard film commentary. There's an palpable sense of desperation as many silent film stars ventured into sound, fearing professional obsolescence—a fate that indeed befell some. Interestingly, Rin-Tin-Tin's performance remained effortlessly natural. Within this vaudevillian collection of disparate segments, certain moments shine, such as John Barrymore's memorable soliloquy from *Richard II*. Confidence on screen largely belonged to those with prior stage experience. Despite these observations, the film remains generally entertaining and is essential viewing for "film buffs" particularly interested in the silent-to-sound transition.

I had initially planned to see this film in theaters, but it was sold out. Instead, I ended up watching *Solaris*, which I consider the worst movie of 2002.

The plot centers on Victor Rosa (John Leguizamo), a tough "street pharmacist" who, after witnessing a shooting, decides to go straight. He invests all his money with Jack (Peter Sarsgaard). Their partnership seems promising until Jack vanishes with his girlfriend, Trish (Denise Richards), late in the film. This twist, however, was unfortunately revealed in the movie’s preview, robbing it of any potential impact.

Indeed, the film offers no surprises. Every plot point is telegraphed in the trailer, rendering the full movie redundant if you've seen even one preview. You could likely infer the entire plot by simply recalling the trailer. I recommend watching the preview online and saving yourself the cost of admission. The only unexpected element in the entire film is the truly dreadful soundtrack.

I can only imagine who was responsible for the music...

"The Cobweb" exemplifies films that, despite showcasing strong performances and notable moments, are ultimately hindered by convoluted plots and a lack of engaging elements. Richard Widmark stars as a doctor at a mental institution whose personal life unravels amidst family issues and a contrived, overblown conflict that feels utterly inconsequential.

The film's preposterous plot centers on the institution's need for new library drapes. A seemingly insignificant disagreement over whether an elderly patient's drapes should be used, or if patients should create their own, escalates into a ludicrous, unintentionally comical conflict that inexplicably endangers lives and fractures families. This trivial dispute more closely resembles a quarrel among young children.

The sheer implausibility of the plot raises significant questions about its logic, making one wonder if only a truly deluded individual could accept it. Despite this, the acting, beyond Widmark, is commendable, featuring a cast of other great performers.

Shaquille O'Neal's portrayal of the genie Kazaam was, to put it mildly, uninspired. His unconvincing rhymes and poorly delivered lines, coupled with a perplexing subplot involving a child's grief, made for a truly cringeworthy experience. The film suffered from a combination of subpar acting, questionable casting choices, and laughably bad special effects. It's difficult to imagine this cinematic endeavor recouping its production costs. Furthermore, the decision to house the genie within a boombox rather than a traditional lamp was as jarring as a sudden cramp, or as unappealing as a soggy food stamp. 

In essence, *Kazaam* is a perplexing cinematic misstep featuring a talentless, rhyming genie. Its abysmal special effects and convoluted plot only add to its notoriety. While it unequivocally belongs in the "so bad it's funny" category, it's perhaps best enjoyed once, with a group of friends, for a shared laugh at its expense. Do not, under any circumstances, anticipate a cinematic masterpiece.

The morning of their wedding anniversary, Dr. Alan Feinstone and his wife Brooke appear to have it all: a beautiful Los Angeles home, and Alan's thriving dental practice. Yet, beneath this veneer, their lives are crumbling. Alan's discovery of Brooke's affair with Matt, their pool cleaner, is compounded by the humiliation of finding out Matt is also involved with their neighbor, Paula Roberts. Adding to his woes, the IRS is hounding him over a substantial debt.

With his grip on reality slipping, Alan becomes convinced that everything around him, much like his patients' teeth, is decayed and rotten, and it's his duty to fix it. At work that morning, his simmering rage boils over. He deliberately injures a young patient, Jody, then sexually assaults April Reign, mistaking her for Brooke in a hallucination. He further inflicts an agonizing, unneeded procedure on another unsuspecting patient.

*How The Grinch Stole Christmas* immediately captivated me, becoming a beloved favorite from my initial viewing. Even after eight watches, its magic remains as potent as ever.

Screenwriters Jeffery Price and Peter S. Seaman, known for *Who Framed Roger Rabbit*, masterfully adapted the classic Grinch story for the big screen. Ron Howard's direction breathed life into the narrative, while Jim Carrey's characteristically vibrant portrayal of the Grinch truly stole the show.

While some critics argue the film deviates from the original story's spirit, I respectfully disagree. Having read the source material, I believe the movie faithfully conveys the enduring message of Christmas and its true meaning. In fact, it deepens the story's impact by personalizing it, revealing the very reasons behind the Grinch's transformation.

*MILD SPOILERS AHEAD* (These are unlikely to spoil your enjoyment, but if you prefer to experience a story with no prior knowledge, proceed with caution.)

The series was a commendable effort. While the storyline could benefit from some refinements, it was largely well-executed, particularly in Season 1. Season 2, however, veered into a "freak show" aesthetic, losing the original charm of *Dark Angel*. The first season's narrative, with its blend of lighthearted moments at Jam Pony and the focused, serious plot of Manticore pursuing the X-series, was more engaging. I, and many others, still eagerly await new seasons. I hope the teams at FOX and the *Dark Angel* production crew recognize the enduring demand for its return. Even two years post-cancellation, *Dark Angel* has the potential for a significant comeback if handled properly. I believe a talent like James Cameron would be ideally suited to spearhead this revival.

*Collusion Course* scrapes the bottom of the barrel, outdoing even the most cliché "evil white male corporate capitalist" flicks. It's an experience more grating than a persistent toothache. While Jay Leno, surprisingly capable in his understated debut *The Silverbears*, delivers a performance perfectly suited to his character's demands, here even his portrayal as a sanctimonious buffoon is less irritating than Morita's equally pious fool.

In this delightful Ealing Studios comedy, Alec Guinness stars as a mild-mannered yet determined chemist who invents a revolutionary fabric—one that never stains or degrades. This discovery, however, poses an existential threat to established industries. Joan Greenwood, with her captivating voice, plays his love interest, while Cecil Parker portrays her beleaguered father. Ernest Thesiger offers an amusing turn as a patriarch of the textile industry. Beyond its engaging narrative, the film provocatively explores the interplay of science, economics, and politics. It is skillfully directed by Alexander Mackendrick, who would later helm "The Ladykillers" and the iconic "Sweet Smell of Success" during the 1950s.

**How far can a once-venerated franchise fall in its desperate attempt to rekindle past glory?** *Star Trek: Human Folly* eagerly provides the answer.

For those who cherish the hallmarks of classic *Star Trek* – insightful storytelling, compelling characters, and meticulous design – this iteration is a profound disappointment. The writing is a chaotic jumble, character portrayals are flimsy, and the visual aesthetics are, frankly, abysmal.

If you appreciate strong, principled Starfleet captains and the unwavering ideals of the Federation, look elsewhere. Here, Starfleet is reduced to a mockery, with ensigns sporting inexplicable spiked hairstyles.

We are presented with a seemingly mentally diminished captain, while within minutes of the opening credits, Ensign Spikey is attempting to proposition an engineer. The decline only deepens from there. Even the uniforms are a chaotic mess – ill-fitting, with collars drooping, and a jarring mishmash of designs from various past series. The strict discipline and cherished traditions of the original *Star Trek* are utterly absent. The only redeeming quality, though a minor one, might be the graphics, which show some marginal improvement with each season. But even that is a fleeting consolation.

I'd readily re-rate this film an eight if Todd Sheets revealed it was a zombie genre parody. Picture a movie where every element—scene, dialogue, even acting—is a deliberate send-up. Frankly, I could scramble alphabet soup and craft a more coherent script. Two scenes, in particular, highlight the absurdity:

SPOILER ALERT: First, Mike's dad and another father *stroll* down a zombie-packed staircase. Despite brushing past flailing undead on this narrow stairway, they emerge untouched. At the bottom, the ex-marine casually remarks, "God, you're a horny bastard," and shoots just one zombie. Second, in the military complex, a girl stabs a zombie with a machete and is instantly encircled. The camera circles her for about forty seconds as she stands, surrounded, yet untouched by zombies just an arm's length away. She then nonchalantly exits the throng to rejoin the other survivors.

SPOILER ALERT OVER: These scenes simply must be...

Robert Wuhl, a multifaceted talent I've followed since his stand-up days and HBO's "Arli$$," is now imparting wisdom to film students at NYU. In his engaging class, he dissects historical inaccuracies and forgotten truths. Wuhl's teaching style is a captivating blend of examples and "show and tell," making complex topics accessible and entertaining. I was particularly struck by his revelation that Paul Revere wasn't the sole rider of his famous "Midnight Ride"—a fact apparently altered by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow for poetic effect. This show is not only highly entertaining but also incredibly insightful. Wuhl, a good actor and comedian, truly shines as an exceptional educator. I wholeheartedly recommend watching an episode; it's an incredibly worthwhile experience.

This film was a letdown. Chrissy, the protagonist, was introduced as a sullen, adrift young woman who did little to advance the plot. This led to a shift in focus towards her relatives, which was a missed opportunity given Chrissy's potential as an interesting character. The story itself was predictable and formulaic. One can only hope for a future where filmmakers like Campion, Jackson, and Tamahori deliver groundbreaking, inspiring cinematic narratives, rather than merely two hours of entertainment. On a technical note, the cinematography was quite unappealing.

Someone or something is leaving puncture marks on victims' jugulars, draining them of blood until dead. Police detective Karl Brettschneider (Melvyn Douglas, before moving to more prominent roles outside B-movie horror) is baffled by these notorious crimes. The village is gripped by hysteria, and Karl relies on his trusted medical genius, Dr. Otto von Niemann (Lionel Atwill, in another effective mad scientist role), for insights into the cause of these deaths. Karl also fears for the safety of his beloved Ruth (the lovely Fay Wray, who previously starred with Atwill in "Doctor X" and "The Mystery of the Wax Museum"), who works as Niemann's assistant.

Dwight Frye delivers a standout performance as a peculiar village eccentric who collects bats and exhibits an unsettling demeanor, making him an easy suspect amidst rising local paranoia. Maude Eburne provides comedic relief as a naive and easily influenced patient of von Niemann's. She imagines various ailments based on medical texts she reads near his laboratory, and von Niemann often humors her constant, fictional illnesses.

Having not seen the first film, and if it's anything like this one, I have no desire to. Hours after watching, I struggle to recall any specifics. From what I dimly remember, the main plot involved a group of highly irritating characters staying in a house with a dubious old woman, perhaps from *Friday the 13th*, while being stalked by a wooden, plank-like figure. Some people died, the film concluded, and I am now considering legal action against the seller for the irreplaceable time I lost. I'd pay someone a pound to take this film off my hands... but I've already pawned it off on a "friend."

The film is an utter failure, devoid of merit even for its niche audience. Only those with a specific interest in bondage might find it remotely engaging, as it offers nothing new or enjoyable for fans of Bettie Page.

Beyond the disastrous technical execution—atrocious screenplay, amateurish acting, nonexistent direction, and shoddy cinematography—the film's fundamental flaw lies in its portrayal of Bettie Page. The lead actress, a zaftig woman with only a superficial resemblance to Page, contributes nothing to the role beyond a willingness to be exploited. This performance, while seemingly beneficial to her own career, is a disservice to the legacy it attempts to represent.

I recently rented and watched this movie, initially expecting a typical story of a girl out to prove something. However, Diane's motivation for joining boxing was purely her own, which I found refreshing. Overall, I thought it was a good film, easily an 8/10. Any movie featuring Michelle Rodriguez is generally a win, even if her filmography isn't extensive.

This film exemplifies a growing issue: the perplexing imbalance between background noise, soundtrack, and dialogue levels. Why is the former dramatically louder than the latter? This isn't an isolated incident; it's a pervasive problem in modern cinema. For two years, I attributed it to my television, but a new TV revealed the same flaw: background noise, even seemingly distant sounds, overwhelms the dialogue.

The issue was particularly irksome in this film due to the female lead's constant mumbling in the English version. I half-expected Jean Reno to interject with a plea for clearer articulation. If you're watching on DVD and have a basic grasp of French, I highly recommend the French version with subtitles.

My rating of 4 stars is solely for Reno's excellent performance, reminiscent of his work in "Léon." While many praise the scenery, having lived in the Rockies, I found it unremarkable on a television screen.

The film opens at a deliberate pace, introducing Wallace Napalm, a man leading an unexciting life as an attendant at a photo-service drop-off. His wife is confined to their home, serving a sentence for arson that dictates she wear an ankle bracelet. Wallace, a dedicated member of the volunteer fire department, takes his firefighting responsibilities very seriously.

Wallace's mundane existence is abruptly disrupted by the arrival of a traveling carnival. Among its star performers is Wilder Napalm, Wallace's brother, a clown with a unique and powerful talent.

Both Wallace and Wilder share a rare ability: they are pyrokineticists, or "pyrotics," capable of igniting fires with their minds. Wallace carefully conceals his powers, while Wilder openly demonstrates his to those around him.

A crucial backstory, revealed later, explains some of their divergent paths: a childhood incident in which their uncontrolled powers inadvertently led to the death of a vagrant. This event shapes their present approaches: Wallace, burdened by guilt, suppresses his abilities, while Wilder, embracing his, yearns for national television exposure.

Further complicating their dynamic, Wilder covets Wallace's wife, a woman they both dated years prior. She becomes a significant point of contention, ultimately fueling the literal "firefight" between the estranged brothers.

The film offers an entertaining experience, though it doesn't...

As an American, though not from the South, I admit country music isn't my favorite, yet I can tolerate it. While I wouldn't don a cowboy hat, I do enjoy wearing hats. And despite not living in a trailer, I occasionally eat tuna salad and own a home. Why share these seemingly unrelated details? Because they challenge the notion that this film only appeals to "country" audiences.

This movie, at its heart, is a raw American love story, skillfully directed by James Bridges, exploring themes of love and loss. In an age of sensationalism and tell-all attitudes, its authenticity resonates more than ever.

The narrative follows Bud as he comes of age, moving to the city with his aunt and uncle to start a new life. He soon finds solace in the local honky-tonk scene, a common escape for blue-collar workers. There, he encounters Sissy, a woman from a similar background, and their relationship unfolds in a tumultuous whirlwind of passion and pain.

*Satan's Little Helper* stands out as one of the stronger B-horror films I've encountered, particularly in its narrative. The movie offers a fresh, unhackneyed plot, a welcome departure from the horror genre's usual clichés. However, it also raises several head-scratching questions that will likely occupy your thoughts throughout.

I first stumbled upon this film while browsing the horror section at HMV. Weary of formulaic Hollywood blockbusters, I was searching for something distinct. The cover art for *Satan's Little Helper* immediately grabbed my attention—its chilling imagery was undeniably captivating. Despite recognizing it as a direct-to-DVD release, I decided to take a chance; after enduring *Boogeyman* the night before, I figured it couldn't be any worse.

Upon watching, I found myself moderately satisfied. The plot was particularly compelling: the killer's chilling pretense of befriending the young boy, all while intending murder, was truly unsettling. In a disturbing, twisted way, the killer genuinely believed they would become partners, a morbid duo.

Branagh stands out for his grasp of the fundamental distinctions between cinema and theater. His *Hamlet* is perhaps the most faithful film adaptation of Shakespeare, yet it pulses with the energy of an action thriller. The indelible encounter between Hamlet and his father's ghost alone is unforgettable.

"Shower" is a cinematic gem, a simple yet profoundly moving film that delivers rich emotional rewards. Its narrative elegantly introduces the timeless clash between old and new, a theme skillfully established from the outset. This core concept is brought to life by a magnificent cast and their compelling characters.

At the heart of the story is Master Liu, the aging patriarch and proprietor of a traditional bathhouse, a symbol of China's pre-modern era. The serene atmosphere of the bathhouse, depicted in every scene, evokes a sense of tranquility and contentment that modern audiences, burdened by stress, can only envy. Even the most jaded viewer would be hard-pressed to find fault with this idyllic setting.

Equally compelling is Master Liu's mentally handicapped son, Er Ming, whose character forms a powerful dynamic with his modern, urban brother. The intricate and heartfelt interactions among these three, along with the diverse patrons of the bathhouse, create scenes brimming with an emotional depth rarely seen in cinema.

Despite its thought-provoking, regime-critical undertones, which led to censorship and limited distribution, "Shower" remains a film of remarkable impact.

While far from a cinematic masterpiece, this film possesses an undeniable, albeit unconventional, charm. It's a B-movie through and through, clearly unconcerned with typical Hollywood polish. The premise alone—a serial killer transforming into a murderous snowman after a toxic waste spill in winter—is inherently absurd and guaranteed to elicit laughs. Despite its overt silliness, the humor is effective, particularly in the delightfully over-the-top kill scenes. I wouldn't recommend a purchase, as I learned the hard way from an appealing cover, but if you stumble upon it on television and are in the mood for some unpretentious, ridiculous fun, it's worth a watch.

"Not a bad start, yet I initially mistook this for an original until I realized it was a 1976 King Kong remake clone. I saw this at nine, years before my first King Kong viewing at fifteen. Prepare for the film's funky disco, especially the Yetians' theme song, to invade your mind. Despite its abysmal creature effects, this film holds a special place as a B-movie holy grail.

Memorable lines include: "Take a tranquilizer and go to bed," and "Put the Yeti in your tank and you have Yeti power." I recall seeing it on Elvira's Movie Macabre. There's a scene that's a delightful inversion of King Kong: instead of climbing up with the girl, the creature descends to catch a falling woman. It reminds me of another 1977 Kong clone, Hong Kong's Mighty Peking Man. The film is packed with traveling matte shots and motorized body parts, guaranteeing a laugh. As I said, it’s just another."

It's disheartening how few viewers truly appreciate imaginative storytelling. This show's unique appeal lies in its creation of a hyper-reality. There's no need to dissect why Ned can revive the dead for precisely one minute. We've lost the childhood wonder found in whimsical tales like "A Wrinkle in Time."

This series stands out as refreshingly original, a stark contrast to the prevalent, overly explicit television that stifles wonder and imagination. It offers a welcome escape from the mundane.

My favorite aspect is the hyper-reality itself: the enchanting 1950s aesthetic, the endearing and unusual characters, and the fantastical settings that are clearly not meant to be realistic.

Unlike other shows that dwell on the morbid, this series masterfully masks the dark nature of death. While I enjoy many other programs, this one has quickly become my favorite, rekindling a much-needed sense of curiosity, imagination, and wonder in television. "Pushing Daisies" quickly rose to the top of my list.

I first saw this film years ago and was impressed, but then again, I was only twelve. Having recently re-watched it, I now wish I could reclaim that time. This movie is, frankly, terrible. While I admire Lee Majors, Chris Makepeace (I recommend *My Bodyguard* (1980) for a genuinely good film he was in, or *Meatballs* for laughs, also starring Bill Murray), and Burgess Meredith, their involvement in this project did nothing to advance their careers.

The plot follows Lee Majors' character, Franklyn Hart, an ex-race car driver who plans to drive his stored race car across the country to California. There's just one problem: the government has outlawed all private transportation. While the core concept isn't the worst I've encountered, its execution was an abject failure.

This film exemplifies how even genuinely funny jokes can be undermined. The trailers promised much, delivering laughs that the movie itself failed to replicate. It's perplexing because individual gags—like the spoofs on the smoking ban or "Jo Bole So"—are genuinely clever.

The film's ultimate failure likely stems from a combination of factors: perhaps the uninspired performances from the cast, the director's vision, or even the casting choices themselves. My advice? If you're utterly desperate for entertainment, give it a watch. Otherwise, save yourself the time and just seek out the much funnier promotional material.

P.S. The only redeeming qualities are Mahesh Manjrekar's performance and the amusing character of Chappu Bhai.

This film is a truly unpleasant experience, with Rick Baker's impressive, albeit stomach-churning, special effects being its sole redeeming quality. Much like other cinema from the 1970s, it leaves one with a lingering sense of grime, as if a long, cleansing shower is in order to scrub away the residue. The characters are uniformly unlikable, and the plot defies all logic.

***SPOILERS AHEAD***

In a malevolent twist reminiscent of a baseball "tinkers-to-Evers-to-Chance" double play, *Omen IV* resurrects the essence of the deceased Anti-Christ, Damien Thorn. This time, the evil manifests as Delia York, portrayed by Asia Vieira. Given to the "deserving" couple Karen and Gene York (Fay Grant and Michael Woods) by the Catholic Church's St. Francis orphanage, Delia immediately begins to sow terror.

Her reign of fear starts subtly: a scratch to her mother at a house party. Later, she narrowly escapes death from a runaway truck, only to be saved by a mysterious "Devil Dog" named Ryder. At school, Delia dispatches a bully by causing him to publicly wet himself. When his father threatens the Yorks with a lawsuit, Delia orchestrates his decapitation in a suspiciously self-induced traffic accident. Clearly, Delia is not someone to be trifled with.

Concurrently, Delia's adoptive father, Gene, rises to prominence, believing his election to Congress as a champion of clean air and green trees is his own independent achievement.

This story lacked a single original idea, brazenly pilfering themes from numerous sources like *The Ninth Gate*, John Carpenter's *In the Mouth of Madness*, and *The Ring*. It even stooped to replicate *The Ring's* iconic glowing circle, shamelessly using it as the film's namesake. Cody Carpenter's score was practically a direct lift from *Suspiria*. I preemptively dismiss any attempts to label these blatant appropriations as "homage," particularly given the on-screen reference to Argento's *Deep Red*. Such a defense would be a disingenuous cop-out for what amounts to bottom-tier filmmaking. The mere inclusion of gore and "disturbing" visuals does not elevate a horror film, a truth John Carpenter once understood. Perhaps he should retire or find a time machine.

Having seen this film at the Sundance Film Festival, I was profoundly moved by its immense power. It delves into the psychological impact on soldiers who join the military with the noble intention of serving their country, often with the expectation of governmental support in return. The film meticulously chronicles the psychological transformation that occurs during boot camp, as recruits are shaped into "killers for their country," and then explores the lingering effects of war upon their return home. It powerfully illustrates the profound impact of killing on the human psyche.

Unlike other films, this one respectfully honors soldiers, never criticizing them, but instead critiques a system ill-equipped to address the comprehensive physical and psychological needs of returning veterans.

This is a powerful, moving, emotional, and thought-provoking film. It serves as a compelling call to action, urging us to support our troops not merely through symbolic gestures, but by actively listening to their experiences and advocating for meaningful changes in their healthcare and well-being.

Vincenzo Natali's stylish direction, characterized by intriguing camera angles and effective close-ups, elevated this film. It was refreshing to see Jeremy Northam and Lucy Liu in leading roles, showcasing their expanded range as performers. The movie also featured one of the most imaginative "escape" scenes in recent memory. The combined efforts of the director and actors resulted in an effective thriller.

Despite its convoluted plotting, the film's narrative unfolded with remarkable clarity as it unveiled layers of corporate greed and skullduggery.

Unlike George Orwell's 1984, which envisioned a future dominated by a totalitarian state, this intriguing futuristic film posited that the corporate world, rather than the government, would be the primary force controlling and devaluing human labor.

I implore every horror and cult movie enthusiast to seek out this film. I did, and it is an exceptional experience: deeply atmospheric, unsettling, and genuinely frightening. It's astonishing what they achieved with such a minuscule — practically non-existent — budget.

The synopsis, from the film's website, reads: "One morning, an old man wanders out into the woods in search of his runaway cat. He finds instead a child without parents and a murder with no corpse..."

While IMDb lacks a trailer, I urge you to visit the film's official website at www.softfordigging.com. The trailer there is quite unsettling and well worth your time.

Initially, I found the Geico commercials somewhat clever and entertaining. However, my patience has worn thin. Is this truly the pinnacle of their creative endeavors? This show is abysmal, a sterile imitation that evokes the feeling of watching "The Office," albeit with characters in cavemen costumes – a comparison I make despite knowing "The Office" has a devoted following, though it personally leaves me cold. The predictable archetypes are all present: the beleaguered everyman, the pseudo-intellectual with barely a brain cell to rub together, and the dim-witted but eager-to-please character. Yet, this familiarity breeds contempt. I've encountered these personality types in real life, and they were just as insufferable then as they are now on screen. Why would I willingly sacrifice another segment of my precious week to endure more of these tired tropes? If you genuinely believe this constitutes entertainment, I urge you to reflect on your judgment.
