This film is a perplexing misstep, a cinematic endeavor so devoid of merit it makes the most cringe-inducing junior-high talent show skit seem like a compelling masterpiece. Only Will Ferrell's brief, wrestling-themed vignettes provide any discernible comedic value in an otherwise utterly abysmal experience.

The film tugs at your heartstrings, leaving you with a sense of tenderness rather than unease. As a fan of such movies, I thoroughly enjoyed it and rated it highly. The performances were exceptional, brimming with genuine emotion. Notably, the minimal violence was a refreshing change. It would have received a 9, had it not been for the ending salute. Overall, it's a commendable film with outstanding acting.

This film was a catastrophic misstep from conception to screen. While the cast delivered commendable performances, it's clear the writing team was the primary culprit. The premise—a rehashed "dance your way out of poverty" trope, much like *Step Up*—felt stale and devoid of any compelling narrative, leaving audiences with nothing to invest in. The casting of Canadian actors in what was clearly intended to be an American setting further detracted from immersion, causing the film to fall flat.

On a brighter note, the direction and cinematography were quite strong, suggesting a significant production budget was at their disposal. My hope is that this team will recognize their strengths and collaborate with experienced screenwriters in the future, allowing genuine storytelling to shine through their impressive technical work. The final product, unfortunately, was a resounding disappointment.

*Bruce Almighty* will sweep the Academy Awards with a record 14 Oscar wins, surpassing *Titanic* as the highest-grossing film of all time! Jim Carrey's fame will reach such a peak that he'll announce his presidential candidacy for the 2004 White House race. These grand fantasies, however, could only transpire if the filmmakers (Carrey included) possessed the powers of God.

That very premise is the paramount ingredient in Carrey's new laugh riot, *Bruce Almighty*. Carrey plays Bruce Nolan, a television reporter utterly obsessed with becoming the main anchor, so much so that he blames God entirely for his misfortunes. God, heavenly played by Morgan Freeman, grants Bruce the "Gift of God" (His powers) to challenge him: can Bruce do God's job any better? Obviously, Bruce gets "Carrey-ed" away with his newfound blissful faculties and uses them selfishly.

Carrey is back in his habitual almighty comedic form in *Bruce Almighty*. Jennifer Aniston was not "mis.pittiful" as Bruce's girlfriend. However, my premier kudos go to Director Tom Shadyac for not letting the dog out for #2, and showing us the most hilarious doggoned bathroom scene.

Undoubtedly, this is the most hilarious of the Curly Stooge shorts. Despite countless viewings, it consistently elicits laughter, thanks to its brilliant pantomime sequences—a masterclass in "musical comedy." Even those typically disinclined to the Stooges recall this particular short with great fondness.

Following the murder of Central City's mob boss, his partner-in-crime, Robert Armstrong (as "Doc" Rogers), takes drastic measures to preserve their criminal enterprise. He recruits the deceased mobster's unassuming son, Richard Cromwell (as Edward "Baby Face" Morgan), to take over the family business. The naive Cromwell is brought to the city and installed as president of his father's "Acme Protection Agency," a front for their illicit activities. While Cromwell innocently sells insurance, his "employees" operate an extortion racket. Cromwell soon falls for a client, Mary Carlisle (as Virginia Clark), and they find themselves in grave danger. *Baby Face Morgan* (1942), directed by Arthur Dreifuss and starring Richard Cromwell and Mary Carlisle, is a quick, light, and inoffensive crime drama, notable for catching its stars nearing the end of their once-promising film careers.

As an Elvis enthusiast, I struggle to comprehend the creation of this film. It stands, unequivocally, as the worst Elvis-related movie ever made—devoid of humor, nonsensical, and riddled with inaccuracies concerning the King. How could Elvis' grave be in a public park? A reference to "Suspicious Minds" in 1958? These are but a few glaring examples. While some cast members strive, Mike Starr delivers a particularly amusing performance (especially as an impersonator), and Tom Hanks' cameo is a pleasant surprise, the actor portraying young Elvis is utterly unconvincing. Ultimately, the movie offers little entertainment and grows progressively tedious. For a truly cheap, quirky, and hilarious Elvis-themed alternative, I wholeheartedly recommend "Bubba Ho-Tep" over this disaster.

I won't offer an in-depth critique of this film, acknowledging the many glowing reviews that precede mine. As a general admirer of Maria de Medeiros, I've long hesitated to voice a disparaging opinion—a year, in fact, has passed. Yet, each time I spot that DVD on my shelf, I feel an internal groan. While I defer to the film's many admirers, I feel compelled to issue a quiet warning to fellow cinephiles.

Put simply: the political upheaval depicted in this film mirrors a period of my own life, experienced through daily newspaper readings at my local Central European pub. Back then, I followed the news, but never quite grasped the full scope of what was unfolding. Reporters often maintained a non-partisan stance or leaned conservative, disapproving of any groups disrupting order or inciting rebellion. This was a time when other currents of unrest swept through Paris, Berlin, Prague, and various parts of the U.S.—issues I understood clearly then. However, whether a dictatorship or not...

For those unfamiliar with Jimmy Stewart's filmography, this represents one of his later, perhaps lesser-known, works. While it doesn't rank among his masterpieces, it's far from bad, serving as an enjoyable, if not particularly profound, diversion.

The plot centers on Kim Novak's character, a witch in New York City, who inexplicably casts a love spell on the unsuspecting Jimmy Stewart. However, a twist ensues as the initially cold and aloof Ms. Novak finds herself genuinely falling for Stewart – a definite breach of the witch's code.

The film presents a peculiar take on witchcraft. These witches are neither the malevolent, baby-sacrificing type nor the omnipotent variety. Their magic is often surprisingly limited and, at times, seemingly trivial (as demonstrated by Jack Lemmon's character using his powers to turn off street lamps). Furthermore, these magical practitioners are portrayed as bohemians, frequenting trendy bars filled with beret-wearing patrons and, inexplicably, "crappy jazz." Given my personal feelings about jazz, one can only imagine the plight of a witch in this cinematic world!

Despite these quirks, the film manages to be quite romantic.

I purchased this DVD for my brother, a devoted Michelle Pfeiffer fan, and decided to watch it myself earlier this week.

The film offers reasonable entertainment, though its two storylines are entirely disparate. Michelle Pfeiffer's segment proved significantly more engaging. She portrays an aspiring Hollywood actress with a history of brief, unfulfilling relationships. A literal collision, a fender-bender with Brian Kerwin (a seemingly ordinary, married family man), initiates their encounter. Initial hostility gives way to an unexpected connection when he offers her a ride home after the accident. A romance blossoms, inevitably leading to tragedy once his wife discovers their affair. The ending, while surprising, is unfortunately undermined by the film's slow pacing and conventional television direction, which strip the plot of any genuine drama.

The second storyline centers on an aging studio boss, played by Darren McGavin. This section boasts a stronger ensemble cast, including Kenneth McMillan, Lois Chiles, Steven Bauer, and Stella Stevens. Each character seeks something from the studio head, but upon his forced resignation, they collectively realize their career aspirations have been dashed.

Eddie Murphy's "Delirious" is an undeniably raunchy and provocative stand-up special. It pushes boundaries with its use of language and explicit humor, often prioritizing shock value over traditional comedic setups. While there are moments where Murphy's comedic genius shines through, the special frequently delves into highly offensive territory, relying heavily on obscenities and crude sexual jokes.

For those who appreciate Murphy's unapologetically audacious style, "Delirious" might be an entertaining watch. However, it's a far cry from the more structured and character-driven humor found in his film work. Personally, I found it difficult to connect with, and it has deterred me from seeking out his follow-up, "Eddie Murphy Raw." My preference leans towards his performances within the framework of a movie script, where his comedic talents are often more refined and accessible.

— Saturday, January 17, 1998

While I eagerly anticipated *Planet of the Apes*, it proved to be a profound disappointment. Though the settings and masks were commendable, they were the film's sole redeeming qualities. Every other element was profoundly irritating. Mark Wahlberg's performance was particularly egregious; he merely occupied space, appearing foolish, and the supporting cast fared little better.

However, the narrative was the film's greatest failing—utterly preposterous. A prime example: the apes lie unconscious, yet the humans inexplicably refrain from attacking, patiently waiting for their adversaries to recover. This is but one instance of the story’s pervasive idiocy, and detailing every flaw would be an exhaustive endeavor.

I'm a big fan of fan productions, seeing them as a way to extend beloved shows long after their official cancellations. *Star Trek: Voyages* and *Star Wars: Revelations* are prime examples of well-executed fan efforts. This inherent appreciation means I tend to be more forgiving of flaws I might otherwise criticize.

Now, regarding *ST: HF*, let's start with the positives. The cast's enthusiasm is palpable, contributing significantly to the show's believability. The visual effects are surprisingly decent for an independent production, avoiding any jarring missteps. The storylines, while not groundbreaking, are solid and benefit from ongoing arcs.

However, the production also has significant shortcomings. While it's understandable that they borrow *Star Trek* footage, sets, music, and effects, I find no justification for the extensive plagiarism of other sci-fi musical scores. Nearly every sci-fi film, from *Aliens* to *Starship Troopers*, seems to have had its orchestral themes lifted at some point.

I just watched a fantastic mystery film on TV that kept me on the edge of my seat until the very end. Sean Connery's performance was, as expected, superb. I'd highly recommend it to anyone who appreciates a well-crafted whodunit.

The film's soundtrack is as uninspired as the movie itself. While not the absolute worst gay film I've encountered, it languishes near the bottom.

Its pacing is relentlessly sluggish. The plot, though not inherently flawed, suffers from predictable turns and could have been far more engaging with a stronger script. Every narrative beat is telegraphed well in advance. The dialogue is insipid, the humor stale, and the characters are an unfortunate collection of one-dimensional, stereotypical gay portrayals.

I found neither the central premise nor the lead couple's relationship remotely believable. There's a glaring absence of chemistry and dynamic between them; their purported love is simply stated, never demonstrated. Given their lack of commonality and sexual incompatibility, their connection remains a mystery—unless sharing an appreciation for the same book somehow suffices.

The acting isn't entirely without merit, but the excruciatingly slow pace is a significant detriment. It approaches Jarmusch-ian slowness, yet lacks any of Jarmusch's artistic merit.

This series introduced me to Deighton's work and the genre at a young age, and I appreciate this adaptation. However, I must respectfully disagree with the preceding comment. My understanding is that Deighton's reluctance to release the series stemmed not from Holm's performance, but from the significant liberties taken with all three books during their screen adaptation. A prime example is the reimagining of the border crossing that ended Samson's field career. This scene is absent from the book, the character who perishes in the minefield is entirely new, and the crossing in *Sinker* was from East to West Germany, not the Polish frontier. This entire storyline is fabricated. Similarly, alterations in *Set* compromise the narrative's integrity.

Regarding Holm's performance, I found his portrayal of Samson's disorientation during his wife's defection to be excellent. He also admirably conveyed the aging field agent's desperate attempts to bridge the class divide. Samson's life is shaped by, and he ultimately pays for, his father's idealism. As Clevemore remarks, had he pursued an education...

Jean Harlow, to me, embodied true star quality. While I don't find her films consistently strong, nor do I consider her a particularly skilled actress, she truly shone in comedies. Her comedic timing in *The Girl from Missouri*, for example, is exceptional, even if the film primarily functions as a love story. Her performance in that movie is captivating, to the point where the rest of the cast feels unremarkable. It's always striking to consider that Harlow's radiant beauty on screen, especially in this film, concealed a sickly body.

We've all been there: settled into the seemingly perfect cinema seat, a spot meticulously chosen for optimal viewing, only to find ourselves an eternity later—what feels like 13 hours—squirming, itching, and silently screaming, "When will this film finally end?!" (Think *A.I.* or *The Village*).

*Visitor Q* evokes a similar, yet uniquely discomfiting, sensation. The first 30 minutes felt like an exercise in cinematic purgatory, leaving me wondering when the actual movie would begin. It's an interminable, almost painfully "arty" experience. As my introduction to Miike Takashi's prolific work, I can only hope his other films aren't similarly self-indulgent. If they are, this will undoubtedly be my last.

While I appreciate certain forms of challenging cinema—David Lynch, for instance, holds a high place in my esteem—*Visitor Q* felt like a cheap, nasty imitation of pretense.

As you might infer, I thoroughly disliked it.

Undoubtedly an improvement over *Death Tunnel*. The film offered some inventive deaths and satisfying gore, reminiscent of *Wrong Turn* blended with *The Hills Have Eyes*.

However, several aspects were problematic:

1.  During the kitchen scene, Shae's lines—particularly those about big-breasted girls—were strikingly similar to direct quotes from *Scream* (1996).
2.  Steve's character felt like a thinly veiled imitation of Randy from *Scream*.
3.  Beyond a mere October setting, the connection to Samhain remained unclear and felt gratuitous. I often find it amusing in 80s horror films how loose ends are conveniently tied up by blaming druids or pentagrams.
4.  A Sam Raimi reference was a pleasant surprise.
5.  Gary and his sister's inclusion was perplexing; their characters served no discernible purpose. Furthermore, for someone so psychic, Gary's failure to foresee his own demise strains credulity.
6.  Finally, during Gary's bathroom death scene (at which point the fatalities devolved into Troma-esque absurdity), it's implausible that his sister could hear his screams from downstairs.

Goldie Hawn, a native of Takoma Park, Maryland, stars in this film, which echoes the spirit of *Mr. Smith Goes to Washington*. I recorded it years ago, largely due to my admiration for Hawn. While the premise—a cocktail waitress securing a significant government position after saving a prominent figure—is highly improbable, the story is engaging. The film evoked both laughter and frustration. Its absurdity, particularly in the scenarios Hawn's character navigates, was genuinely amusing. However, the notion of the government so shamelessly exploiting an ordinary citizen, as depicted, was infuriating. Despite this, her concluding speech was truly inspiring, a testament to courage rarely seen.

This film evokes the low-budget "erotic thrillers" that populated late-night Cinemax during my pre-teen years. It registers as "softer-core," primarily due to the absence of simulated sex. However, nudity abounds: the opening is set in a strip club, we get a glimpse of Kane Hodder's backside (or a stunt double's), followed by an inexplicable ten-minute lesbian dance sequence mid-film, and finally, a nude female werewolf whose appearance suggests she pilfered a costume from *The Munsters*. One can practically hear the cheers of thirteen-year-old boys.

Beyond that, the werewolf transformation sequences feature some of the most abysmal CGI in recent memory, akin to the quality of full-motion video from early *Resident Evil* games. The werewolf itself is poorly conceived, and despite the subpar quality of the suit, it's overused.

The plot and acting are equally nonsensical. There's a convoluted backstory involving werewolves and "hybrid-werewolves," with the "Darkwolf" belonging to the latter category. Yet, from what I could discern, these hybrids behave identically to regular werewolves: they appear human, transform into wolves, and kill people.

This film is a spectacular failure. Beyond the laughable CGI gore, its true shortcomings lie in the abysmal acting, nonexistent atmosphere, and directionless plot.

The narrative is dreadful, particularly the main character's absurd arc. His rapid descent into a haunted, weepy mess after a few nights of stalking Vinnie Jones strain credulity; are all New York photographers so childish and weak? His character development is completely unearned, culminating in a ludicrously predictable, yet utterly absurd, twist that elicits more laughter than shock.

The attempts at gore are a transparent, self-conscious grab for the modern MTV aesthetic. Composed entirely of CGI blood with no emotional impact, these scenes are unintentionally comical and distracting in their self-awareness, complete with gratuitous wacky camera angles.

Ultimately, this film squanders a promising concept. What could have been atmospheric (until the nonsensical monsters appear) is sacrificed for self-indulgent, "look at me" directing. This film wasn't made for an audience; it was a testament to cinematic self-sabotage.

Beyond its superb direction, production, acting, and predictable drama, the film's script delivers a profound message: "Listening leads all the way." It posits that listening is fundamental — for a voice to flourish, for harmonious collaboration, for self-discovery, and for understanding the needs of any situation or others. The script writers seem to unveil a vital "life's secret": listening fosters self-awareness, awakens other senses (especially vision), broadens horizons, and can even lead to the discovery of one's soul. The artistry of "As It Is in Heaven" beautifully illustrates life's unfolding, encompassing its joys, sorrows, and ultimately, its hope. This profound insight is powerfully conveyed through the leading character's initial instruction to the choir: "Just Listen, it leads all the way."

"The Return of Chandu" stands out for its unconventional casting of Bela Lugosi as the hero, a departure from his typical villainous roles. He even ends up with the leading lady.

The plot revolves around the Black Magic Cult of Ubasti, who seek to capture the last Egyptian princess, Nadji (played by the captivating Maria Alba), to sacrifice her and resurrect their ancient leader, who bears a striking resemblance to Nadji. Lugosi, as the magically-powered Chandu, endeavors to thwart their nefarious plans.

Director Ray Taylor skillfully navigates limited resources and extensive stock footage. Viewers may recognize the colossal doors from "King Kong" (1933), repurposed here to restrain the titular ape. While the acting is largely subpar, the high priest ( Lucein Prival) exemplifies the affected, over-enunciated delivery common in early sound films. The performances of the remaining cast are best left unmentioned.

It remains a puzzle why Lugosi opted for roles in independent quickies at this juncture of his career, especially given his continued star power at Universal.

I'm left wondering if this film had a coherent purpose.

For a movie touted as "rebellious" and "controversial," Maddox's distributed materials are surprisingly insipid. The students are inexplicably swayed by vague anti-authoritarian platitudes and illegible scribbles on leaflets. "Rebel, everyone," indeed.

Perhaps it's too much to expect a teen rebellion film to omit the obligatory school fire alarm scene.

Apparently, a "huge fight up on the football fields" translates to a skirmish involving two individuals.

Character personalities are jarringly inconsistent. The football jock Maddox fought and stapled in the face is inexplicably cordial and apologetic the following day.

The lack of a meaningful plot resolution suggests this entire production could have been condensed into a half-hour after-school special, especially with the removal of most of the pseudo-glitch soundtrack.

*Private Lessons II* stands as the pinnacle of cinematic achievement in my viewing experience. This Japanese import, despite a notoriously poor English translation, offers an unparalleled viewing pleasure. Its narrative often defies logic, yet this only enhances its charm. It's a comedic masterpiece, remarkable for achieving its humor entirely unintentionally.

This rare film remains unavailable on home video, though I've been fortunate enough to catch late-night showings on premium cable on a few occasions. My treasured taped copy has endured countless viewings, as I assiduously introduce this hidden gem to new audiences, one person at a time.

Joanna Pacula portrays Ken's tutor and lover, a role she seemingly undertook purely for financial gain. Ken, our protagonist, is brought to life by Goro Inagaki of the Japanese pop group SMAP, who delivers an earnest performance and maintains impeccably coiffed hair throughout. Stacy Edwards, known for *In the Company of Men*, also appears in the film and likely found solace in subsequent film roles.

Unraveling the plot of *Private Lessons II* typically requires at least three viewings. Subsequent rewatches reveal delightful nuances, such as the astounding number of vases—at least 50—adorning Ken's home.

"I truly hope the person who hailed 'Dream Machine' as one of Corey Haim's best and 'the movie of the century' was being sarcastic. My own sarcasm, however, might have gone unnoticed. 

'The Dream Machine' sadly set the tone for a series of mediocre films that would characterize much of Corey Haim's career, with the notable exception of the surprisingly decent 'Prayer of the Rollerboys.' In this film, Haim plays Bernie, a laid-back college student convinced a cool car will win over his dream girl. Conveniently, a wealthy woman, seeking revenge on her unfaithful husband, impulsively gifts her loyal piano tuner—Bernie—a sleek Porsche Turbo. Unbeknownst to her, and unfortunately for Bernie, her deceased husband's body is hidden in the trunk. Fortunately for the plot, bodies in this film don't seem to decompose or emit any odor, so Bernie remains blissfully unaware. He also completely misses the numerous suspicious events unfolding around him, particularly the persistent, grizzly man trailing him, desperate to retrieve the body unnoticed.

This film is, at best, a low-grade action fizzle."

I'm generally not a fan of Westerns, having never watched one from start to finish. So, I challenged myself to watch "My Darling Clementine" all the way through, anticipating a painful experience. Initially, it was as excruciating as expected: the acting seemed laughable, the desert scenery with its horses and cowboys was boring, and the music felt awkwardly timed, almost painful.

However, after a mental pep talk, I persevered. Roughly twenty minutes in, it became more tolerable. I began to appreciate the cinematography, noting how John Ford could elevate even the most mundane scenes (in my opinion) into something visually striking.

Ultimately, I can't claim to have enjoyed the film. Yet, its quality was sufficient to hold my attention to the very end, and that, in itself, is impressive.

This film, starring Eva Longoria and Paul Rudd, delves into the humorous haunting of a new girlfriend by her deceased predecessor. Fans may recognize Longoria as Gabrielle from Desperate Housewives and Rudd from his memorable role as the "Sex Panther cologne" enthusiast in Anchorman. While not vying for Golden Globe nominations, the movie offers a delightful ninety-minute escape for those willing to embrace its comedic premise. The ensemble cast delivers consistently funny performances, with a particularly strong dynamic between Paul Rudd and Lake Bell. Rudd channels the charm and wit he exhibited in Friends, while Bell captivates with both her humor and presence. My wife and I thoroughly enjoyed the experience.

Famous Studios cartoons were renowned for their signature tension-and-release style, wherein a secondary character faced dire peril, only to be saved by the hero at the eleventh hour. This particular Casper cartoon stands out as the sole instance I recall where death itself intervenes, yet still culminates in a happy ending.

A recurring theme in Famous Studios' productions is the triumph of virtue. Popeye invariably consumes his spinach just in time, Baby Huey consistently outsmarts the fox, and Little Audrey reliably learns her lesson. While some Famous Studios cartoons delve into darker, more somber themes, their overall quality is undeniable.

Paramount deserves commendation; even with my affection for Looney Tunes and Tom and Jerry, I believe no other studio produced superior animated content during that era. Their cartoons consistently showcased exceptional color, animation, music—thanks to the brilliant Winston Sharples—editing, and voice acting. They represented the pinnacle of the art form.

In an era of digital fabrication, the irreplaceable human element of acting and writing shines through in films that prioritize character-driven narratives, a rarity in today's cinematic landscape. This film, featuring outstanding performances from Duvall and James Earl Jones, fully lives up to high audience expectations. Its intimate, "close-up" narrative quality suggests a television movie, yet its impact transcends the small screen. The exceptional acting elevates the film, making its lack of masterful cinematography a minor flaw; indeed, visual grandeur is not always paramount. One wonders how talents like Jones and Duvall continue to deliver such profound work when many actors are reduced to mere digital models.

This is a beautiful and haunting film, particularly recommended for fans of equestrian cinema, WWII dramas, and the stark beauty of the Hungarian Plateau. It's a powerful story of courage, compassion, and loyalty that resonates across generations. The horsemanship is stunning, particularly the captivating training sequences involving the main character's horse.

I highly recommend this as a family film and plan to buy it for repeat viewings. While there are some violent scenes, they are a stark portrayal of the Nazi occupation of Hungary. The resilience of the native people is compelling, as they bravely stand their ground even against a Nazi officer with a personal vendetta.

"Things were simply better in the past, and children's television is a prime example. *Fraggle Rock* effortlessly proves my point. As a fourteen-year-old, I'm still captivated by its charm.

For those unfamiliar (have you been living under a rock?), *Fraggle Rock* centers on the Fraggles, a group of playful, goofy creatures living in a magical rock. But they're not alone. The rock also hosts industrious Doozers and countless sentient plants. Outside, one side is home to the inventor Doc and his dog Sprocket (who later befriends Gobo Fraggle), while on the other resides a family of Gorgs, who fancy themselves rulers of the universe.

The five main Fraggles—Gobo (the fearless leader), Mokey (artistic and serene), Wembley (indecisive and Gobo's friend), Boober (a pessimistic domestic god), and Red (sporty and feisty)—find themselves in peculiar situations each episode, all while singing and dancing their worries away.

*Fraggle Rock* is undoubtedly a family show. While infants might miss the intricate plot details, the musical numbers..."

I'm baffled by the negative reviews for this film. While it's a classic boy-meets-girl romance, its exceptional flair and polish make the time fly by. Henstridge is as captivating and alluring as ever, proving that the golden age of cinema is far from over, and Vartan delivers a strong performance.

The chemistry between the leads is palpable; the film truly comes alive whenever they share the screen, which is often. Their dynamic is so well-executed that you can't help but root for them to end up together.

Disregard the naysayers—if you're feeling down, this movie is sure to lift your spirits. If you're already happy, it will leave you euphoric.

George Gershwin's 1928 orchestral piece, "An American in Paris," culminates in a dazzling seventeen-minute dance sequence—an undisputed masterwork. Gene Kelly's precise and uniquely stylish choreography, combined with vibrant color, music, and dance, remains strikingly impressive. The sequence unfolds through scenes inspired by renowned artists: Dufy for the opening Place de la Concorde, Manet in the flower market, Utrillo on a Parisian street, Rousseau at the fair, Vincent Van Gogh in the spectacular Place de l'Opera, and Toulouse-Lautrec at the Moulin Rouge, where Kelly dons his iconic white bodysuit. While the preceding 97 minutes of this 1951 Oscar-winning musical are considerably less thrilling, the full viewing experience offers its own charms.

Director Vincente Minnelli and screenwriter Alan Jay Lerner crafted a surprisingly sophisticated, if somewhat insubstantial, romantic narrative centered on Jerry Mulligan, a former G.I. who stays in Paris post-WWII to pursue painting. Gene Kelly, with his boastful demeanor and athletic dance style, can be a polarizing screen presence—both endearing and vexing—yet he seemingly finds his stride here.

At a concise yet fulfilling runtime, *Cat Soup* offers a truly bizarre viewing experience. I stumbled upon it while browsing the anime section of my On-Demand service and, on a whim, decided to watch. For its duration, I was utterly transfixed, my jaw agape. My mind oscillated between complete blankness and fleeting urges to "TURN IT OFF!!!" Yet, I persisted, and I'm genuinely glad I did.

The animation is breathtakingly artistic, peculiar, and dark. While its striking visuals were a primary draw for me, the seemingly elusive narrative proved equally captivating.

The story follows a young boy—or rather, a cat—on a quest to retrieve his sister's soul. Initially, we see her ill in bed, visited by a grim reaper figure. Her soul is then split, with the cat boy recovering one half but losing the other.

Frankly, much of the remaining film blurs in my memory. I recall them returning to a world that seemed to be...perhaps slowly unraveling? It's possible her missing soul is the cause, as the rest of the film hints at...

This film was a profound disappointment. I engaged with it purely for amusement, never anticipating the depth of its failures. It transcends the realm of "so bad it's good," seeming instead to have been crafted with the express purpose of provoking ire, a goal it achieved with remarkable efficacy.

It felt as though the creators distilled the most grating elements of the film "PRIEST," augmented them with an abundance of unappealing male characters, stripped away any semblance of intrigue, humor, or even a hint of wit or allure, and then liberally infused the remaining void with the essence of aged, spoiled cheese. That's its entirety: an unpalatable, curdled mess.

There is not a single demographic for whom this film could conceivably resonate, nor any conceivable reality in which its narrative could plausibly unfold. One is left to ponder why such a production couldn't simply aim to be a source of enjoyment and levity. Why did an already ill-conceived premise need to be amplified to such an extreme of absurdity? Why was no effort seemingly made to elevate it to even an acceptable standard, not even as a B-movie?

Reflecting upon it, the true intent behind its creation remains utterly baffling. I had anticipated a campy love story, and instead…

First encountering this film in the 1980s, during my mid-teenage years, I initially felt a reluctance to watch it, having outgrown what I perceived as the "Sesame Street/Muppets" era. My memory of my initial reaction is hazy. However, a rewatch in college transformed my perspective, solidifying its place in my personal "Best Films Ever" collection.

The film overflows with humor that transcends typical Muppet expectations. While the Muppets have always masterfully blended humor for both children and adults, this film takes it a step further. Moments like Janice's overheard declaration, "I don't take my clothes off for anyone, even if it IS artistic," a father's quip to his son about being in love with Kermit, or Gonzo's hilarious post-mouth-to-mouth resuscitation announcement, "I think we're engaged now," had me in stitches. This, coupled with incredibly smart dialogue and witty New York/Broadway "wink wink" humor, elevates the film considerably.

This film is an utter failure, devoid of genuine emotion in every frame. Its characters are one-dimensional, predictable caricatures, and the plot is a trite exercise in Hollywood escapism.

William Holden, tragically miscast at 55, attempts to portray a character in his early forties, yet appears closer to sixty. His romantic interest, a 20-year-old Kay Lenz, is scripted to find him irresistibly attractive – a notion less convincing than the allure of a stray dog.

Holden's character, coincidentally the same age as director Clint Eastwood at the time, is surrounded by clichéd symbols of 1960s pre-hippie coolness: the bachelor pad, the high-fidelity sound system, lunches at Yamashiro. Yet, the film itself is an embarrassingly uncool, clunky attempt by an older generation to appropriate the vibrant youth culture of Sunset Boulevard and Laurel Canyon, seemingly hoping their material possessions would compensate for their lack of genuine appeal.

The film's portrayal of youth culture is frankly insulting, and one cringes to imagine the desperation that led William Holden to accept such a demeaning role.

This four-hour remake of H. Rider Haggard's classic tale, "King Solomon's Mines," expands on the original with the addition of a female character and a superfluous subplot involving Russian soldiers on a quest for a "Stone of Power" hidden alongside Solomon's treasure. Despite these narrative deviations, the film is visually stunning, masterfully capturing the vastness of the African landscape, and boasts strong performances. Patrick Swayze shines as Alan Quatermain, while Alison Doody delivers an engaging portrayal of Elizabeth Maitland, who enlists Quatermain's help to rescue her father. Notable supporting performances include Sidede Onyulo as Umbopa and Gavin Hood as McNabb and the unnamed leader of the Russian soldiers. While Hollywood's penchant for altering source material often disappoints, this adaptation is well-crafted and engaging, though its excessive length is a notable drawback. Overall, I found it enjoyable. 6/10.

With an IMDb rating of 8.1, my expectations for this film were considerably higher. It opens with a charming, humorous, and spontaneously energetic tone. However, it quickly devolves into a sluggish and disappointingly predictable narrative before even reaching the halfway mark. While the office characters were initially delightful, their continued development led them to become one-dimensional caricatures rather than relatable individuals. This felt like a recycled plot, merely presented with minor situational variations. A predictable love story might have been tolerable, but the stale dialogue made it unbearable.

Adding to its flaws, *Dead Letter Office* also suffered from inconsistent and unbelievable character motivations. I sincerely hope this film is soon relegated to the cinematic "dead letter office."

The film's prolonged ambiguity and lack of exposition lead to a series of baffling sequences that, despite hints of deeper meaning, ultimately come across as merely strange and incomprehensible. This narrative approach, while perhaps intended to encourage rewatching, instead creates a frustrating viewing experience; I'm certain that had I watched it in the evening, I would have fallen asleep. It felt like a low-budget imitation of "Blade Runner."

The movie's abundance of unanswered questions and improbabilities leaves it feeling pointless and forgettable.

Furthermore, the film's unusual aesthetic is a detriment. Its blend of CGI and live-action elements is executed poorly, lacking the impressive, spectacular, and imaginative quality seen in films like "Sin City" and "300." The decision to animate half of the characters via computer seems particularly odd and unnecessary, especially given the unconvincing character animation.

This film languishes near the bottom of my cinematic experiences, spared true rock bottom only by the likes of *Haunted Mansion* and *Nothing But Trouble*. It suffers from a rushed pace, a flimsy narrative, and amateurish performances. While some blame undoubtedly lies with the source material—the novel it's based on is remarkably ponderous and illogical—the film itself fails to elevate it. Even Oprah, typically a compelling presence, delivers a surprisingly unremarkable performance as "Bigger's" mother, far below her usual standard. Other well-known actors, too, seem to be operating at their least effective.

The plot follows an African American man who takes a job as a chauffeur. While driving the family's daughter to a communist dinner, an acquaintance forms. One event leads to another, and the girl becomes intoxicated. Though his employers aren't prejudiced, he perceives them to be. Upon returning home, he puts her to bed, but she begins to wail. The blind mother, hearing the commotion, prompts Bigger to attempt to silence her, but he inadvertently smothers her. Fearing the repercussions of killing a white girl, he takes a tragically desperate and illogical step, disposing of her body...

Even with low expectations, this film was a profound disappointment. Its narrative suffered from poorly conceived motivations, and the performances were largely uninspired—a point underscored by P. Diddy's surprising turn as a standout. The plot offered little intrigue, its twists easily foreseen. While some nods to *Carlito's Way*, like the protagonist's Caribbean dream, were mildly effective, most felt tenuous. The romantic subplot, in my view, was misjudged, though reasonable minds may differ. I particularly feel for Jay Hernandez, a genuinely capable actor (as seen in *Friday Night Lights*), who was let down by this project. Fortunately for him, it's unlikely many will witness this cinematic misstep. Though I'm usually generous with ratings for films that pique my interest even slightly, this one barely managed two stars. Here's hoping for a better next attempt. (And yes, *Carlito's Way* remains a classic.)

As a devoted admirer of Neil Young's music, I eagerly sought out the earliest screening of "Greendale," drawn in by both my personal appreciation and the enthusiastic reviews circulating within indie media. However, my initial excitement quickly dissipated. The film's cumbersome narrative and uninspired lyrical progression seemed to lull much of the audience into either slumber or dissatisfaction.

Young himself has stated that the project originated as a soundtrack, with the characters evolving so vividly that filming the soundtrack became the logical next step. This approach, however, proved detrimental to storytelling. Character development is virtually nonexistent, and even pivotal moments fail to resonate with the audience, largely due to the film's increasingly frustrating technical execution. The entire film unfolds as a series of songs, with characters perpetually lip-syncing the lyrics. While this technique holds a fleeting novelty in its initial moments, it rapidly devolves into an irritating distraction. It creates a sense of artificiality that is neither engaging nor believable, simply unwelcome.

The acting is uniformly poor, with performers settling into a single emotional state and maintaining it throughout. Lighting is often subpar. The only commendable aspect of the film lies in several scenes presented as newscasts, though this technique has become considerably overused in contemporary cinema.

For a debut episode of a new series, I believe it was exceptionally well executed. It was thoroughly entertaining and featured brilliant performances from the cast. I find it baffling when people criticize it, especially regarding historical accuracy, as it's clearly intended as Saturday night entertainment, not a history documentary. The costumes and settings were perfectly suited to its purpose. It was a brilliant start, and I'm eagerly anticipating future episodes! Many at my school share my enthusiasm, finding it to be superb entertainment with compelling storylines.

This past weekend, I rented a movie and was impressed by its audio quality on my surround sound system, particularly the impactful special effects. It's an excellent choice for a rental, with remarkably frightening special effects that even startled my fiancée. While some effects appeared noticeably computer-generated, it's still a perfect film for a scary, late-night movie experience at home. Highly recommended!

This exceptionally well-crafted film captivates from start to finish. The brilliant performances by the entire cast, particularly Salman, Rani, and Preity, breathe life into a compelling narrative. The story, a poignant journey of love and loss, follows Raj and Priya, whose marital bliss is tragically short-lived after a devastating pregnancy loss. Raj's subsequent, morally complex encounter with Madhu, leading to an unconventional pregnancy outside of marriage, adds a compelling layer of drama.

Beyond its engaging plot, the movie shines in every technical aspect. The dialogue is wonderfully penned, the songs are melodious and perfectly complement the visual storytelling, and the picturization is nothing short of spectacular. The wedding song, in particular, is a vibrant explosion of color. The excellent cinematography beautifully captures the picturesque landscapes of Switzerland, enhancing the film's overall aesthetic. This cinematic experience is a true testament to the power of a strong cast and exceptional filmmaking, making it well worth both your time and money. Rating: 8/10.

"Kameradschaft," an early German talkie with English subtitles, remains a powerful docudrama, drawing its chilling effectiveness from an actual mining disaster. This film, featuring many non-professional actors, vividly portrays the unwavering camaraderie among mine workers, transcending the French/German border. A catastrophic accident unleashes the best in everyone, rendering official orders obsolete as miners prioritize helping their comrades, even at immense personal risk.

The selfless heroism depicted in "Kameradschaft" resonates strongly with the actions of the NYFD after the 9/11 attacks. Much like the firefighters who disregarded regulations to save lives and find their fallen comrades, the miners in the film demonstrate an unyielding dedication to one another. More than 70 years on, "Kameradschaft" continues to deliver its timeless and potent message: a friend in need is a friend indeed.

Having encountered this film multiple times across various short-film festivals, I'm consistently left with the distinct impression of having watched a movie trailer rather than a complete narrative.

For a student production, its execution in terms of direction and production quality is commendable. However, the story itself feels underdeveloped, lacking the depth needed to elevate it into a more compelling and substantial work. Specifically, the character of Tim Watcher would have benefited from a more in-depth exploration. This superficiality in character development is a recurring issue I've observed in some Portuguese short films, where the script often remains at a surface level.

Despite these reservations, I did find myself enjoying the film.

Parabéns!

While many prefer *Antz*, I found *A Bug's Life* to be the more enjoyable film, despite *Antz* being a strong contender. I can't recall laughing so consistently at a Pixar film since the first two *Toy Story* movies. The animation is polished, the story is fresh, and it avoids being overly didactic.

The voice cast truly elevates this film. Dave Foley brings a heartfelt earnestness to Flik, an ant who frequently finds himself in sticky situations. Kevin Spacey delivers a superb, wonderfully villainous performance as Hopper, while Hayden Panettiere shines as Dot. The supporting cast is equally stellar, featuring Dennis Leary, David Hyde Pierce, and Madeline Kahn, among many other talented actors.

The script is exceptionally well-crafted, offering consistent humor and moments of genuine poignancy. Unlike *Antz*, it doesn't burden itself with overt social commentary, instead focusing on delivering rock-solid entertainment. I give it a 9/10. - Bethany Cox

Jason Lee's physique returns to the screen! If that's your primary interest, this film delivers. Otherwise, you might want to skip it.

Regarding the movie itself, it's a collection of clichés, featuring poorly executed yet somewhat unique fight sequences (utilizing Jeet Kune Do), alongside generally weak acting and subpar special effects. Lee appears to be in discomfort throughout, making for an unenthusiastic return.

This film struggles to even qualify as a decent B-movie. While it features a blonde, Rutger-Hauer-esque antagonist, it lacks the usual B-movie staples like gratuitous sex scenes or even a single suggestive shot. This absence is notable, especially when compared to films like *Starship Troopers 2*, which understood the necessity of such elements (and for more on that cinematic masterpiece, please see our upcoming review of its mind-blowing sequel). I suspect the writer may have been settling a personal score, so I won't delve into the plot or other specifics. However, it's worth noting the presence of non-heterosexual undertones.

On a positive note, at least Jean-Claude Van Damme isn't in it.

First, scrawl your script on a napkin – who needs more for a non-Hollywood film?

Next, cast amateurs to generate festival buzz; after all, who values years of honed craft? Then, hire a cinematographer oblivious to lighting, ensuring that "unrealistic" polished look is avoided and professional-level photography dismissed. Finally, entrust your camera to a ten-year-old novice. This guarantees an amateurish aesthetic, which festival screeners will mistake for "reality," leading critics and a niche, over-intellectualizing audience to hail it as "genius," even as it alienates most viewers.

With these steps complete, you're ready for the "Festival of Bad Movies," also known as Sundance.

What a lamentable waste.

Michael Rooker, while a competent actor, struggles as a leading man unless operating within the confines of a low-budget production; his subdued charisma is particularly evident when contrasted with Ryo Ishibashi's significantly more engaging screen presence. Unfortunately, Ishibashi's compelling performance is sidelined, with the majority of screen time dedicated to Rooker's less expressive portrayal.

Danielle Harris, known for her roles in "Halloween 4 and 5," delivers a charming and amusing performance as Rooker's daughter. However, her character's lack of intelligence is a narrative misstep, leading to a pivotal foolish mistake that directly results in the death of a main character. The film also features surprising and memorable turns from comedians Fred Willard, Bobcat Goldthwait, and Stephen Furst; observing their characters' fates is a highlight.

Vincent Schiavelli's portrayal of the Consigliere to the local Mafia Godfather adds an intriguing ambiguity, leaving the audience to ponder whether his performance is intentionally comedic. Tim Thomerson, a familiar face in the realm of ultra-low-budget, direct-to-video action and comedy films, also appears. The unexpected assembly of so many comedic actors lends the film a distinct, almost spoof-like quality, raising the question of whether it's intended as a parody of Yakuza cinema. It's difficult to ascertain.

I was genuinely surprised and disappointed by how much this film failed to deliver. As a long-time admirer of Peckinpah's work, I picked up this drastically discounted DVD, thinking it was worth a gamble. The opening credits, a familiar hallmark for Peckinpah aficionados, skillfully intercut between human and animal imagery. What truly impressed me was the use of non-diegetic ambient noise—children playing in a schoolyard, eerily juxtaposed with the planting of a bomb, building fantastic suspense.

Later, as Caan and Duvall drive to their next assignment, Duvall casually drops a bomb of his own on Caan: his date from the previous night has an STD, a discovery made by snooping through her purse while Caan was intimately involved with her. The ensuing, uproarious laughter is brilliant and clearly influenced the similar scene in Brian De Palma's *Dressed to Kill*, albeit at the fleeting expense of Angie Dickinson.

The unfortunate truth about *The Killer Elite* is that after its compelling opening, the movie completely loses its momentum. Even *Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia*, a film notorious for its rough edges (and that's saying something for those in the know), boasts stronger production value. While I often use Peckinpah's masterful opening sequences as teaching material, for *The Killer Elite*, I recommend turning it off once those credits conclude.

"Greetings from the darkness once more. This film immediately brings to mind 'The Princess Bride,' and while it doesn't quite reach that classic's heights, it stands on its own as remarkably entertaining and well-crafted. The plot is admittedly a bit unusual, and the 'wall' concept remains largely unexplained, yet the execution is solid, even managing to build considerable suspense.

Charlie Cox portrays Tristan, who, smitten with the rather unsuitable Sienna Miller, pledges to retrieve a fallen star. This 'star' turns out to be the captivating Claire Danes. While their eventual connection is fairly predictable, the true suspense stems from the wicked witch, played by Michelle Pfeiffer, and the pursuit by Prince Septimus (son of King Peter O'Toole), both vying for the ruby necklace adorning our celestial heroine. It's a classic tale of good versus a whole lot of bad.

Along Tristan's journey, he encounters the most unconventional pirate imaginable—yes, even more so than those from the Caribbean. Robert De Niro shines as Captain Shakespeare, a character who is outwardly formidable but surprisingly in touch with his more delicate side. Another memorable meeting involves the brilliant Ricky Gervais as a fast-talking trader, providing a welcome dose of humor."

The show subjected me to an excessive amount of teenage, high school angst and family conflict. I have no interest in adolescent girls' relationship woes, having personally navigated similar, agonizing experiences. My expectation was science fiction, the sole reason I watched. While a brief moment of sci-fi appeared late in the episode with the introduction of a proto-Cylon, a critical detail was overlooked: its red eye-dot fixated on an object. Canonical Cylon eye-dots continuously scan, mapping their surroundings, never ceasing their back-and-forth motion. I trust the writers will rectify this inaccuracy in future episodes.

A colossal misfire, this film exemplifies what happens when a director is creatively disengaged, merely fulfilling a contractual obligation. Despite promising intentions, boasting impressive locations and an epic scope, the execution is shockingly amateurish.

The performances are abysmal. Extras are routinely caught staring directly into the camera or gawking at the main actors, clearly clueless about their roles once "Action!" is called. The battle sequences are laughably incompetent; one wonders if the combatants could inflict more harm by simply embracing. Slow-motion shots inadvertently reveal extras aimlessly wandering or gesturing, utterly undermining the supposed intensity.

Focus is inexplicably placed on foreground action, yet to what end? The narrative is a jumbled mess, illogical and discontinuous, often feeling like a random collection of moments strung together, if even that. Dialogue is insipid, and the romantic subplot manages to be even more cringeworthy and absurd than those found in the most outlandish Hong Kong action films.

With a reported budget of $40 million, every penny of which is visible on screen, the culmination of this immense effort is, at best, nothing more than a shiny, round laser disk.

Twenty minutes in, boredom struck. The characters, frankly, were dull. Fleeting moments of entertainment punctuated stretches of tedium. My persistence eventually paid off with a not-bad ending, though it hardly redeemed the ninety-minute slog that preceded it. Overall, a mediocre film and, given the talented cast, a significant disappointment.

Panic In The Streets immediately establishes a classic film noir atmosphere. The opening shot, a gaze down a dark street culminating in an upward tilt to a window, reveals a seedy card game in progress. This initial flourish, along with the subsequent on-location shooting, recalls the evocative mood Welles would achieve years later in Touch of Evil. A player flings open the window, a symbolic gesture that not only ushers in the film's events but also literally provides our first glimpse into the criminal underworld.

Filmed in stark, high-contrast black and white, Panic In The Streets is significantly elevated by its powerful cast and exceptional location work in New Orleans. The coroner's office, the bustling shipping office, and the decaying "Frank's Place" all contribute to a distinct, often stifling atmosphere that could not have been replicated on a soundstage. These elements demonstrate Kazan's indebtedness to Dassin's groundbreaking 1948 film, Naked City, which pioneered a gritty, almost documentary approach within the noir genre. Notably, Widmark had previously appeared in Dassin's superior Night And The City, a film where...

We purchased this film as a joke for a friend, a jest that nearly backfired spectacularly. It's barely watchable, plagued by dire acting, especially from what might be the worst child actor ever to grace the screen. Even Hasselhoff delivers a substandard performance. The plot is disgraceful, at times so boring it left us utterly bewildered. What attempts to be gruesome often devolves into unintentional comedy. Frankly, it's just terrible.

Who would have thought these two could be so hilarious? Christopher Meloni and Janel Moloney, primarily recognized for their stellar performances in acclaimed television dramas like "Law & Order: SVU" and "The West Wing," prove their comedic chops in this surprisingly engaging and laugh-out-loud romantic comedy.

Their ability to build the characters' evolving relationship is remarkable. Despite Barry Singer (Meloni) being a mean-spirited, sexist stand-up comic, the actors make it impossible not to root for him. You'll find yourself cheering him on as he confronts his insecurities and pursues Thea (Moloney) across the country to win her affection. While they seem to have little in common, Barry's eventual vulnerability will leave you wondering why Thea keeps her distance.

"The Souler Opposite" is a truly wonderful film, boasting an incredible cast and brilliant writing. It's time well spent.

I've never seen any of the "Santa Slasher" films, like 'Silent Night, Deadly Night,' the original 'Black Christmas,' or 'Christmas Evil.' I know their reputation, often described by groups like M.A.D.S. (Mothers Against Deranged Santas). I rented 'Christmas Evil' because I heard it referenced on 'Fat Guys At the Movies.'

Mothers should object to this film, not for its "killer" Santa, but because it's simply awful. It's boring, drawn-out—even at just 92 minutes—and utterly terrible.

The movie begins in 1947, with a young boy witnessing Santa deliver presents, eat treats, and then seemingly float up the chimney. Later, the boy returns to find his mother and Santa in a compromising position. This apparently traumatizes him for life, though the scene itself is about as steamy as the "Leg Lamp" in 'A Christmas Story.' Disturbed, he goes to the attic and cuts his hand.

Fast forward to 1980. The now-adult, troubled boy works in a toy factory.

For fans of derivative, predictable rape-revenge thrillers, this film offers a unique experience. Personally, I found it irredeemable, a peculiar relic seemingly unearthed from the straight-to-video era of the 1980s. While Gillian Anderson and Danny Dyer deliver competent performances despite a weak script and tedious premise, one wonders why Anderson, fresh off her brilliant portrayal of Lady Deadlock in the BBC's "Bleak House," chose to participate in such a project. The director's purported inspirations—witnessing a near-rape and his documentary work—fail to excuse bizarre moments, like the bewildering scene where a pack of dogs attacks Dyer, which elicited laughter from the audience. More perplexing still is the involvement of FilmFour and Verve Pictures, companies responsible for recent acclaimed British independent films such as "Bullet Boy," "Code 46," and "Red Road." This film simply doesn't belong in their distinguished catalog.

That summer, I spent several days watching the filming of this movie at Sylvan Lake in the Black Hills, only for it to result in just two scenes in the final cut. Despite the limited screen time, I eagerly anticipated its release and was thoroughly impressed. The authenticity was striking; the buffalo herd culling portrayed on screen was, in fact, real—a grim reality where animals were harmed during filming. I even suspect the ending might have inspired Jack Nicholson's iconic scene in *The Shining*.

This 1950s film stands as a powerful Western and social commentary. It deserves recognition alongside *High Noon* for its dramatic depth, and its societal impact mirrors that of *Blackboard Jungle* or *Rebel Without a Cause* for the youth of its era.

This film is a reasonable effort at a summary of the era, a decent sixties film that ultimately lacks a sense of achievement. Maggie Smith delivers a believable performance, though perhaps not her strongest, while many of her co-stars are dreadful, leading to a terrible overall portrayal. The movie struggles to land its comedic and dramatic elements, failing to be particularly funny or impactful. Romance is the only genre consistently depicted at a satisfactory level. The film misses its target audience, sending confusing messages through its basic plot and storyline, which are poorly executed. Viewers may be left wondering about the film's shortcomings and its intended demographic. Despite these flaws, Maggie Smith's performance is a highlight, and there are moments of capability within the storyline.

As a white individual, I approach discussions on race with caution. This film, however, presents a problematic double standard: portraying white-on-black hatred as unequivocally wrong, while seemingly condoning black-on-white animosity.

My critique of this movie extends beyond its racial politics. Its few redeeming qualities are limited to unintentional comedic moments, such as the absurd scene where Ice Cube and his companions effortlessly defeat a group of seemingly formidable Neo-Nazis who are twice their size. The chase sequence is similarly laughable.

Far from being a film about race, tolerance, or understanding, this movie is, in fact, deeply racist. It reinforces harmful stereotypes, exemplified by the implausible transformation of a meek white character into a skinhead after a confrontation with his Black roommate. I genuinely regret having watched it.

Spare yourself the tedious and biased experience of this poorly written and acted film. If you're interested in the subject of racial dynamics, I highly recommend "American History X" instead—that's a worthwhile movie.

Allen, in a setting he personally disdains, spends a weekend with his typical cast of successful, middle-class, and often whiny white characters.

Normally, I can unearth some humor in a Woody Allen comedy, but this one completely misses the mark. Even his signature one-liners are absent. The plot is virtually nonexistent, save for a few misguided attempts at Shakespearean pastiche. Allen seems to lean on the rural location to inject a semi-mystical vibe, which only adds to the film's witlessness and underdeveloped feel.

Ultimately, it fails on every conceivable level and is a colossal bore. The most redeeming quality of this film (besides its merciful conclusion) is the hope that its overwhelmingly negative reception will serve as a wake-up call, prompting Allen to realize that a haphazard script and a familiar cast do not inherently equate to entertainment.

Viewers approaching older films should adjust their expectations to account for the cinematic conventions of the era, which can enhance their tolerance for elements that might otherwise detract from the experience. This was certainly the case when viewing "Revolt of the Zombies." One must anticipate the pervasive use of cumbersome dialogue and exaggerated acting prevalent at the time, as well as the rudimentary, if not absent, special effects. The film heavily relies on the viewer's imagination—perhaps excessively so.

The plot itself is convoluted: During WWI, zombified Southeast Asian soldiers inexplicably demonstrate exceptional combat prowess. A subsequent expedition is dispatched to investigate, ostensibly to prevent the knowledge of their transformation from falling into the wrong hands. A member of this expedition acquires the ability to perform long-distance hypnosis, which he immediately exploits—among other uses—to temporarily sideline a romantic rival. In a misguided attempt to prove his devotion, he relinquishes his hypnotic control over everyone. This proves to be a critical error, as many of the newly un-zombified individuals immediately seek to kill him, fearing his renewed control.

Even with a considerate perspective, the film remains below average. It is recommended only for those with an exceptionally high tolerance for cinematic antiquities.

This film, initially presented as a mysterious, serious thriller about a man searching for a missing girl, devolves after merely thirty minutes into an absurd, comedic farce populated by irritating characters and nonsensical scenes. It's impossible to imagine anyone maintaining a straight face during moments like Cage's random karate kick to the blonde woman or his "bear" punch of the elderly lady. From the outset, the dialogue, character portrayals, and performances are all notably subpar. While I've generally held Nicolas Cage in high regard as an actor, his recent cinematic choices have been unfortunate, with this particular movie standing out as the absolute worst to date.

I wholeheartedly advise against this film if you're seeking an intense, gripping thriller. For a truly enjoyable experience of this narrative, I recommend renting the original. However, should you still choose to watch this version, be prepared to find humor in its lines and climactic moments rather than taking them seriously; it’s the only way to endure, let alone “enjoy,” this cinematic misstep.

What was the creative team thinking? Over the years, the "Columbo" series experimented with its successful formula, but this particular installment pushes those deviations to an unfortunate extreme. It stands apart from previous "Columbo" films, and not in a positive way.

The most striking departure is the complete absence of a murder, which fundamentally alters the show's core premise. This places Columbo in an entirely new environment and situation, giving the film an overall "modernized" and unfamiliar feel.

It's particularly perplexing that Alan J. Levi, who previously directed "Columbo" movies that faithfully adhered to the traditional formula, was chosen for this project.

Even Columbo's character feels somewhat off, likely due to his unusual circumstances: assisting his nephew whose bride vanished immediately after their wedding. The characteristic and much-loved Columbo humor is also noticeably absent.

Richard Dix's retirement led to Michael Duane stepping into the role of Ted Nichols. The story introduces Ted's whirlwind romance with Alice Dupres Barkley (played by Lenore Aubert), a young French woman. After only two days, the couple decides to marry, and in a downpour, they arrive at the Justice of the Peace's home, only to discover he's away until the following day. Inside, a mysterious figure is seen pilfering a part from their car engine, hinting at impending trouble for the couple. This act foreshadows a deeply mysterious event surrounding Alice, marking a tumultuous beginning for Ted and leaving their marriage plans in limbo. While the mystery is compelling, Richard Dix's absence was felt. Enjoy.

Released in 1984, at the height of Prince's superstardom, this film was a cultural phenomenon. Though essentially an extended music video, its massive appeal was undeniable. While the acting, particularly from the musical newcomers, was rudimentary, the movie undeniably delivered entertainment. Morris Day and Jerome Benton's comedic timing, especially their memorable "The Password" routine, offered classic moments reminiscent of Abbott & Costello.

The film also featured Appolonia, who, in her mononymous debut, contributed a brief yet striking moment of nudity, adding to her undeniable allure. Crucially, the accompanying soundtrack stands as one of Prince's most acclaimed works. This period marked a pinnacle in his career, predating his well-documented disputes with Warner Bros. and subsequent name change.

While not an all-time cinematic masterpiece, the film remains a thoroughly entertaining experience.

I was nine when my parents took me to see "Elephant Walk," a film that left an indelible mark. Elizabeth Taylor, then twenty-two, captivated me completely. Her beauty was unlike anything I had ever witnessed; it wasn't a sexual attraction, but pure admiration. I was so enthralled that I barely registered anything else on screen, wishing only to sit at her feet like a devoted puppy, gazing up at her. Even now, with her nearly seventy-four years showing, I still consider her one of the most breathtaking women to have ever lived.

Watching the film again as an adult, I recognize it as a rather sappy melodrama. Yet, it's redeemed by several elements: Taylor's undeniable allure, the magnificent scenery, an impressive elephant stampede, and a poignant lesson on human arrogance confronting the power of nature.

Despite its flaws, "Elephant Walk" remains a worthwhile viewing experience, whether it's a casual watch on a movie channel or a rented video.

For a debut, this film delivers riveting and chilling moments. It masterfully tightens the pit of your stomach, in the style of the best horror films, from start to finish. The ending is superb; its influence on *The Blair Witch Project* is evident, offering not a definitive conclusion but a terrifying prelude to the end. This is a great movie, a standout in Japanese horror, and earns a perfect score for its ability to provoke thought and induce sheer terror.

"Rosenstraße" tells the story of courageous women during the Nazi era in Germany, but its excessive length, emotional detachment, and periodic dullness detract from its impact. The film is plagued by an overreliance on clichés and a lack of compelling performances.

The narrative structure is fundamentally flawed. Similar to James Cameron's "Titanic," the story employs an elderly woman reminiscing about her past. However, the introduction of a second woman who also recalls events, often those of others, creates significant confusion. This demonstrates a clear misunderstanding of basic storytelling principles. For instance, it's illogical for Riemann to recount the fate of the little girl's mother and her interrogation, as she couldn't possibly have first-hand knowledge of these events.

The chronological presentation of scenes is haphazard, making it difficult to discern the timeline. A prime example is the proposal scene between Riemann and Fabian; its anachronistic setting, appearing more like the 1920s, further disorients the viewer.

Riemann's character, predictably, is a gifted pianist and, remarkably, a Baroness. Her brother, a "Ritterkreuz" recipient returning from the Eastern Front, is frequently seen displaying his war hero status.

*Kimi wa Petto* tells the charming story of a woman who one day discovers a young man in a box outside her apartment. After bringing him inside to tend to his injuries, she leaves him food and a note, expecting him to be gone by the time she returns from work. To her surprise, he's still there and expresses a desire to live with her, offering to be like a brother or cousin. Desperate to have him leave, she jokingly suggests he can stay only if he becomes her "pet," with no rights, and obedient to her every command (though not in a kinky way). To her astonishment, he agrees, and from then on, he is known as Momo, her peculiar pet.

This film, a glossy remake, stands in relation to the original Zatoichi movies much as the Star Trek films did to their television predecessor. However, unlike Star Trek, the original Zatoichi films surpassed this modern iteration in entertainment, interest, and even craftsmanship, especially if one values substance over superficiality. Had I approached this movie without prior knowledge of the originals, I might have found it visually appealing but ultimately hollow. Having seen the originals, I found its stylistic choices jarring and its narrative lacking. The decision to resurrect the character in such a lavish production likely seemed promising, but its sole purpose appears to have been financial gain. The film largely misses the essence of Zatoichi's world and offers no new trajectory for the character, merely rehashing familiar ground (and the lead actor's performance was unremarkable). My hope had been to see a mature Ichi, with a story providing a graceful conclusion to his journey and reflecting on his accumulated experiences. Instead, this film merely cobbles together elements from previous movies, adding a dash of gratuitous sex and stylized violence, resulting in a fundamentally different and less satisfying experience.

An underappreciated gem from the 80s, this soundtrack conjures images of John Travolta crooning its tunes. The film itself, a veritable embodiment of 80s kitsch, thrives on mechanical bulls, bartending antics, and awkward romances – a clear reflection of the era's cinematic trends. Travolta's lackluster Texas accent, especially when juxtaposed with the authentic portrayals in *Friday Night Lights*, is particularly noteworthy.

For those interested in tracing the "dumbing down" of cinema, I recommend starting with *Cocktail* and *Stir Crazy*. On a related note, *Made in America*, starring Ted Danson and Whoopi Goldberg, is another wonderfully awful film that I was surprised to have missed. *Cadillac Man*, with Robin Williams, also fits this peculiar subgenre of cinema. It's a striking reminder of how many major stars – Tom Cruise, Richard Pryor, Robin Williams, and John Travolta – took on prominent roles in these undeniably cheesy productions.

This Chinese film resonated deeply, bridging the gap between my own culture and one seemingly distant. With an almost meditative quality, it masterfully draws viewers into the lives of its characters, celebrating the quiet joy found in everyday routines.

The entire cast delivers brilliant performances. Xu Hzu, in particular, radiates a compelling blend of kindness and wisdom, yet also vulnerability and even harshness. Er Min, the brother with intellectual disabilities, movingly illustrates that intelligence and wisdom are distinct, and that profound wisdom can emanate from the most unexpected corners of the universe. This is a portrayal of China far removed from conventional Chinese realism, yet it overflows with humanity and a unique, profound form of realism.

See it. You will not regret it.

This awful movie holds a surprising personal connection for me. Filmed in 1976, it utilized Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff and Oak Creek Canyon near Sedona as its backdrops. Many of the extras were NAU drama students at the time. Though a freshman theatre minor myself, I wasn't involved in the production. However, several friends were, and they shared a rather peculiar behind-the-scenes tidbit:

In a scene depicting a hazing ritual, two main characters are shown running naked into the woods, viewed from behind. Those aren't the actors, though. Instead, they're two acquaintances of mine from the theatre department. The identities of these "stunt posteriors" shall remain a secret, at least on this site, unless they decide to, um, "reveal" themselves!

My admiration for Anthony Hopkins as an actor fueled my anticipation for his foray into writing and directing. Unfortunately, the experience was profoundly disappointing. The film suffered from extreme disorganization, and its cinematography was so excessively stylized that it became a distraction. Despite strong performances from the cast, their talent felt squandered. This film serves as a clear illustration that not all actors are suited for roles behind the camera, a category into which Mr. Hopkins, regretfully, falls. In my five decades of movie-watching, this stands out as unequivocally the worst film I have ever encountered. Mr. Hopkins, for the sake of your audience, please continue to grace us with your exceptional acting and entrust the writing and directing to those with a proven aptitude for it. If a rating below one were possible, this film would undoubtedly receive it.

Michael Ironside's involvement in this low-budget film suggests a career downturn. It's surprising he'd accept such a role, given his talent.

The movie's limited budget is consistently evident. A scene at what's supposedly an outpost clearly appears to be filmed outside a railway station, likely because of financial constraints.

The film's sole redeeming quality, and the reason for a slightly elevated rating, is a beautifully executed sequence depicting a spacecraft landing and taking off over a lake nestled within a forest. Beyond this, the rest of the movie falters.

Another scene, presented as a space outpost, is clearly an industrial plant, further highlighting the film's budgetary limitations and lack of authenticity.

Ultimately, this is a nonsensical, poorly funded film, and one can only feel for Michael Ironside's role in it.

I watched this extraordinary film last night on cable. Its understated, low-key approach belies a deeply heartfelt core. Henry Thomas, known for his role as the child in E.T., delivers a masterfully inarticulate performance, perfectly portraying a man of few words. David Strathairn is a wonderful, unhinged villain. Remarkably for a Hollywood production, a baby serves as a central character, not through acting or dialogue, but simply by existing, and is luminous in the role. It's interesting to note the parallel between Thomas's mysterious connection with E.T. in that film and his bond with the baby in "A Good Baby," both forming the emotional crux of their respective stories.

The music is simply breathtaking. Gillian Welch's tunes are wonderful, and the entire score, rich with gorgeous hill country music, is a highlight.

This film is wonderfully atmospheric, and I highly recommend it.

The film appears to advocate for Muslimization, a conclusion drawn from several narrative choices. The protagonist, born to a Muslim father and Christian mother, spends his formative years in a Christian village. Yet, by the film's conclusion, his attire—specific headwear, an amulet, and general clothing—strongly suggest he has embraced Islam. Furthermore, his six-year-old child, whose mother is Christian, is depicted wearing identical headwear, implying the child is also being raised Muslim. This suggests a deliberate choice by the protagonist to convert and raise his offspring in the Islamic faith. Notably, other prominent male characters, who are Christian, are not shown to have children, leading to the impression that the film's world experiences an increase in its Muslim population by its end.

Walt Disney, the legendary film producer, adapted three of the world's most beloved fairy tales into animated classics that remain enduringly popular. His first groundbreaking feature, "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs," premiered in 1937, followed by the then-underappreciated "Sleeping Beauty" in 1959. Nestled between these two, "Cinderella" (1950) stands out as perhaps his most satisfying and faithful adaptation.

While "Snow White" became the definitive version of its story for many, "Cinderella," despite its critical and financial success in revitalizing Disney's fortunes, never achieved the same iconic status it deserved. Remarkably, Disney chose to elaborate upon and enrich the original "Cinderella" narrative rather than significantly altering it, resulting in an enchanting cinematic experience.

The film's radiance, which continues to captivate audiences, is a testament to its superb animation—rendered in beautifully soft Technicolor—and the perfectly cast voice talents that brought the timeless tale to vibrant life.

Television profoundly shapes societal trends, as evidenced by the sudden proliferation of cappuccino shops following the debut of this superficial program. Moreover, the characters' seemingly perfect lives are unrelatable, as genuinely attractive individuals rarely encounter significant challenges.

Furthermore, it strains credulity to believe these characters, given their ostensible professions, could afford lavish Manhattan lofts. NBC, it seems, takes pleasure in underestimating its audience's intelligence, regardless of their intellectual capacity. For instance, I know a web designer earning $100,000 annually who resides in a cramped, $2200-a-month, one-bedroom Manhattan apartment.

I'd be far more inclined to watch a series titled "Phriends," depicting six unattractive, ordinary individuals stuck in dead-end jobs, living in a dilapidated neighborhood plagued by constant sirens and weekly muggings, only to face continuous rent increases. Now *that* would be compelling television.
