For the first twenty minutes, *Alienator*—which I watched on a PS2, so precise timing is elusive—establishes an engaging premise. I don't recall encountering a slasher film where the antagonist is an extraterrestrial alien. Yet, intrigue swiftly gives way to bewildered disbelief as the "alien" is revealed to be a hulking bodybuilder in a metal bikini. *Alienator* is, undeniably, absurd.

This absurdity, however, isn't necessarily a flaw. In the realm of schlock-horror, patent ridiculousness can often be a virtue. Unfortunately, the film's overt silliness is its sole redeeming quality. While hilariously camp, *Alienator* is also an utter shambles. The actors struggle ineptly with attempts at gravitas, potentially brilliant lines of cheesy dialogue are fumbled with unsettling lack of skill, and the direction fails to deliver a single memorable scene. By the film's conclusion, the initial concept is buried beneath layers of pure nonsense.

Compounding this, the "Alien" simply vaporizes its victims, rather than...

I had hoped for an in-depth exploration of the Apollo 11 mission. While the program offered decent interview segments with key figures like Buzz Aldrin and Gene Kranz, these were unfortunately connected by an over-sensationalized, disaster-focused voice-over – a regrettable example of poor television production.

With a different narrative approach, one that celebrated overcoming challenges to achieve extraordinary goals, and without the sensationalized narration, this program could have been truly compelling. Instead, I regret spending approximately 45 minutes of my time on a 60-minute broadcast.

I seem to be an outlier among American viewers, as this film simply didn't resonate with me. It bafflingly falls short of the cinematic masterpiece many claim it to be, barely registering as entertainment.

The narrative, at its core, traces a man's rise from obscurity to drug lord — a premise I found undeniably simplistic and ultimately, the extent of my engagement with the film. The pervasive belief that themes of mafia, drug trade, or criminal organizations inherently elevate a movie to greatness is, in my opinion, a fallacy; compelling storytelling remains paramount.

Having experienced numerous compelling Korean films, particularly thrillers and those with darker themes, I found this particular movie profoundly disappointing. It entirely lacked entertainment value and failed even as a thriller. The director's approach seemed gratuitously sadistic, resulting in a production I can only describe as cinematic junk. Despite adequate acting, the storyline and its lasting impression were utterly dreadful.

I will actively avoid any future films by this director. Their filmmaking sensibility is severely lacking, and the supposed thriller elements were a complete letdown. The film devolved into poorly shot scenes of psychopathic acts, relying on excessive blood and violence to compensate for an absence of genuine thrills. This was a deeply unsatisfying viewing experience, and I strongly advise against watching this film or any others of its kind.

This film, a standout in Amitabh Bachchan's resurgence, captivated me during a period when Govinda and David Dhawan were at their peak. Its fantastic, "masti"-filled songs, coupled with Anupam Kher's multifaceted performance, make it an evergreen entertainer. True to David Dhawan's style, the storyline is packed with hilarious twists and turns. Madhuri Dixit's timely cameo added to the riotous climax. It was truly wonderful to witness Bachchan's forceful and humorous performance after his long hiatus. While some might label it a typical "Bollywood Masala" film, I'd readily watch it again. For its sheer Bollywood spirit, I easily rate it an 8 out of 10.

This "movie" is an abomination, so bad it would make a non-believer exclaim in despair. Previous reviewers, those who rated it three stars or less, have already articulated its many failures, and I wholeheartedly concur. Allow me to add a few observations.

While characters endured gruesome fates—ingesting their own waste, dismemberment by axe, sexual assault with a broomstick, and castration—the ex-boyfriend suffered the most excruciating torture: enduring the girl's interminable and meaningless kitchen table prattle. We, the audience, shared this torment, though thankfully, we had the blessed mute button.

Had the director excised the superfluous and seemingly endless graveyard and inverted scenes, our ordeal could have concluded a mere thirty minutes in. The singular redeeming quality, providing a modicum of bearability, was Emily Haack's breasts, which earn it a paltry point.

Seriously, avoid this at all costs. Do not buy it. Do not waste your time. Do not sacrifice your sanity. My brain is so thoroughly fried from this viewing experience that I feel compelled to immediately watch, and likely suffer through, "Scrapbook" as a palate cleanser.

Like many devoted Trekkers (or Trekkies, the nomenclature matters not!), I endured seven seasons of *Star Trek: Voyager*, yearning for its conclusion and lamenting the 1999 finale of *Deep Space Nine*. My prayers were answered with *Enterprise*. This series is fantastic: a fresh perspective, radically different characters, stunning new visuals, and surprisingly, a pop song for its intro! I can genuinely say there's nothing I disliked. Sign me up for ten seasons of this show. *Star Trek* is back—*Voyager*, you are not missed! Keep on Trekkin'!

Rob Roy excels in every aspect, from its superb cast and intelligent, quotable script, to its lavish cinematography and Carter Burwell's beautiful score. It's a rare cinematic experience, virtually faultless.

Unlike Braveheart, its contemporary, Rob Roy foregoes self-conscious epic grandiosity for immersive, tightly edited storytelling. Every scene is essential, contributing to a perfect balance of drama, action, and humor. Its well-developed characters, anchored in authentic period detail through their vernacular and mannerisms, offer a refreshing departure from simplistic good-vs-evil caricatures often seen in film. We root for the heroic Rob Roy, understanding his struggles are products of his circumstances.

Many criticisms here compare this film to "The Mortal Storm" or "Casablanca." While film comparisons are subjective, the former shares a clear thematic link with "Watch on the Rhine" through their focus on refugees fleeing Nazi oppression. The comparison to "Casablanca," however, often centers on perceived historical injustices regarding Humphrey Bogart's 1943 Oscar loss to Paul Lukas for Best Actor.

I don't find this outcome entirely unjust. Lukas, a seasoned actor with a notable career in both Hollywood and British cinema (including his villainous role in "The Lady Vanishes"), delivered what was arguably his career-best performance. Bogart, despite his iconic turn as Rick Blaine, had already given—and been overlooked for—several other outstanding performances, such as Sam Spade in "The Maltese Falcon" and Roy Earle in "High Sierra" just two years prior. Furthermore, he would go on to deliver even more masterful, yet un-Oscared, performances as Fred C. Dobbs in "The Treasure of the Sierra Madre," the writer/murder suspect in "In a Lonely Place," and Captain Philip Francis Queeg.

While some elements of this film, such as its all-white male crew, are undeniably products of their time, and its pacing occasionally mirrors the self-indulgence common in pre-Star Wars science fiction, it remains unparalleled in its capturing of Golden Age Science Fiction's essence. Its use of "electronic tonalities" for the score perfectly evokes the era, and Robbie the Robot stands as an iconic precursor to beloved androids like C3PO and Data, embodying the spirit of Asimov's creations.  Furthermore, by expertly weaving in Shakespeare's "The Tempest"—with Morbius as a clear Prospero figure—the film elevates science fiction to a sophisticated, adult genre, arguably for the first time.

Aspiring filmmaker Aldolpho (Steve Buscemi) inhabits a rundown NYC apartment, dependent on his mother for rent. He's captivated by his beautiful neighbor, Angelica (Jennifer Beals), whose marital status is ambiguous but whom he dreams of casting in his film. A sudden offer of funding from a mysterious man named Joe appears to be Aldolpho's big break. However, Joe's unorthodox methods, including a brazen Porsche heist as part of the "financing," quickly challenge Aldolpho's moral compass. The central questions become: will Aldolpho's film ever see the light of day, and will Angelica grace his screen, before he completely loses his integrity?

In this viewer's opinion, the film is an unmitigated disaster. The script is dreadful, a meandering mess with no discernible direction. Beals' performance is practically a series of snarls, and while Buscemi is inherently likable, his character is utterly bland. The film is rife with distasteful content and unsavory characters. To make matters worse, abysmal production values consistently lend the film a second-rate appearance. Even with time to spare, this movie is best avoided.

I adore movies and typically commit to watching them in their entirety, always striving to give them a fair chance. However, I've finally encountered a film I simply cannot endure from start to finish. The acting is remarkably bland and monotonous, the CGI appears amateurish, as if crafted by a novice in a basement with rudimentary software, and then there are the incredibly drawn-out scenes of... just walking! And this movie clocks in at three hours! I barely lasted fifteen minutes before resorting to fast-forwarding the DVD. The alien encounters are disappointingly brief. Perhaps a more fitting title than "War of the Worlds" would be "War of the Walking Long Distances." This film reportedly cost five million dollars to produce! One can only wonder what justified such an expenditure—perhaps the dramatic opening song?

On a slightly different note, there's one scene worth watching: the aliens' initial assault on humans. It's unintentionally hilarious, not due to the deaths themselves, but because the victims continue to writhe for a full twenty seconds after being reduced to skeletons.

So, if your cinematic taste leans towards dull, uninspired, and action-deprived features, this film might find a place in your DVD collection. However, I didn't write this review for you; I wrote it for the...

This film boasts a compelling story and superb animation, clearly influenced by the works of Frazetta and Bakshi—a definite plus. Fans of *Conan the Barbarian* or *Dungeons and Dragons* will particularly appreciate it. The classic battle between good and evil is refreshingly clear-cut, even if the hero occasionally seems neutral. Breaking from typical fantasy tropes, the film defies the common portrayal of elves as fair-skinned and goblins/orcs as dark-skinned. Like the works of Frazetta, Bakshi, and Tolkien, this film is devoid of racial undertones.

A must-see for fantasy enthusiasts, though its violence and sexual innuendo make it unsuitable for young children. The casting is excellent, complementing the first-rate cinematography and musical score. I eagerly await its DVD release and consider myself fortunate to own a well-preserved VHS copy of this cinematic gem.

**ALMOST GOLDEN: THE JESSICA SAVITCH STORY**

**Aspect Ratio:** 1.33:1
**Sound:** Stereo

This biographical drama, chronicling the ascent and decline of America's pioneering female TV news anchor, falters as a bland, almost soap-operatic rendering. While the production boasts the typically polished, if impersonal, values of a TV movie, its superficiality ultimately mirrors "old fluff," offering little genuine engagement. A more incisive script, tighter direction, and a stronger cast might have elevated the material beyond its flimsy execution. Indeed, a documentary approach might have better served the compelling subject matter.

While the true crime story at the heart of *In Cold Blood* may seem less sensational to those accustomed to the grizzly narratives of serial killers (Gein, Bundy, Dahmer) or infamous Hollywood cases (O.J., Manson), its power lies elsewhere. The core facts are relatively straightforward: Perry Smith and Dick Hickock (portrayed by Robert Blake and Scott Wilson, respectively) met by chance, plotted to rob a Kansas farmhouse safe, and ultimately murdered a family of four with a shotgun and dagger, escaping with a mere $43.

The resolution, too, holds little mystery. After a brief flight to Mexico, they were apprehended by a stroke of ironic fate: a police officer, observing them after they had helped a boy and his father collect bottles for change, stopped them for driving a stolen car. Sentenced to hang, their story concluded in 1965.

Yet, it's the masterful handling of this narrative—the poignant moments, the compelling performances, and the sheer cinematic brilliance of director Richard Brooks and his extraordinary cinematographer, the late Conrad Hall—that elevates *In Cold Blood* beyond a simple recounting of facts.

This film recounts the disturbing odyssey of a deranged scientist. Following his fiancée's decapitation, he embarks on a grotesque quest, frequenting strip clubs in search of a suitable body to reattach her severed head. Every character in this narrative, especially the protagonist, radiates an unsettling repulsiveness.

This film is a must-see for romantics and sports enthusiasts. Drew Barrymore delivers a captivating performance, a welcome return after a string of less successful projects. Jimmy Fallon, surprisingly, shines as Ben, the endearing, sports-obsessed comedian. The movie is genuinely funny, with several laugh-out-loud moments.

Their first date takes an unexpected turn when Ben arrives with flowers to find Lindsay battling food poisoning. Instead of leaving, he gallantly tends to her, helping her into pajamas and cleaning up after her, later quipping, "You were very lady-like... no chunks." Their romance blossoms throughout the winter, but the arrival of baseball season reveals Ben's intense devotion to the Red Sox. Lindsay begins to understand why such a seemingly perfect man might still be single. Initially, she dismisses his obsession, even seeing it as beneficial given her demanding work schedule.

*Robot Jox* isn't hindered by its story or visual effects. For a 1990 film, its effects were par for the course. Many blockbusters of that era, including *RoboCop 2*, still relied on stop-motion animation, pushing the boundaries of available technology. The true leap in cinematic special effects wouldn't arrive until *Terminator 2: Judgment Day* the following year, which subsequently influenced countless filmmakers.

Fans of *Transformers*, *Gundam Wing*, or *Power Rangers* will find plenty to enjoy here. The antagonist robot is particularly menacing, inspiring a healthy dose of caution. The film also features compelling plot points, including a compelling traitor storyline. The unsettling thought that someone you trust implicitly could be working against you adds a layer of suspense that resonates throughout the movie.

While its historical accuracy is debatable—a characteristic now more readily overlooked, perhaps due to the widespread acceptance of works like *The Lord of the Rings* despite their own inaccuracies—I found its artistic merit commendable, even if it doesn't strictly fit the art house genre. The film occasionally delivers genuinely emotionally charged moments.

My primary criticisms are its brevity and the unexplained, intermittent whispering voice.

Overall: 8/10
Quality: 10/10
Entertainment: 7/10
Reusability: 5/10

"My Left Foot" is an absolute must-see, even if you're completely unfamiliar with Ireland. Daniel Day-Lewis's transformative portrayal of Christy Brown, a man with cerebral palsy, is particularly captivating. Brown, ostracized for most of his life and dismissed even when attempting to communicate, finds his sole means of expression and connection through his left foot. With this one functional limb, he paints and writes poetry, ultimately achieving recognition.

This film stands as a testament to the successful collaboration between Day-Lewis and director Jim Sheridan, a partnership revisited in the equally powerful "In the Name of the Father." "My Left Foot" evokes a spectrum of emotions—sadness, hope, and more—but what remains undeniable is Day-Lewis's truly unforgettable, career-defining performance. It is, without question, a cinematic masterpiece.

American author Edgar Allan Poe's visit to London takes an unusual turn when British journalist Alan Foster challenges Poe's claim that his macabre tales are rooted in reality. Accepting a wager from Poe and his friend, Sir Thomas Blackwood, Foster attempts to spend a night in Blackwood's reputedly haunted castle. Once inside, Foster discovers he's not alone; he encounters beautiful women, handsome men, and a metaphysicist who reveals them to be lost souls, replaying their deaths on the anniversary of their demise. This classic horror film captivated me from the outset, proving both genuinely creepy and sorrowful. Barbara Steele's beauty is undeniable, and the musical score amplifies the terror. The unexpected topless scene was surprising. Synapse appears to have done an excellent job with the picture enhancement, as the uncut international version of the film looks remarkably good for its age.

Intrigued by the widespread acclaim for this play, I tuned in when I found it airing. However, I struggled to understand how its focus "elevates" women or their "struggles." While it might appeal to those interested in narratives centered on women's private lives, I personally found it quite dull and, at times, even degrading. My perspective was echoed by a female friend who also viewed it and shared my disappointment, confirming that my reaction wasn't simply a case of a male viewer "not getting it."

"This movie held so much promise: my favorite actor, a historical drama set during the American Revolution. It evoked the sweeping landscapes, Native American presence, and military action of "Dances With Wolves," while the British aesthetic and candlelit ambiance brought "Barry Lyndon" to mind.

However, the script proved to be its undoing. The narrative continuity was jarring, punctuated by abrupt time jumps ("5 months later," "3 years later"), and the romantic subplot was laughably improbable—despite the vastness of America, the characters continually, coincidentally, crossed paths. The ending, in particular, was an astonishingly misguided choice, effectively sabotaging the entire story (imagine such a twist in "Titanic").

A brilliant director can sometimes salvage a weak script, but unfortunately, Hudson is not that filmmaker. His previous work, "Greystoke," exhibited similar flaws: a singular lack of dynamism in the scenes, editing, and score. The result here is equally protracted, tedious, and lifeless.

I'd long heard this film marked a low point in Pacino's career; now I understand why. As my final viewing of 2006, it sadly mirrored the year itself: a painful experience."

It's a good thing I didn't watch this while pregnant. I definitely would have been a mess, either from crying or nausea. The film was less gruesome and more profoundly disturbing. Interestingly, I found the baby oddly endearing in its own twisted way. However, as a mother, I winced during Beth's self-inflicted stab wound to the stomach and Virginia's horrifying, third-trimester abortion with rusty implements. And as an animal lover, the scene where the cat was brutally scratched nearly brought me to tears. Despite the baby's creepy and sinister nature, I surprisingly found myself rooting for its survival. And as twisted as the movie was, I'm now incredibly curious to see the sequel.

The film's shoestring budget is evident in its sets, staging, and editing, perhaps masked by Bela Lugosi's presence. Young brides inexplicably drop dead at the altar, their bodies then absconded with by the renowned horticulturist Dr. Lorenz (Lugosi) and his two grotesque henchmen. His aging wife, Elizabeth Russell, requires injections of glandular fluid from these virginal victims to maintain her eternal youth and beauty. A sharp cub reporter, Luana Walters, connects the disappearances to a unique orchid worn by each bride—an orchid Dr. Lorenz would undoubtedly recognize. A classic horror movie storm enhances the eerie atmosphere of the Lorenz estate, especially with a dwarf and slobbering hunchback lurking about. The cast also includes Angelo Rossitto, Tristram Coffin, Minerva Urecal, and Frank Moran.

Despite my anticipation, fueled by the compelling cast, picturesque Italian setting, and the involvement of director Michael Winterbottom, this film ultimately disappointed. From the outset, it carried a familiar echo of "Don't Look Now," hinting at a narrative where new surroundings might offer solace from grief. I eagerly awaited a twist, a development to subvert expectations for this family abroad. Yet, nothing unfolded. The characters remained stubbornly one-dimensional and unengaging. The slow pacing, which initially promised an impending revelation, led nowhere. Opportunities for compelling plotlines—the eldest daughter's flirtations, the youngest daughter's visions of her deceased mother, and the father's budding romantic interests—were introduced but ultimately abandoned, leaving them as hollow, unfulfilled narrative threads.

I saw this film at the Esquire Theatre in Cincinnati, OH, and it was a truly soul-chafing experience. Honestly, Christopher Reeve would have been more convincing as a boxer.

The movie itself was painful to watch, but witnessing Bret Carr in person was to see desperation personified. My personal highlight was a slow-motion shot of BC getting hit in the face with what looked like a "C" battery from a dildo. The jury's still out on that, but it certainly seemed to be the case.

Bret Carr's quote, "Shoot the left side of the face only...people become famous by demanding things!" oddly resonated amidst the chaos. He even donned a chicken suit and roamed the streets of Clifton, publicly denouncing his own film – a perfectly justified reaction, in my opinion.

My enduring impression is that Bret Carr lacks the charisma or intelligence to lead even a cult, which is the bizarre feeling one gets from the trickle of brainwashed, impressionable neo-yuppies who came to see this "Bret Carr Piece of Work." Just recalling it is an emotionally draining experience.

I'm not typically a Sylvester Stallone enthusiast; indeed, my appreciation for his work was largely limited to a nearly vanishingly small role in the French film *Taxi 3*. Yet, I must confess, *Cliffhanger* genuinely surprised me, defying my low expectations.

The film opens with a harrowing scene: Gabe (Stallone) attempts a perilous mid-air rescue, only for his friend's girlfriend to plummet to her death from 4,000 feet. This tragedy shatters him, driving him from his work as a mountain ranger. For nearly a year, he avoids the reserve, but ultimately returns. Soon after, an emergency call comes in—a group of hikers supposedly trapped in a blizzard. The rangers believe they're responding to a rescue, but the truth is far more sinister. It's a team of ruthless robbers whose daring mid-air heist of government funds went awry, scattering cases of money across the treacherous mountain landscape. They now need skilled climbers to recover their ill-gotten gains.

While *Cliffhanger* certainly isn't a masterpiece of intellectual cinema, it delivers...

Forced to view this in school, I found the experience dreadful. The film is woefully outdated. Its blend of fact and fiction, intended to spice up the narrative, often muddles the episodes. Teachers touted it as a treat, but it was a painfully dull ordeal. 

I've since learned that few of the on-screen personalities are professional actors; most perform their real-life roles within the film. This explains the frequent, cringeworthy acting. Moreover, the story often veers into the outrageous and far-fetched. The dialogue felt poorly crafted, lacking depth and significance. 

Despite intentions to be educational, humorous, suspenseful, and hip, it devolved into a boring, dry, far-fetched, and antiquated mess. I strongly advise against wasting time on this film; you'll miss nothing by skipping it.

This series, intended as an improvement over *Batman: The Animated Series*, falls woefully short. The character designs are, to put it mildly, disappointing—Catwoman's portrayal is particularly egregious. However, my primary frustration stems from how it diminishes Batman, portraying him as a anemic fighter incapable of handling himself in battle without the constant intervention of two or even three sidekicks. This is Batman, for crying out loud! While I understand Nightwing and Batgirl are indeed his comic book allies, alongside Robin, depicting Batman as explicitly *needing* their assistance undermines his legendary prowess. The Batman of *The Animated Series* could effortlessly dispatch a dozen foes; here, he struggles with a few punches. Is he suddenly old? Nonsense.

Furthermore, it's highly uncharacteristic for Batman to send a young Tim Drake into battle so prematurely, without years of rigorous training. This is both irresponsible—a trait utterly foreign to Batman's character—and a departure from the established comic book canon.

*Batman: The Animated Series* set a benchmark with its animation, storytelling, and character development. It remains a true legend.

I endured this film only out of a prior commitment. Unlike many bad films, it offered no unintentional amusement whatsoever. It may well be the worst movie I've ever seen; I'm astonished any distributor attached their name to it.

This movie, a dismal failure as a horror film, was a comedic masterpiece by accident. Its nonsensical plot and undefined characters only heightened the humor, guaranteeing side-splitting laughter with every scene. The minimal dialogue suggests a production without a script, a choice that inadvertently created a versatile viewing experience. Whether watched linearly or in reverse, the film's chaotic charm will leave you delightfully bewildered. A personal highlight is the scene where inmates, in what the doctor bafflingly terms "treatment," gleefully assault each other with sticks. Pure genius!

RKO's "Of Human Bondage" vividly brings Somerset Maugham's characters to the screen, though the film itself is a somewhat sparse adaptation of the novel. Bette Davis' star-making performance as Mildred Rogers dominates the energy, at times overshadowing other aspects. The narrative primarily follows Leslie Howard as Philip Carey, initially an aspiring painter who, upon being told he lacks artistic talent, shifts his ambitions to medicine. This pivot from art to medicine, despite his eventual success in the latter, subtly highlights the earlier misguidance regarding his artistic pursuits. Notably, the film also incorporates the symbolism of his "club foot" disability.

Early in this adaptation, Philip becomes infatuated with Mildred, a waitress portrayed by Davis. Davis' portrayal of Mildred is extraordinary, culminating in a memorable scene where she shockingly declares, "I had to WIPE MY MOUTH!" after kissing him. While Howard delivers a solid performance, the film struggles to adequately explain Philip's enduring fascination and love for Mildred, which ultimately diminishes the impact of both actors' efforts.

Nevertheless, "Of Human Bondage" remains a must-watch for its exceptional acting, including strong supporting performances. Bette Davis' iconic characterization was so impactful that it reportedly launched a write-in campaign for her Academy Award nomination.

Hour-long ape-gazing left me feeling like a primate myself — specifically, the kind who'd shell out cash for this film. Save your money, folks; a comedy like *Bridget Jones's Diary* would be a far wiser investment.

This lyrical, free-flowing film captivates and delights, even as it navigates truly shocking events. The mistreatment of women elicits gasps, yet their ultimate triumph is a testament to the cast and crew's skillful navigation of potentially disastrous scenes. Depardieu's performance is arguably his most natural, and possibly his best. Jeanne Moreau delivers an outstanding performance in a challenging role, including vigorous sex scenes with much younger men. Miou-Miou is consistently captivating, expertly handling demanding scenes. What initially appears to be a misogynistic romp evolves into a tender and honest portrayal as the story and characters unfold. Ultimately, this uncompromising and daring film commands respect.

*An Inconvenient Truth* presents a narrative that, while aiming to inform, shares a simplistic and demagogic tone reminiscent of the most ardent political rhetoric. It argues for impending environmental catastrophe, a claim that, while perhaps scientifically sound, struggles to resonate with a human nature often characterized by self-interest and a short-term perspective.  The film ultimately posits a future of dire consequences, yet the proposed solutions come from the very political establishment that many view as complicit in the current state of affairs. This leads to a cynical outlook: that despite any proposed "new society," fundamental power structures and human flaws will ensure the continuation of existing problems.

The film's messenger, Al Gore, also faces scrutiny. His personal lifestyle, including travel in a large vehicle, reliance on technology, and expansive property holdings, is seen by some as contradictory to the urgent environmental message he espouses. Critics point to the historical use of his land for practices like cattle ranching, tobacco and pig farming—activities associated with environmental degradation and methane emissions—as further evidence of this apparent disconnect. This perceived hypocrisy undermines the film's intended impact for certain audiences.

A film as predictable as it is dreary, unfolding in the bleak landscape of the lower Coachella Valley. The acting is remarkably amateurish, and the script feels like a first draft from a screenwriting novice. Its only redeeming quality is its effectiveness as a sleep aid.

Here's an indie film that, despite my hopes, ultimately disappointed. The absence of a script, prominently announced in the opening credits, is painfully evident and undermines the entire production. The narrative is a confusing jumble, not worth the effort to decipher. My interest waned within the first ten minutes, and I endured the subsequent forty—holding onto a sliver of hope—before resorting to chapter skips to reach the conclusion. Even that expedited viewing proved unrewarding. *OZARK SAVAGE* strains to be ingenious, borrowing its most compelling scenes from *EVIL DEAD 2* and *THE MATRIX*. Consequently, the film offers little originality and what it does offer has been executed with greater success elsewhere. This movie might have been enjoyable as a 10-20 minute short; as a feature, it feels distended and contrived. Naturally, short films offer limited financial return, so I grasp the presumed economic rationale for its expansion to over 75 minutes. Director Matt Steinauer demonstrates considerable potential, and I wish him well.

Neither the unmitigated disaster critics proclaimed nor the misunderstood masterpiece its ardent admirers championed, Guy Ritchie's *Revolver* stands as a commendable effort to imbue his signature con-artist narratives with greater depth. However, few things draw more derision than an ambitious film that overreaches, particularly one built upon the familiar gangster/con-artist framework.

Given Luc Besson's producer credit, *Revolver* predictably exhibits a strong "Cinema de look" aesthetic. Set in a stylized, almost fantastical world where American and British sensibilities seamlessly merge, the film boasts stunning visuals, a few brilliantly edited and conceptualized action sequences, and an undeniable allure of style. These qualities might ordinarily brand it as mere disposable entertainment. Yet, Ritchie clearly aimed for more than a quick rehash of his previous successes. He plainly invested considerable thought and research into themes of life, the universe, and everything in between. Indeed, *Revolver*'s central flaw might be its very ambition: an overwhelming attempt to weave in too many influences—from Machiavelli and Godard to the Principles of Chess—alongside diverse motifs and cinematic techniques, bombarding the screen with an array of quotes. The film was originally conceived to...

*3 lbs* feels like a vanity project for Stanley Tucci, who appears to have taken on the role of producer and resident brooding, insightful doctor. Unlike *House*, the lead character lacks any compelling personality, and in contrast to *Grey's Anatomy*, the neurological cases themselves fail to engage. For a show supposedly set in a premier neurological center, the storylines are remarkably uninspired. Even the weak "feud" with a rival and the protagonist's hallucinations add nothing to the narrative. A fleeting glimpse into the lead's life as a father in the pilot was utterly forgettable and contributed nothing meaningful.

Ultimately, *3 lbs* is a disappointment. In today's crowded landscape of medical dramas, this show does absolutely nothing to distinguish itself.

Catching the latter half of this film on cable, I was immediately struck by its profound morbidity. Even as one of the two victims reaches the most advanced state of deterioration, the camera unflinchingly maintains its gaze. The extended shots of his corpse being unearthed and his concentration-camp-like figure being zipped into a body bag are both deeply moving and profoundly depressing. This is not a film to watch if you're already feeling low; then again, it's equally unsuitable if you're in high spirits.

"Werewolf Woman" is a misnomer; the film is a prime example of European horror's tendency to prioritize sex and nudity over genuine scares, often to an excessive degree. While the initial scenes of the titular character's violent outbursts might offer fleeting amusement, 100 minutes of repetitive sex and murder quickly devolve into monotony. The protagonist isn't even a werewolf, but rather a schizophrenic woman whose ancestor was accused of lycanthropy. The film's tone is wildly inconsistent, shifting from supernatural horror in its opening flashback to a troubling character study of abuse, and finally, a revenge thriller. The director's claim of a "true story" basis is dubious at best.

Despite its flaws, the film offers a few redeeming qualities. The lead actress is striking, and there are some commendable gore effects and nude scenes, though even these become tiresome. The dubbed dialogue also provides unintentional comedic relief, adding to its camp appeal.

*City Hall* presents a mixed bag, oscillating between vignettes of New York City political life and a moralizing tale. Al Pacino, portraying a Dukakis-esque boss with presidential aspirations, delivers a performance that is often sullen or subdued. He truly shines, however, in the rare moments he chews the scenery. In contrast, John Cusack gives a generally flawless and understated performance, deftly avoiding caricature with his New Orleans dialect and steering clear of melodrama during the film's climax. Danny Aiello also impresses as a borough political chief. (On a personal note, I'm quite fond of showtunes.)

Despite its many merits, the primary flaw in *City Hall* is its pervasive lack of momentum. It feels more like a documentary than a motion picture, presenting the story from a detached perspective. This distance prevents viewer involvement, leading to apathy towards the characters and, ultimately, the plot. This alienation is particularly evident in what should have been a riveting, detail-rich finale, which instead lands with a disappointing "Hmmm...uh...okay." As the saying goes, "You can't fight city hall," a maxim that unfortunately applies to the film's narrative inertia.

At the close of the 1980s, Warren Beatty delivered two vastly different cinematic experiences. Earlier in the decade, he wrote, directed, and starred in "Reds," an intelligent historical epic chronicling the birth of the Soviet Union through the lens of radical journalist John Reed. This profound film, both entertaining and message-driven, featured an ensemble cast. Later, Beatty helmed "Dick Tracy," a different kind of epic, unabashedly pure entertainment, where a stellar cast gleefully embraced flamboyant roles under layers of makeup.

That both "Reds" and "Dick Tracy" emerged from the same individual underscores Beatty's remarkable versatility as a filmmaker. In "Dick Tracy," Beatty successfully assembled numerous iconic characters from the original comic strip into a cohesive, original screenplay.

The film opens with the city's reigning mob boss, Big Boy Caprice, strategically eliminating rivals. He orchestrates a "Valentine Massacre"-style shooting to eradicate Lips Manlis's henchmen, soon after ensuring Lips himself meets a watery end. These aggressive maneuvers, however, draw the immediate attention of Tracy.

Meanwhile,

This animated short, the first in a series, chronicles the history of the Matrix, from the genesis of AI and humanity's exploitation of machines to the robot rebellion and the subsequent war that led to the Matrix's creation. The animation style blends Japanese anime with contemporary American aesthetics, a testament to the renowned directors behind the film.

Setting aside any behind-the-scenes drama, we'll evaluate this film purely on its own merits.

In short: this movie is terrible. Rather than delve into what passes for a plot, I'll spotlight some of its most bizarre elements.

Our story begins with a history class of five students on a field trip to rural Ireland, though their nationality and the Canadian filming location are glaringly inconsistent. Among them is a "dumb jock" who inexplicably transforms into a horror-savvy character, a possible Chris Klein look-alike whose girlfriend's fate is left ambiguous, a brooding and unexplained recluse, and a generic blonde.

In this cinematic Ireland, the population seems to consist of two cousins and a character named Gary.

As a newcomer to US television, my initial encounter with this program on my in-laws' cable left me utterly bewildered. It began as what I presumed was a low-budget sci-fi flick. Moments later, I considered it a sharp satire on Christian fundamentalism's most outlandish aspects. Then, the shocking realization hit: they were serious! I haven't witnessed such unintentional comedy in ages.

I initially hesitated to review this, fearing I might offend religious sensibilities. However, after seeing other reviews, I decided they could handle it. This film presents a fascinating dilemma: how do you critique a genre without directly showcasing its flaws? The answer, it seems, is to craft something so specific that only those who despise the genre will fully grasp its humor. While some might be put off by the filmmakers' apparent disdain for viewers not steeped in biblical lore, I found it utterly hilarious.

This film proved surprisingly thought-provoking. While the central twist felt somewhat predictable and dated, it effectively sparked contemplation about a world devoid of vegetation and livestock, fostering a deeper appreciation for our own. Charlton Heston and the supporting cast deliver strong performances, grounding the narrative in a surprising degree of realism. Though occasionally lacking direction and sufficient explanation for its settings, the movie ultimately stands as a remarkably intelligent and engaging experience. My main critique is that I wished it hadn't ended so abruptly; I was eager to see what unfolded next.

7/10

Having seen this film only once, I can confidently say that a single viewing was more than sufficient. It struck me as a relentless parade of psycho-sadistic violence, with barely a whisper of plot or character development. My initial draw was Zoe Trilling, known from "Night of the Demons 2," as I hoped to see her in a more conventional role. However, Tobe Hooper's script felt embryonic and directionless, overshadowed by Robert Englund's overbearing performance. One can only imagine Zoe Trilling's current whereabouts—perhaps in self-imposed exile from this cinematic misstep.

This film is among the worst I've ever seen, yet it's made entertaining by the performances of the young enslaved girl, Alice, and Jared Harris's imitation of Christopher Walken. Alice's smoking, drinking, and uncanny ability to appear when her name is called are strangely captivating. Jared deserves praise for his Christopher Walken impression, and Christopher Walken for allowing it to be featured in the film.

This film is another regrettable example of Lifetime TV's tendency to portray the reprehensible actions of morally bankrupt women with misplaced empathy. Like other problematic films such as "The Burning Bed," "Enough," or "Monster," it attempts to sanitize the image of a deplorable criminal and convince the audience of her inherent goodness. This approach is deeply flawed and disingenuous.

I pose this question to the filmmakers: Had LeTourneau been a man and Vili a 12-year-old girl, would you have crafted a narrative that sympathized and empathized with the aggressor? The unequivocal answer is no.

Consider the hypothetical scenario of reversed genders in this film, and the fundamental issues with its premise become glaringly apparent. Were the genders switched, there would be no attempt to elicit sympathy for the perpetrator. Instead, we would undoubtedly witness a depiction of a monstrous individual preying on a vulnerable child, their depravity leading to their incarceration, and their traumatized victim grappling with the complexities of Stockholm Syndrome. The only reason LeTourneau receives preferential treatment in this narrative is solely due to her gender.

Let's be frank: LeTourneau is a criminal.

Even for devoted fans of Al Pacino, this film was a difficult watch. What appeared to be the regrettable conclusion of a once-distinguished and principled career, his performance felt like a publicity stunt. Pacino's disheveled appearance and an utterly unconvincing, fluctuating Southern accent were significant distractions.

The narrative itself was a tangled mess, progressing erratically with numerous unresolved plotlines and implausible scenarios that were frankly mind-numbing.

Kim Basinger's presence was largely inconsequential. Her interactions with Pacino lacked any believable chemistry or emotional depth, making their supposed bond unbelievable.

In contrast, Téa Leoni was a standout, bringing an electric energy to the screen. Her scenes with Pacino were by far the most engaging in the film, though even her performance couldn't salvage Pacino from what felt like an embarrassing turn.

Franco Rossi’s 1985 six-hour Italian mini-series adaptation of *Quo Vadis* is a peculiar film. It meticulously recreates ancient Rome with an almost documentary-like straightforwardness, favoring intimate shots over grand vistas. Yet, this commitment to historical allusion and classical literature often overshadows the narrative, relegating the main story to the background.

The series' unconventional structure—with much of the first episode unfolding through voice-over letters—and a noticeable lack of narrative urgency make the six-hour runtime both challenging and curiously undemanding, and often uninvolving. Nevertheless, it possesses notable strengths. Chief among these is the portrayal of Petronius (voiced by the aptly dubbed Frederic Forrest), depicted as a man so consumed by courtly survival tactics that he has become emotionally numb. Equally compelling is Klaus Maria Brandauer's distinctive interpretation of Nero as a performative emperor, meticulously calculating every action for his perceived audience. Furthermore, Max Von Sydow makes a brief, yet impactful, appearance, delivering the series' most moving scene in an encounter with a child.

This is an amazing film! Chinese folklore is incredibly complex and philosophical, often embedding stories within stories. While I didn't grasp every nuance, my studies in Chinese folklore have taught me just how intricate it is. Embrace the experience for what it offers, and enjoy the ride!

Attending a small screening hosted by my college's gaming club, I was told to expect the "reefer madness" of gaming. This film certainly delivered on that promise.

Tom Hanks stars as Robbie, a student returning to college after a semester-long "rest." We soon learn Robbie was once deeply addicted to the role-playing game "Mazes and Monsters," a game he reconnects with when a gaming group recruits him for a campaign.

The movie is hilariously absurd on multiple fronts. One memorable scene depicts the group "gaming by candlelight," which perfectly encapsulates the film's tone. While likely intended to convey a sense of cultishness, this portrayal is wildly inaccurate to anyone familiar with gaming. Most role-playing sessions occur in brightly lit rooms, typically accompanied by snacks and soda.

The acting, though not Oscar-worthy, isn't terrible either. This was an early role for Tom Hanks, preceding "Bosom Buddies" and "Bachelor Party" by a year or two. The supporting cast, while not particularly memorable, delivers competent performances.

While I recognize Fassbinder's esteemed place among post-war German directors and the critical acclaim many of his films have received, revisiting "Lili Marleen" in 2004 left me questioning its widespread admiration. The performances, particularly Hanna Schygulla's unsettlingly perpetual smile, struck me as inadequate. The shifts between wartime glamour and battlefield scenes felt jarring and nonsensical. The overall aesthetic suggested a rushed, low-budget production, perhaps even made in an attic. Although some might interpret this as artistic authenticity, I found the film to be simply poor and inauthentic. Compared to the nuanced artistry of Visconti's "The Damned," "Lili Marleen" pales significantly, challenging any assertion of its quality.

Having never read "A Wrinkle in Time," and after seeing the film adaptation, I question whether I ever truly want to. While I'm not here to offer a formal review, I'll start by admitting that the TV movie is remarkably forgettable. My inability to recall its plot serves as testament to that. No TV movie, in my honest opinion, will ever surpass "Merlin."

How does one even review a TV movie? I haven't before. Typically, they feature a few recognizable faces. "A Wrinkle in Time" only boasts one: Alfre Woodard (or Woodward, I'm unsure of the spelling), an Oscar winner.

The film suffers from cheesy special effects, a mildly engaging plot, and moments that elicit a resounding "WTF." It is, in essence, an incredibly bad movie that consistently prompts such exclamations. But what did I expect? It's a TV movie; they rarely impress, and this one is no exception. "A Wrinkle in Time" is a colossal waste of time, and you'll likely forget it the moment the credits roll – or shortly thereafter.

Many reviewers have unfairly dismissed this film as awful, a sentiment I wholeheartedly disagree with. The acting is strong, and the direction flows smoothly. I found the interwoven narrative, reminiscent of Tarantino's style, to be a compelling and fresh approach that significantly enhanced the film. While minor script refinements could be made, they are the only flaws I noted. Nestor Cantillana delivers a remarkable performance as Sylvio, and Antonella Rios is captivating, making the film a worthwhile watch for her presence alone.

Casey Affleck is a talented actor whose work I deeply respect, and I wish he appeared in more films that truly showcased his abilities. However, "Soul Survivors" was an exceptionally poor movie.

I attribute most of the film's failings to its weak script. Despite a cast that included the talented Affleck, Wes Bentley (who delivered an outstanding performance in "American Beauty"), Melissa Sagemiller, and the then-popular Eliza Dushku, it's clear the actors struggled with the material. This movie's classification as horror is a stretch. While it featured the expected twists, they ultimately led nowhere but to further confusion. The ending was anticlimactic, failing to provide any sense or answer the many questions I had about the storyline.

Regrettably, I cannot give this movie a positive review. The only truly frightening aspect of "Soul Survivors" is...
This film, despite its significant flaws—including a nonsensical plot, poor performances, and glaring inconsistencies—does offer occasional glimpses of impressive female anatomy.

I'm writing this because I was somehow led to believe *Dark Remains* was a good movie. While not the worst I've seen, it certainly isn't good.

The film suffers from a weak script, subpar acting, and uninspired directing. Even without a big-name cast, one might hope for a more engaging lead actress; it was painful to watch such a plain performance throughout the film. The story itself was a clichéd and poorly scripted affair, with minimal special effects and repetitive, unconvincing attempts at suspense.

In fairness, *Dark Remains* is no worse than some episodes of *Masters of Horror*, but it falls far short of quality cinema. *Dark Remains* is only recommended for the most dedicated horror fans who feel compelled to see every film in the genre, regardless of quality. For everyone else, your time would be far better spent on almost anything else.

This romantic fantasy, adapted from John Van Druten's Broadway hit, boasts an impressive cast to tell the story of a contemporary witch in New York City who enchants a successful publisher. While James Stewart leads the bill, Kim Novak truly captivates as a memorably alluring cinematic witch. The primary duo, however, presents one of the film's rare drawbacks: Stewart, with his gray hair, appears somewhat overaged for the part. While his infatuation with Novak is believable, her reciprocal attraction to him is less so, given their apparent disparity in temperament and perspective. (An enjoyable aspect of the narrative is its portrayal of witches and warlocks as Greenwich Village beatniks and bohemians.) Intriguingly, the chemistry between Stewart and Novak would be far more palpable in *Vertigo*, released the same year, a film that benefited from a compelling suspense plot and Alfred Hitchcock's direction.

The film's humor primarily stems from its exceptional supporting cast, featuring a young Jack Lemmon (as Kim's warlock brother), Elsa Lanchester (as their eccentric aunt), and Ernie.

1985 stands as a remarkable, perhaps even legendary, year in cinema. Yet, the Academy's snub of this particular film, denying it any accolades despite eleven nominations, solidified for many fans the belief that the Oscars are merely a decorative nod for those in favor.

This outright disregard for one of their most celebrated directors was palpable. He would endure another eight years before the Academy, seemingly overcoming whatever biases had previously held them back, bestowed upon him seven statues for *Schindler's List*—a film, arguably, not its equal (and I say this as someone of Polish descent).

To be clear, *Schindler's List* is a classic, and I hold no disdain for *Out of Africa*, which claimed the top prize that year. However, in my estimation, *The Color Purple* surpassed it. This epic portrayal of suffering and resilience moved me to tears, a rare occurrence for me.

Perhaps it was the magnificent score, or the lavish cinematography, but most likely, it was the performances that elevated it. Whoopi Goldberg transcended her comedic persona, proving her profound dramatic depth. Danny Glover, then an unknown to me, delivered a powerful performance, as did Oprah Winfrey.

The film's legacy speaks for itself.

Having seen most of Ryuhei Kitamura's films, I've concluded he possesses a remarkable talent for action. His scenes are consistently kinetic and fast-paced, blending elements of martial arts, gunfights, and samurai combat. The camerawork skillfully captures the onscreen chaos. With "Versus" and "Aragami," Kitamura proved his creativity and ability to deliver compelling cinema even on a limited budget. This makes the profound lack of action in "Alive" all the more perplexing. To put it bluntly, "Alive" is a two-hour-plus film where virtually nothing happens, featuring undeveloped characters and a negligible plot.

Adapted from Tsutomu Takahashi's comic, "Alive" centers on Tenshu Yashiro (Hideo Sasaki), a death row inmate who inexplicably survives his execution. Offered a choice between another attempt at execution or submitting to a series of bizarre experiments, he chooses the latter. He is then confined, first with a rapist, and later with a young woman infected by a strange parasite that grants supernatural powers in exchange for its host's humanity.

Having heard much about the 1990s *Cracker* series but seen none, I eagerly anticipated this installment, confident that the collaboration of Jimmy McGovern and Robbie Coltrane couldn't fail. I was mistaken.

The overwhelming polemics, punctuated by frequent, repetitive, and violent flashbacks, dominated the viewing experience. The production's attempt at modernism, with its flashing boxes and even a childish font, proved irritating. Robbie Coltrane seemed to sleepwalk through the two hours, offering unexplained and improbable "insights," while the police were depicted as one-dimensional, bumbling idiots. Consequently, tension never materialized, and the penultimate scene (to avoid spoilers) was among the most laughably poor pieces of television drama I've encountered in a long time.

I have no desire to see further episodes of this iteration. However, I will revisit the DVDs of the 1990s series to assess if they live up to their reputation.

As a Swedish viewer who just watched this film, I found it to be okay. While I've seen many negative comments, it's important to remember that this miniseries reaches a global audience, not just the USA. Many viewers, especially those outside the US, may be unfamiliar with the original 1960s film or even the historical events (murders) it depicts. The original movie can be difficult to find, and some people simply don't enjoy black and white films. This version, being in color and feeling fresh, will likely find its own audience. Although it's 12 years old, I only just saw it for the first time. I plan to seek out the original to compare them, though I haven't found it available in Sweden. Of course, the internet exists, but it's not universally accessible. This story is largely an American crime history, significant in the 1950s and 60s in the US, but it likely passed by much of the rest of the world.

While I grasp the impulse to connect this film with the Eighties, it hardly reflects the reality of life for most people then, even in the most deprived Bradford estates. Instead, it epitomizes the crude agitprop often produced by the Royal Court Theatre during that period. This was art designed to appeal to a niche, politically-minded audience, bolstered by an incestuous network that guaranteed further work for mediocre playwrights. For a more authentic portrayal of everyday life, one need only look to 'Gregory's Girl,' a film that resonates with a far wider audience.

To label this a "kitchen sink" drama would be an insult to the genre itself, let alone the plumbing industry. The script is, in a word, dreadful. Despite its inexplicable cult following among certain Guardian readers – who, one can only assume, derive some perverse pleasure from cinematic poverty tourism – I urge you to avoid it. This is a poorly written film, utterly convinced of its own profundity.

Fifteen years ago, this video captivated me, and its power hasn't diminished. As a former English teacher, particularly fond of Romantic poetry, I hold Coleridge in high esteem. My appreciation for this video stems from its ability to enhance, rather than detract from, the poem's beauty and narrative strength. It masterfully engages viewers, especially high school students, by visually interpreting the story—a significant advantage for a generation raised on television. Michael Redgrave's narration further elevates the production, lending it authenticity and authority.

While acknowledging the project's modest budget and lack of modern CGI or blockbuster aesthetics, one cannot overlook the integral role of Gustave Doré's illustrations. To summarily dismiss this video as "trash," as a previous comment did, strikes me as both unfair and unperceptive. My defense of this work isn't born of personal connection to the producer, but from a genuine belief in its artistic merit and its effectiveness as a tool for introducing Coleridge's poem to students.

An extraordinary crime thriller, this film captivated my wife and me at last week's Toronto International Film Festival, standing out as the best in an exceptionally strong lineup. It has already secured its place as my second favorite film of all time, just after DR. STRANGELOVE, leaving me on an emotional high as my wife and I debriefed the experience on our walk home.

To preserve the viewing experience, I'll avoid revealing plot details, as thrillers of this caliber are best enjoyed without preconceptions. A safe synopsis involves two brothers, portrayed by Philip Seymour Hoffman and Ethan Hawke, planning a jewelry store robbery in Westchester, New York. The narrative fluidly shifts through a two-week period, encompassing events before, during, and after the robbery. Notably, a pivotal scene is revisited multiple times—a technique that, in lesser films, might disrupt momentum. Here, however, it only intensifies the experience within this masterpiece. The film's excitement, tension, and even the caliber of its acting consistently escalated, culminating in a breathtaking climax that had me on the edge of my seat.

In 1999, I completely dismissed the show "Protesting Hippies" after its dismal first episode, so much so that I avoided the rest of the series. However, years later, while browsing "The Paramount Comedy Channel," I stumbled upon it again. Deciding to give it another chance, I watched the entire series and was pleasantly surprised to find it genuinely hilarious. (A valuable lesson learned: never judge a comedy series by its pilot!)

Set in 1969, "Hippies" features Simon Pegg as Ray Purbbs, editor of "Mouth," an underground magazine reminiscent of "Oz." His eclectic group of friends includes Jill, a staunch feminist; Alex, a laid-back free spirit; and Hugo, the lovable half-wit. The show masterfully captures the incredible optimism prevalent among young people in the late '60s—a belief that they could change the world, even through magazines few would read. Rather than mocking the hippies' naiveté, the series embraces it with warmth and affection. Arthur Mathews' witty scripts cleverly parody iconic elements of the era, from "Hair" and "Woodstock" to "The Graduate" and even the infamous "Oz" obscenity trial of the early '70s. The cast delivers excellent performances, with Julian Rhind-Tutt's portrayal of Alex oddly reminding me of Richard O'Sullivan's character in "Man About The House." It's a shame that a second series never materialized, perhaps due to initial reactions like my own. If you missed "Hippies," I highly recommend giving it a watch.

By the mid-1930s, Hollywood had largely recovered from the disruptive shift to sound. While the technical hurdles of "talkies" were swiftly overcome, it took more time to define the visual language, narrative structure, and acting styles suitable for this new medium. *The Informer* stands out as a pivotal film, demonstrating how wordless sequences can powerfully advance a story, showcasing the potency of visuals without diminishing the crucial roles of sound and dialogue.

This doesn't imply *The Informer* is simply a return to the silent era. Many silent films, in fact, relied heavily on intertitles rather than pure visual storytelling. Rather, *The Informer* confidently stretches moments between dialogue, prioritizes reactions over speeches, and allows shots to unfold purely for atmospheric effect.

Director John Ford, a filmmaker of immense talent, often invested effort commensurate with his interest in the material. If a story failed to captivate him, his commitment wavered. Fortunately, *The Informer*, with its exploration of community, honor, and working-class life, clearly engaged him.

Were a negative rating possible, this film would earn it. It is, without hyperbole, the most atrocious cinematic experience I have ever endured. The viewing was agonizing, a testament to boredom of epic proportions. Any semblance of a plot is buried beneath layers of impenetrable ambiguity. My friend and I rented this film, and after a hopeful thirty minutes, we resorted to fast-forwarding, desperate for improvement. Our efforts were futile; the film never redeemed itself. The premise—a man kidnapped by two women—sounds intriguing, but the execution is utterly devoid of engagement. Nothing remotely interesting ever transpires. Should you ever encounter the opportunity to watch this, do yourself a favor and opt for "Plan Nine from Outer Space" instead.

*Bedknobs and Broomsticks* is an enchanting film, one of the most charming and delightful movies a child could ever experience. This unforgettable adventure follows two adults and three spunky children on a quest that, while perhaps appearing a bit dated, is well worth the watch. Neither my mother nor I found it lacking; in fact, I was thoroughly captivated by the story and the exceptional animation.

This wonderfully comedic and musical film is a delight for the entire family, especially children aged seven and up. The animation, in particular, stands out with its beautiful movements and layouts, earning high praise. *Bedknobs and Broomsticks* is a terrific musical for all to enjoy. So what are you waiting for? Seek out *Bedknobs and Broomsticks* today!

Having seen this movie at the 2006 Palm Springs International Film Festival, I can confirm it's a made-for-TV movie, likely produced by HBO for cable release later this year. The film portrays Bettie Page primarily as a figure of bondage and discipline fetish, a pin-up and stag film actress who, despite her niche, possessed the talent for a broader acting career. While the movie briefly acknowledges her other modeling work, it doesn't adequately explore the full scope of this 1950s pin-up icon's career.

Reportedly based on Richard Foster's book "The Real Bettie Page," the film employs black and white cinematography to evoke a 1950s nostalgic aesthetic. As someone who owns "Bettie Page The Life of a Pinup Legend," a book rich with photographs chronicling Page's career, I was struck by how accurately the movie, with Gretchen Mol as Page, recreates many of those iconic images. Mol, with her black Bettie Page wig and brown contact lenses, embodies Bettie Page; she captures not just the look, but also the distinctive smile and mannerisms.

Orphaned young, the three youngest Gaylord daughters, heirs to one of America's most prominent families, face an uncertain future. Their father, before leaving to fight in WWI, extracts a promise from the eldest, Fiona, that she will never sell their ancestral land. As adults, the sisters find their inheritance depleted by legal battles fought to protect their property. A loophole in their father's will threatens to transfer ownership of the Gaylord estate to Charles Barclay, who plans to erect a development called Barclay Circle. Barclay, a character inspired by John D. Rockefeller's acquisition of New York properties for Rockefeller Center, looms as their primary adversary.

The film largely focuses on the dramatic plight of the sisters. Fiona, portrayed by Barbara Stanwyck in a performance that, while solid, isn't among her most celebrated, appears as a cold, controlling figure with hidden secrets. Nancy Coleman plays Susanna as flighty and deeply enamored with a modern artist, Gig Young.

This film is arguably the most profoundly moving and inspiring I've ever encountered. Though not religious, I find that exceptional art, like this movie, can evoke an almost spiritual awakening, revealing life's deeper meaning.

Initially, I approached it with skepticism, fearing a contrived plot and banal storytelling. However, as a devoted David Lynch fan, I felt compelled to watch. Within half an hour, I was utterly engrossed, captivated by its profound wisdom and warmth. I left the cinema with a sense of having gained invaluable insights into life.

This stands apart from Lynch's typical works, making its creation, after years of exploring humanity's darker facets, quite astonishing. Yet, it's unsurprising that he conveys such deep emotions and profound human insight, a testament to his consistent ability to do so.

The delightful Bugs Bunny cartoon features the return of the as-yet-unnamed Marvin the Martian and his loyal companion, K-9 the green dog. This time, Marvin's objective isn't Earth's destruction, but rather to land, capture an Earth creature, and transport it back to Mars. Naturally, his chosen quarry is Bugs Bunny. Initially, Bugs mistakes Marvin and K-9 for trick-or-treaters, but the illusion shatters when Marvin dramatically expands Bugs' rabbit hole with a ray-gun. Bugs attempts to outwit his captors through various schemes, including convincing Marvin that K-9 is planning a mutiny. Ultimately, he is subdued by an Acme strait-jacket-ejecting bazooka. Surprisingly, for an Acme product, it functions exactly as advertised. Forced to rely on his cunning, Bugs manipulates K-9 into releasing him, swiftly turning the tables. The two disgruntled Martians end up trussed, while Bugs endeavors to pilot their saucer back to Earth.

I thoroughly enjoyed this short, despite an ending that felt a bit anticlimactic compared to the build-up. Notably, Marvin's voice has a slightly different inflection in this installment, and he displays visible emotion when enraged.

A promising premise can unravel when forced to cater to an audience with a short attention span, leading to an illogical jumble. This unfortunate fate befell a film starring three respected actors, a regrettable outcome given their past and future successes.

The initial concept—a doting couple in an idyllic home terrorized by a rogue cop—held significant intrigue. A subtly unsettling intruder, as effectively portrayed in films like *The Hand That Rocks the Cradle* and *Single White Female*, is a proven recipe for a compelling thriller.

The challenge, then, was whether to craft a genuinely disturbing narrative that maintained a sense of reality, or to escalate the shock value by transforming the antagonist into an over-the-top, cartoonish super-villain.

The filmmakers opted for the latter. The resulting film is a poorly executed mess, with the cast struggling to make sense of their roles.

This film stands as my undisputed favorite, a masterpiece of cinematic artistry. Every individual involved, from the actors to the crew, delivered Oscar-worthy performances. The screenplay is a perfect distillation of the narrative, expertly crafting a far more satisfying relationship between Lady Caroline and George Briggs than the original novel. Peter Barnes' meticulous character development for the supporting cast is truly commendable, and the film's stunning visual aesthetic, a testament to director Mike Newell and cinematographer Rex Maidment, was undeniably deserving of Academy Awards. Josie Lawrence delivers her finest performance to date in this film, and it completely reshaped my appreciation for Joan Plowright's talent. Even after more than fifty viewings, I can discern no flaws. Richard Rodney Bennett's score is simply magnificent.

This film, with its exaggerated performances, feels like a lost silent-era masterpiece. The acting, while undeniably theatrical, captivates in its sheer earnestness.

Every element is amplified: emotions are immense, dialogue is weighty, and each scene is punctuated by dramatic human suffering.

Despite a strong urge to recoil, the spectacle held me in a morbid fascination. The dialogue, perhaps suited for the stage (though I have my doubts), felt cluttered, disjointed, and clichéd on screen – a catalog of every negative descriptor for a poorly executed drama.

If you have an insatiable appetite for melodrama, this film *might* appeal to you. Be warned, however, that despite its dramatic intensity, the pacing is incredibly slow.

One can only imagine the script reading differently in the actors' minds; its delivery on camera simply fails to land.

IMDb's "weighted score" system does a disservice here. *Curse of the Starving Class* deserves a rating lower than a 1.

While character-driven storytelling is valuable...

Am I missing something here? "Unexpected plot developments"? "Plot twisting with subversive glee"? Are these viewers watching the same Arquette film I just endured (in an obvious subconscious bout of masochism)? I joined this site simply to ensure no one else rents this stinker. This movie was an embarrassment to everyone involved.

Quick question: Did Sir Stevie read the script before giving Kate C. the thumbs-up? If so, it must be the same Spielberg who greenlit "Howard the Duck." Don't give me that "it was a hit play" crap—I'm guessing Mssr. Reddin isn't too pleased.

The DVD cover promised "surprising corners" and a "twisted story." Story?! It's content like this that makes old Robert McKee and his band of Structuralists sound like geniuses. Sundance? Berlin? Toronto? I have a home video of my cat farting that evokes more interest than Arquette's one-dimensional portrayal of anguished loss.

And talk about *deus ex machina* for Mr. Stanley T.—thank God, just in the nick of time, he thought to have Dave call the cops! And thank Shiva the cops had just caught the true killer! What?!? Up until the credits, I was still waiting for it to...

As Rome erupts in a frenzy of parades, uniforms, and fanfare for Hitler's visit, two strangers remain in their building, their paths converging. She is Sofia Loren, portraying the beleaguered wife of a brutish civil servant and mother of six. He is Mastroianni, a radio speaker recently dismissed due to his homosexuality. Both yearn for companionship and understanding, finding solace in their unexpected connection.

The film unfolds over a mere few hours, its muted palette and a continuous soundtrack of military marches and frenzied radio broadcasts setting the scene. Remarkably, the Nazi anthem, "Horst-Wessel-Lied," transforms into a poignant romantic motif.

This is a beautiful film, masterfully evoking a pivotal era in Italian history, and weaving a deeply touching, melancholic narrative. Mastroianni delivers his consistently superb performance, while Sofia Loren shines in a role far removed from her familiar, boisterous personas. A must-see.

This film ranks among the poorest I've ever endured.

Contrary to another reviewer's opinion, the special effects were far from "okay"; in fact, they were quite terrible. Their lack of realism and obvious artificiality constantly pulled me out of the narrative.

Perhaps this distraction contributed to my difficulty in comprehending the plot. The archaeologists' quest for "the set" remained vague – its nature and significance, along with the rationale for searching in California given the Egyptian-set intro, were never adequately explained.

For a movie set in a desert, the lack of on-location shooting was glaring. The opening scene, depicting an ancient ceremony, conspicuously appeared to be shot indoors rather than amidst desert landscapes.

The action maintained a flat, unvarying pace throughout, devoid of peaks, valleys, or a discernible climax. This constant level ironically made the movie feel shorter, which, in this particular instance, was a welcome relief.

This film transcends cultural barriers, offering a relatable narrative that resonates with individual experiences, community dynamics, societal structures, and global issues. It not only provokes thought but also inspires a quest for deeper understanding and the pursuit of essential questions, ultimately leading to personal conviction and empowerment. The film's depiction of stereotypes illuminates the archetypes prevalent in our world, exposing them as recurring cycles of destruction that stand in opposition to innovation, creativity, and growth. It underscores the urgency of identifying and confronting forces that disrupt natural order. "The Idea" is more than just a film to be watched; it's an immersive experience that engages one's inner voice and conscience, evoking profound feeling rather than passive observation.

Predicting cult classics is a futile exercise. Who could have foreseen the enduring popularity of films like *Vision Quest*, *Fight Club*, and *2001: A Space Odyssey*, all initially dismissed by critics and audiences? As a self-proclaimed film aficionado, I often find myself at odds with popular opinion, particularly when it comes to movies like *Envy*, which, despite its abysmal 4.4 IMDb rating, I consider one of the funniest films of the last decade.

The film's plot is absurd, its dialogue pedestrian, its scenes disjointed, and its script seemingly penned by a child. Yet, these very flaws are what make it so uproariously funny. To truly appreciate *Envy*'s accidental brilliance, one must approach it with a sense of ironic detachment.

My affection for *Envy* stems from its paradoxical transformation: it is so bad that it becomes good. This, I contend, is the very essence of a cult classic, and *Envy* embodies it perfectly.

MGM, an underdog in the animated short market dominated by Warner Bros.' Looney Tunes and Merry Melodies, occasionally released hidden gems like "To Spring."

This remarkable cartoon envisions spring not as a natural phenomenon, but as a fabrication by subterranean male elves. As snow melts, these elves spring into action, felling rainbow rock columns, crushing them into rubble, and transforming them into vibrant color fluids. These fluids are then transported to the surface, bringing forth grass, flowers, and all the hallmarks of spring.

The first half of the short details this intricate process of spring's creation. However, the latter half introduces a conflict: Old Man Winter returns, attempting to prolong winter by destroying the elves' work, leading to an epic battle between them.

The accompanying music is simply delightful, with melodies that linger in the mind long after the cartoon ends.

**SPOILER WARNING!** As a dedicated fan of *Homicide: Life on the Street*, I may be biased, but I found this film to be excellent. It delivered numerous surprises and brought a satisfying sense of closure to the series. Despite my disappointment at Bayliss's transformation into a murderer, the overall experience left me feeling content.

Joanne's review:

This film offers a fascinating perspective on human behavior. It brilliantly illustrates how our relentless pursuit of perfection can inadvertently undermine the very foundations we seek to build. The narrative also astutely highlights our tendency to overlook quieter voices, potentially costing us valuable opportunities. The added layer of comedy makes for a truly enjoyable viewing experience.

This is a must-see for anyone who appreciates a reflective yet humorous take on life. I eagerly await your next production and hope you continue to deliver such quality entertainment. Excellent work!

Govind Nihalani's masterful adaptation of Vijay Tendulkar's novel stands as a cinematic classic and his most discussed work. Om Puri, in a National Award-winning performance, portrays Inspector Velankar, compelled to protect the formidable underworld don Rama Shetty, brought to life with brilliant dominance by debutant Sadashiv Amrapurkar. Despite only appearing in four scenes, Amrapurkar's portrayal commands the film. Smita Patil delivers a strong performance as the female lead opposite Puri, while Naseeruddin Shah shines in a brilliant cameo. The film garnered significant acclaim, winning Filmfare Awards for Best Film, Story, and Supporting Actor for Sadashiv Amrapurkar.

This film isn't just the worst gay-themed movie I've ever seen—it's the worst movie of any genre, period.

A "personal note" from the director at the outset, pleading for "understanding" for a first-timer's "many challenges," is an immediate red flag. The audio is frequently so poor, even on DVD, that dialogue is unintelligible. Combined with abysmal lighting, sets, and cinematography, a weak script, and generally poor acting, the result is an unwatchable "film." Though I struggled through to its terrible conclusion, I promptly gave away the DVD I regrettably purchased. While first-time directors undoubtedly face hurdles, this anemic effort is far from a finished product. IMDb reveals this was Richard Natale's sole directorial attempt, which, ironically, is the only redeeming quality of this so-called "movie."

Words like "amazing," "fantastic," "disturbing," or "hilarious" fail to capture the unique cinematic event that is *White Fire*. From its shaky, bewildering opening to its profound conclusion, this film promises relentless entertainment.

The movie opens in an unnamed country's woods, where a family hides from unmarked soldiers in ill-fitting uniforms. When the father separates from his wife and children, the film immediately reveals its distinct tone. The father, dressed entirely in white, tumbles down hillsides and politely gains people's attention before shooting them. Tragically, he is then burned alive in a stunt that appears both unsupervised and incredibly unsafe. Meanwhile, the mother and children flee along a beach, pursued by an armed soldier who trails just five feet behind. He delivers a bizarre, stern "HALT!" before promptly executing the mother. This opening sequence sets the stage for the unusual childhoods of our protagonists, Bo and Ingred.

We then fast-forward approximately two decades (or thirty, if one is honest about the hero's age) to...

A thrilling, thought-provoking journey! Sharon Stone reprises her role as the captivating, drop-dead gorgeous author Catherine Tramell with impeccable skill. While the original *Basic Instinct* unfolded in San Francisco, the sequel transports Catherine—and us—to the bustling, high-fashion world of London. Both cities, vibrant hubs of excitement and haute couture, provide the perfect backdrop for a character like Tramell. David Morrissey (*Derailed*) delivers a smooth performance as psychiatrist Dr. Michael Glass. David Thewlis, playing Roy Washburn with Scotland Yard, offers a refreshing departure from his beloved role as Lupin in the Harry Potter series. This film is a feast for the senses, packed with flashy cars, designer clothes, sex, drama, humor, and tension—all the "basic instincts" you could ask for. It's a mind-bending experience from start to finish, boasting a great screenplay. From its climactic opening to its surprising conclusion, boredom is simply not an option. The audience was captivated, glued to the screen throughout.

Last night, I had the unexpected pleasure of seeing "Cracker Bag," shown before a preview of Disney's "Holes."
